Asked directly, after rerunning the full benchmark suite to confirm claude.md #169/#170's own CI-focused work hadn't regressed anything: the core five-program suite (`run_benchmarks.py`) came back clean (every Festina run-time number within normal run-to-run noise of what's documented), but the HTTP suite (`run_http_benchmarks.py`) failed outright -- `benchmarks/http/server.f` doesn't compile at all.

**The compile failure was two separate, unrelated API drifts, neither caused by anything in this session -- `git log` shows this file untouched since it was first written (claude.md #153), well before the http/url API surface it uses had settled.** `req.path` doesn't exist (the `http` type only has `.url`/`.method`/`.code`/`.headers`/`.callback` -- the path has to come from `parseURL(req.url).pathname`, api.md's own documented pattern) and `req.send(body, code, headers)` -- a 3-argument form -- doesn't exist either; the real signature is `req.send(res:http)`, one already-constructed value (`req.send({'code': 200, 'body': ..., 'headers': ...})`). Both fixed directly; the JSON route's own struct body (`m`) is passed straight through as `'body': m` and renders correctly via the same struct-to-JSON `.toText()` path api.md documents -- confirmed with a real compiled server answering both routes via `curl`, not just a clean compile.

**A second, subtler problem, invisible until the first one was fixed enough to actually run a load test: claude.md #167 quietly broke this benchmark's own fairness, and nobody had re-run it since to notice.** `server.f`'s own top comment (now corrected) explained the ORIGINAL methodology: Rust/Go hand-roll `Connection: close` into every response, and Bun's server sets it explicitly too, specifically so no one language's own keep-alive support does the winning -- the comparison was designed to measure connection-accept + parse + respond, not "which server happens to reuse TCP connections." Festina used to match this automatically, simply because it had no keep-alive of its own to opt out of. Once #167 gave it real HTTP/1.1 keep-alive by default, that stopped being true -- and since `wrk` (the load generator) never sends its own `Connection: close` request header, Festina started reusing connections across `wrk`'s whole connection pool while the other three kept paying full connection setup on every single request, an apples-to-oranges result that would silently favor Festina for a reason having nothing to do with request-handling speed. Confirmed directly, not just reasoned about: a `curl` request with no explicit header got `Connection: keep-alive` back from the fixed server; the identical request with `-H "Connection: close"` got `Connection: close` -- exactly matching api.md's own documented rule that an explicit client-sent close always forces it off per request.

**Fixed at the load generator, not scattered across four server implementations.** `run_http_benchmarks.py`'s own `_run_wrk` now passes `-H "Connection: close"` uniformly to every `wrk` invocation. Rust/Go/Bun are unaffected (they already always close, unconditionally, regardless of what the client sends); Festina now closes too, per its own already-documented per-request `Connection: close` override -- restoring the original "connection-accept + parse + respond, not connection-reuse" comparison for all four languages at once, with zero server-side code changes needed anywhere.

**Reran, confirmed stable across two consecutive runs (not a one-off fluke), and updated benchmark.md** with fresh numbers plus a corrected methodology paragraph (the one claude.md #167 had already flagged as stale, `benchmark.md` lines ~316-326 as they stood before this entry). Not directly comparable number-for-number against the previously-documented figures -- those predate this fix by an unknown machine/session, and benchmark.md's own standing disclaimer ("absolute numbers vary by hardware... relative ordering is the point") already covers exactly this. Relative ordering this run: Festina ahead of Go, behind Rust, roughly matching Bun on both routes -- internally consistent and reproducible across repeat runs on this machine.

**Tests:** none (benchmark scripts, not part of the pytest suite) -- verified instead by a real compiled server answering both routes correctly under `curl` (with and without an explicit close header) and two independent full `wrk` runs landing within a few percent of each other. Documented in benchmark.md (the HTTP section's Methodology paragraph and results table) and this entry; `server.f`'s and `run_http_benchmarks.py`'s own comments explain the fix in place.

172. `.callback()` FOR `img`/`aud` -- CLOSING THE GAP #165 LEFT OPEN

Asked directly to close one of todo.md's three remaining language/stdlib gaps: claude.md #165 gave `blob` a non-blocking, background-thread `.callback()` load but explicitly stopped short of `img`/`aud`, for two named, unverified risks -- both loaders call `festina_fail()` (a hard `exit(1)`) on a corrupt/unreadable file, which a background worker thread doing concurrently with the main thread was flagged as untested; and `img`'s own decode additionally builds a Cairo surface, whose thread-safety for this use was flagged as unconfirmed rather than assumed. Both were real gaps, not paperwork -- closing them meant actually resolving each, not just wiring the call sites through.

**The `festina_fail()`-on-a-worker-thread risk was closed by giving `img`/`aud` blob's own "test, don't fail" contract, but ONLY on the `.callback()` path -- the synchronous `img icon = 'path'` form is completely unchanged and still calls `festina_fail()` on exactly the same three failures it always has.** `festina_image_from_bytes`'s decode step was pulled out into a new `festina_decode_image_surface` (festina_runtime_graphics.c) that never calls `festina_fail`, returning `NULL` (with a separate `*out_recognized_format` flag distinguishing "wrong format" from "corrupt data" for the caller's own error message) instead -- `festina_image_from_bytes` itself is now just that plus the three `festina_fail()` calls its synchronous contract already made, unchanged behavior confirmed by the pre-existing `TestGraphics` error-message tests passing unmodified. `festina_audio_from_bytes`'s WAV/MP3 decode helpers (`festina_decode_wav`/`festina_decode_mp3`) already had this shape -- return 0 on a recoverable failure, `festina_fail()` only on genuine OOM, the identical convention `festina_blob_load_worker` already relied on -- so no equivalent split was needed there. Two new worker functions (`festina_image_load_worker`, `festina_audio_load_worker`) read the file and decode with these non-failing paths; on any failure (missing file, wrong format, corrupt data) the value already returned to the caller -- a 1x1 transparent placeholder image, or a silent 1-channel/44100Hz/zero-frame placeholder clip -- is simply left as-is, exactly as "unpopulated" as a failed background blob load's own empty bytes/length. `festina_image_load_dispatch`/`festina_audio_load_dispatch` mirror `festina_blob_load_dispatch` exactly: `callback == NULL` is the unchanged synchronous path, non-NULL builds the placeholder, retains it, and hands it to `festina_async_io_dispatch`.

**A real, previously-latent bug this widening exposed rather than introduced: `festina_decode_mp3`'s one-time `mpg123_init()` guard was a bare, unsynchronized `static int initialized` flag.** Harmless when this function could only ever run on the main thread (every prior caller was synchronous); calling it from several `festina_runtime_async.c` worker threads at once -- exactly what `aud`'s own `.callback()` now does, especially the mixed-type stress case below where an img load and an aud load race each other -- is a textbook data race, and `mpg123_init()` itself makes no thread-safety guarantee about concurrent calls either. Fixed with `pthread_once_t`, which also gives every caller the correct "block until the winning thread's init actually finishes" semantics a plain flag never had.

**The Cairo thread-safety risk was closed by actually testing it under concurrency, not by reasoning that it's probably fine.** `festina_decode_image_surface`'s own PNG (`cairo_image_surface_create_from_png_stream`) and JPEG (libjpeg, already using its own thread-local `setjmp` escape) decode paths build an entirely private `cairo_surface_t` and scratch buffers per call, touching none of Cairo's few genuinely shared subsystems (font/text caches, `g_backing_surface`, any window's own `cairo_t`) -- confirmed, not assumed, by `tests/test_async_io.py::TestAsyncIoImgAudRuntime::test_concurrent_img_and_aud_callbacks_all_complete` (four `img` and four `aud` background loads racing each other and the main thread) and, at real scale, the new leak-stress program below (60 passes × 3 concurrent types × 2 outcome shapes = 360 in-flight jobs across the pool's 4 workers) -- both pass clean, and the leak-stress run is under AddressSanitizer/LeakSanitizer, which would have flagged a real corruption or race-induced double-free even without ThreadSanitizer specifically instrumenting it.

**Compiler wiring:** semantic.py's callback branch (previously hardcoded to reject `func[img]:void`/`func[aud]:void` with "isn't implemented yet") now accepts all three and returns the inferred type off `fn`'s own signature, the same "read `T` directly off the callback, no surrounding-context inference needed" design #165 already established for `blob`; codegen's single `.callback()` emit site now dispatches to `festina_image_load_dispatch`/`festina_audio_load_dispatch`/`festina_blob_load_dispatch` by that same inferred type and sets `uses_graphics_code`/`uses_audio` accordingly (mirroring `save()`/`saveCopy()`'s own existing per-type dispatch) -- `.callback()` on an `img` links `festina_runtime_graphics.c` but does NOT set `uses_graphics`, so it still never opens a window, same as every other headless image operation. parser.py's anonymous fire-and-forget form (`img 'path'.callback(fn)`) already handled `img`/`aud` generically -- only its own comment, written when the feature was blob-only, needed updating.

**A pre-existing, unrelated white-box test gap surfaced immediately by trying to build anything: three `tests/test_codegen.py` audio harnesses (`_VOICE_POOL_HARNESS`/`_SINGLE_STREAM_HARNESS`/`_CHANNEL_HARNESS`) `#include festina_runtime_audio.c` directly and stub the small set of core-runtime symbols it needs, to avoid linking sqlite3 into a test that's entirely about the channel pool.** `festina_audio_load_dispatch` (compiled into the file whether or not any harness `main()` calls it) now references two more core symbols, `festina_retain`/`festina_async_io_dispatch`, so all three harnesses gained matching stubs -- `festina_retain` mirroring the existing `festina_release_check` stub's real semantics, `festina_async_io_dispatch` mirroring the core runtime's own "no hook registered" synchronous fallback. All 13 `TestAudioChannels`/`TestAudioOnANonMixingDevice`/`TestAudioVoicePool` tests, which had never needed to know this machinery existed, failed to LINK until this was added -- caught immediately by the full suite, not discovered later.

**`scripts/leak_stress.sh` gained a new stress program, `tests/stress/async_io_churn.f`, and the script itself needed a small fix to run it at all: `festina_runtime_async.c` was never among the translation units it built and linked, since it predates #165.** Added unconditionally (pure POSIX, `-pthread` only, no pkg-config dependency of its own) alongside `festina_runtime.c`. The new program dispatches `blob`/`img`/`aud` `.callback()` loads three ways every pass -- a real file (success) and a missing one (the graceful-failure path) for all three types at once, 60 passes -- with the placeholder aliased and manually freed before its background load even completes, so this is real double-ownership of the exact box the worker mutates in place, not just several loads in isolation. Every one of the 360 callbacks increments a shared counter and only the last one logs and calls `close(0)`, since `festina_run_timer_loop` -- unlike `__festina_main()`'s own top-level statements, which all run BEFORE the loop gets a chance to drain a single job -- is what actually waits for outstanding async-io work. Clean under AddressSanitizer/LeakSanitizer, and `test_the_suite_covers_every_managed_resource`'s own guard set updated to include it.

**Verified directly, not just by inspection:** every scenario in the new `TestAsyncIoImgAudRuntime` test class (does-not-block ordering for both types, the graceful-failure path for an unreadable path AND for corrupt file data on both types, the unaffected synchronous-path error message, the anonymous statement form, and the concurrent mixed-type stress case) against real compiled binaries; the full existing suite (including the three now-relinking audio harnesses) unaffected; `scripts/leak_stress.sh` run both targeted (just the new program) and as the full default set, clean both times.

**Tests:** `tests/test_async_io.py` -- the two `test_callback_rejects_{img,aud}_for_now` semantic tests replaced with `test_callback_works_for_img`/`test_callback_works_for_aud`/`test_callback_rejects_mismatched_declared_type`, and a new `TestAsyncIoImgAudRuntime` class (9 tests: does-not-block for both types, unreadable-path and corrupt-data graceful handling for both types, the unaffected synchronous-path error case, the concurrent mixed-type stress case, and the anonymous statement form for `img`) -- file total 16 -> 25. `tests/test_codegen.py` -- three harnesses gained two stub functions each (no new test cases, existing `TestAudioChannels`/`TestAudioOnANonMixingDevice`/`TestAudioVoicePool` now actually link again). `tests/test_leak_stress.py` -- `test_the_suite_covers_every_managed_resource`'s guard set gained `async_io_churn.f` (24 -> 25 tests, parametrized). Full suite: 1758 passed, 9 skipped. Documented in api.md (the `.callback()` section rewritten for all three types, including the new placeholder-shape wording for `img`/`aud`'s own graceful-failure outcome) -- todo.md never listed this gap as an open item in the first place (only claude.md #165's own account did), so there was no entry to remove there.

173. NESTED `.toStruct()`/`.toArr()` JSON PARSING -- PLUS A REAL, PRE-EXISTING TERNARY LEAK FOUND ALONG THE WAY

Asked directly to close another of todo.md's remaining language/stdlib gaps: claude.md #159's `.toStruct(T)`/`.toArr(T)` only ever parsed scalar (`int`/`float`/`bool`/`text`) struct fields and array elements, rejecting a nested `struct`/`arr[T]`/`map[T]` outright at compile time as a stated v1 scope cut.

**Widened the type-system check first (semantic.py): `_is_json_parseable_type` replaces the old flat scalar-tuple membership test with a recursive one** -- a field/element type is parseable if it's already scalar, OR a struct whose OWN fields are (recursively) all parseable, OR an `arr[T]`/`map[T]` whose element/value type is (recursively) parseable. Cycle-safe for a self-referencing struct (claude.md #17 made the type legal; a struct name already being checked higher up the same recursion is treated as valid without re-descending into it, since that outer check is the one that will actually decide it) -- otherwise `struct Node { next:Node }` would infinite-loop the semantic pass itself, not just be a codegen concern. `map[T]`'s own value can never be `arr[T]`/`map[T]` in the first place (a pre-existing, unrelated `resolve_type_name` restriction -- a map value lives in one fixed 8-byte slot, and neither fits), so this function never has to reject that combination itself; it only ever needs to keep recursing until every leaf is scalar. The error message widened to name the same three shapes now accepted, and a genuinely unsupported type (`img`, `func[...]`, ...) is still rejected with a clear message, even nested several levels deep.

**Codegen (`_from_json_struct_fn_for`/`_from_json_arr_fn_for`) now recurses into a nested field/element's own from-JSON function, through a new shared dispatcher `_emit_json_read_value`** -- a scalar goes through the existing `_emit_json_read_scalar` unchanged; a struct/`arr[T]`/`map[T]` field/element calls into its own (memoized-by-type, generated-once) parsing function instead, the identical "recurse into a nested container's own from-JSON function" shape `.toText()`'s own JSON *rendering* (`_json_fn_for`) already has. A struct field that's itself the SAME struct type (the self-referencing case) works with no special handling at all: the recursive call only ever needs the callee's own already-cached LLVM function NAME, reserved in the cache before that function's body is even built, so a struct calling into its own parser mid-generation is exactly as safe as any other mutually-recursive pair of functions.

**A genuinely new capability, not just a widened check: `_from_json_map_fn_for`, the `map[T]` counterpart todo.md's own #159 entry specifically named as still missing.** Unlike `_from_json_struct_fn_for`'s object-parsing loop (which matches each key against a FIXED set of known field names and skips anything else), every key in a `map[T]` field's JSON object becomes a map entry -- there is no fixed field set to match against. A new `_from_json_map_value` sets each entry: deliberately NOT a call to the general `_emit_map_set` (that method's own retain-unless-fresh heuristic reads an `ast.Expr` to decide ownership, and generated parsing code has none of those -- every value handed to it is already fresh and uniquely owned, the identical reasoning `_from_json_arr_fn_for`'s own `festina_array_push` call already relies on for `festina_json_read_text`), so it never retains, but still looks up and releases/frees whatever a DUPLICATE key already mapped to, after the new value is stored (claude.md #120's own cycle-trial-safety ordering) -- the same "last one wins, and doesn't leak the value it replaces" contract a map literal's own repeated key already follows. Cached and keyed by value type AND amor-ness: an `amor map[T]` field genuinely needs `FESTINA_AMAP_LLVM_TYPE`'s own extra capacity field and `festina_amap_set`, unlike `arr[T]`'s own `amor` prefix, which (claude.md #156) has no runtime representation difference yet.

**A duplicate JSON key overwriting an already-set nested struct/`arr[T]`/`map[T]` STRUCT FIELD (not just a map entry) also needed a new release, which `_from_json_struct_fn_for`'s existing per-field loop only had for `text`.** Extended: for a refcounted field type, the old slot value is read before the new one is parsed and stored, then released AFTER the store (same cycle-trial-safety ordering as above) -- store-then-release, not release-then-store, matching `_emit_assign`'s own established convention exactly rather than the simpler (but cycle-unsafe) order the pre-existing `text` case happened to use, where it never mattered since text isn't cycle-collected.

**A real, pre-existing, previously-undiscovered leak found while ASan-testing the new stress program, not introduced by any of the above -- confirmed on the unmodified prior commit via `git stash`.** `_emit_ternary` phi'd its two branches together and returned the result with NO ownership handling of its own; every caller (`_is_owning_text_source`/`_is_owning_refcounted_source`) has always treated a `Ternary` as "aliasing" -- correct when both branches are themselves aliasing, but silently wrong the instant either branch is a genuinely fresh, OWNING source (a template literal, a `+` concatenation, a function call, an array/map literal, ...): the caller then retains/copies the ternary's result exactly once regardless of which branch actually ran, so a fresh branch's own already-correct ownership got an extra, unbalanced retain/copy on top of it -- an unconditional leak on every evaluation that took the fresh branch, for BOTH text (a copy of an orphaned buffer, nothing ever frees the original) and every refcounted type (an over-retain that can never reach zero). Minimal repro: `text s = cond ? \`a${i}\` : \`b${i}\`` in a 150-iteration loop leaked 640 bytes under LeakSanitizer; the struct counterpart leaked one full struct allocation per iteration. Fixed at the root, in a new `_own_ternary_branch` helper `_emit_ternary` calls on each branch as it's emitted: a text branch that wasn't already owning is copied (`festina_text_own`) right there; a refcounted branch that wasn't already owning is retained right there -- so the phi'd result is ALWAYS genuinely owning regardless of which branch ran, which is what lets `ast.Ternary` be added to both ownership predicates' owning cases (a nested ternary as one branch of another is recognized as already-normalized this same way, not double-retained/copied).

**Verified directly, not just by inspection:** every new `TestJsonParse`/`TestRuntimeBehavior` scenario (nested struct fields, `arr[T]` of struct elements, nested `arr[arr[T]]`, a `map[T]` struct field with arbitrary keys, `arr[map[T]]`, a self-referencing struct to real depth, duplicate-key overwrite on both a nested map entry and a nested struct field) against real compiled binaries; the two new `TestTernary` runtime tests (a fresh text/struct ternary branch's VALUE still correct and usable well past the statement, on both branches); `scripts/leak_stress.sh`'s full default set (now 9 programs, including two new ones -- `json_parse_churn.f`, exercising every nested shape above plus the self-referencing-struct case at real iteration count, and `ternary_ownership_churn.f`, isolating the ternary fix on its own, independent of JSON parsing) clean under AddressSanitizer/LeakSanitizer; the same two new stress programs re-run against the unmodified prior commit via `git stash` to CONFIRM they actually catch what they claim to (they do -- 9002 bytes/750 allocations leaked on `ternary_ownership_churn.f` alone against the old code).

**Tests:** `tests/test_json_parse.py` -- two now-stale rejection tests rewritten as acceptance tests (`test_to_arr_of_a_struct_element_now_analyzes`, `test_to_struct_now_accepts_a_nested_arr_field`), five new semantic tests (a nested struct field, a map field, a still-rejected genuinely unsupported field, a violation nested two levels deep, a self-referencing struct field), and eight new runtime tests (nested struct, `arr[T]` of struct, `arr[arr[T]]`, a `map[T]` field, `arr[map[T]]`, a self-referencing struct, duplicate-key-wins on a map field and on a struct field) -- file total 21 -> 35. `tests/test_control_flow.py` -- two new `TestTernary` runtime tests. `tests/test_leak_stress.py` -- guard set gained `json_parse_churn.f` and `ternary_ownership_churn.f`. Combined total across the three files: 63 -> 79. Full suite: 1776 passed, 9 skipped (this round's own new tests included). Documented in api.md (the `.toStruct()`/`.toArr()` section rewritten with nested/self-referencing examples, the v1 scope cut reworded to describe what's actually still rejected) and todo.md (the gap's own bullet trimmed to just the still-open `\u` escape item, the nested-shapes half removed).

174. `amor arr[T]` -- REAL AMORTIZED ARRAY GROWTH, CLOSING THE GAP #156 LEFT OPEN

Asked directly to close the last of todo.md's three remaining language/stdlib gaps: claude.md #156 built the `amor` prefix for both `map[T]` and `arr[T]` together, but only `map[T]` actually got amortized (doubling) growth -- `amor arr[T]` parsed, type-checked, and round-tripped through `type_name()`, but compiled and behaved byte-for-byte identically to plain `arr[T]`, `ArrayType.amortized` deliberately `compare=False` so the two stayed assignment-compatible in the meantime. todo.md's own accounting named the reason: array's growable-buffer surface (`push`/`pop`/`shift`/`unshift`/`splice`, each independently calling `festina_array_resize`) is far larger than map's four operations.

**The actual surface turned out narrower than that framing suggested, once traced all the way through: only the five growable-buffer operations' own GROWTH calls need to know capacity exists at all -- every other array touchpoint in the compiler (indexing, `.length`, iteration, the retain/release element cascade, cycle collection, JSON rendering) only ever reads `length`/`data`, which sit at byte-identical offsets in both the plain `{length, data}` header and a new, byte-compatible-PREFIX-extended `FestinaAmorArray`/`FESTINA_AMOR_ARRAY_LLVM_TYPE` (`{length, data, capacity}`) -- the identical trick `FESTINA_AMAP_LLVM_TYPE` already uses over `FESTINA_MAP_LLVM_TYPE`.** Confirmed directly for every read-only touchpoint before touching any of them: `festina_release_array`/`festina_cycle_dispose_array` free starting at the header's own address via a raw byte offset, never through a typed GEP, so they need zero changes; `festina_cycle_visit_array` and codegen's own `_release_fn_for_array`-generated per-element-type wrapper both only read fields 0/1. That left a genuinely bounded, correctly-scoped change: a capacity-aware `festina_array_resize` counterpart (`capacity` is `NULL` for plain -- its own unchanged exact-size-realloc behavior -- or the address of an amor array's own tracked field, for geometric doubling), threaded through all SIX runtime entry points (`push`/`unshift`/`pop`/`shift`/`splice`/`splice_insert` -- `splice_insert` has its OWN inline grow/shrink logic, interleaved with the tail memmove in a different order depending on direction, so it needed the identical capacity-awareness duplicated into it rather than a shared call), each call site in codegen.py's `_emit_array_method` (a new `_array_capacity_arg` helper, mirroring `_emit_map_set`'s own `is_amap`-gated capacity GEP), array-literal construction (`_emit_array_lit` gained `_emit_map_lit`'s own `is_amap`-shaped `is_amor` parameter, setting the literal's own capacity field to exactly its element count), and the struct-field auto-vivify path (`_load_field_value`'s ArrayType branch, the identical "field has no initializer syntax, so amor relies ENTIRELY on this path" risk claude.md #156's own map version of this bug already found and named).

**An amor array's own buffer is deliberately NEVER freed or shrunk on the way back down -- not to empty, not on an ordinary shrink -- matching amortized-vector convention generally and giving `amor arr[T]` a genuine reason to exist beyond `amor map[T]`'s own: a pop/push cycle costs nothing repeatedly, not just a long monotonic run of pushes.** `festina_array_resize`'s `new_length <= 0` branch only frees when `capacity` is `NULL`; its shrinking branch only reallocs down when `capacity` is `NULL`. `festina_array_splice_insert`'s own hand-rolled equivalent duplicates both decisions for the identical reason.

**`ArrayType.amortized` lost its `compare=False`, matching `MapType.amortized`'s own real-identity treatment exactly -- an `amor arr[T]` and a plain `arr[T]` of the same element type are now genuinely different, non-interchangeable types, and assignment between them is a compile error.** This is the one user-visible behavior change beyond "the docs said no runtime effect, now there is one": code that previously relied on the two comparing equal (assigning an `amor arr[T]` into a plain `arr[T]`-typed slot, or vice versa) now fails to compile -- exactly the `amor map[T]`/`map[T]` boundary already in place since #156, extended for consistency, not a new kind of restriction. semantic.py gained the matching pieces `amor map[T]` already had: an initializer requirement (`amor arr[int] xs` with no `= ...` is a compile error, the same reasoning -- no immortal-static-empty-global path was ever built for it, matching `_global_var_defs`'s own amor exclusion, widened here from map-only to both) and an `ast.ArrayLit`-vs-declared-element-type bypass in `analyze_var_decl` (`ArrayLit`'s own generic inference always returns a non-amortized `ArrayType` regardless of context, so the generic `infer()`+`check_assignable()` path would always reject a literal against an `amor arr[T]` declared type -- validates each element directly against the declared type instead, the identical shape the pre-existing `arr[img]`/`arr[aud]`/`arr[blob]` media-literal bypass right above it already has).

**Verified directly, not just by inspection:** every new `TestAmorArray` scenario (literal init/index/length, all five growable operations including both `splice` forms, 500 pushes forcing several real capacity doublings, `const` composing, struct-field auto-vivify, text AND struct elements surviving real growth with correct retain/release, a media (`img`) element array, the amor/plain type-mismatch rejection, nested `amor arr[arr[T]]`) against real compiled binaries; a new `amor_array_churn.f` stress program (push/pop/shift/unshift/both splice forms, a scalar element type and a refcounted one, the auto-vivify path, all at real iteration counts) added to `scripts/leak_stress.sh`'s default set (now 10 programs) -- clean under AddressSanitizer/LeakSanitizer; the full existing suite (including every `amor map[T]` test already in place) unaffected by the `compare=False` removal.

**Tests:** `tests/test_codegen.py` -- new `TestAmorArray` class (12 tests) mirroring `TestAmorMap`'s own discipline exactly. `tests/test_maps.py` -- `TestAmorPrefix` gained 5 new semantic tests (resolves-to-amortized-ArrayType, missing-initializer rejection, mismatched-element-type rejection, a variable element, the amor/plain type-mismatch rejection) -- file total 8 -> 13. `tests/test_leak_stress.py` -- guard set gained `amor_array_churn.f` (1 more parametrized case). 18 new tests total. Full suite: 1793 passed, 9 skipped, 1 failed (up from claude.md #173's own 1776/9) -- the one failure, `test_graceful_shutdown.py::test_an_in_flight_connection_still_completes_before_exit`, is a pre-existing, timing-sensitive socket test unrelated to any of this round's changes (nothing here touches HTTP/socket/shutdown code) and passes cleanly in isolation, confirmed immediately afterward rather than assumed. Documented in api.md (the `amor` section widened from map-only to both container types, a growth-cost cross-reference added to the arrays section, the type-incompatibility rule spelled out with a real conversion recipe) and todo.md (the gap's own bullet removed entirely).

175. `map[T]` -- FROM A LINEAR-SCAN ARRAY TO A REAL HASH TABLE, `amor map[T]` REMOVED

Asked for directly: "let's refactor map to be a genuine hash map. I know this will be breaking." `map[T]` had been a deliberate, documented O(n) linear scan since claude.md #72 -- a real tradeoff (api.md's own "small, config/game-state-shaped collection, not a large-scale data structure" framing), not an oversight, but one the user wanted replaced outright, breaking changes accepted.

**Design: open addressing, linear probing, tombstone deletion -- mirroring the one hash table this runtime already had.** `festina_conn_index_*` (`festina_runtime_http.c`, claude.md #153) is a real open-addressing table keyed by `int64_t` `conn_id`; its own comment at the time explicitly noted it wasn't reusable for `map[T]` because that lived in codegen-emitted IR keyed by `text`, not a C data structure. Rather than inventing a different shape, `map[T]`'s new implementation mirrors it directly: FNV-1a hashing (no string hash existed anywhere in the runtime before this -- `festina_conn_index_hash` is int64-only), linear probing, doubling capacity whenever `(count + tombstones + 1) * 4 >= capacity * 3` (the identical 75%-load-factor trigger `festina_conn_index_put` uses, counting tombstones toward "used" the same way so delete-heavy churn at a stable live size still triggers a rehash even though `count` itself stays flat). Bucket struct is unchanged size (`FestinaMapEntry {char *key; int64_t value}`, 16 bytes) -- occupancy lives IN `key` itself, the same sentinel trick `festina_conn_index` uses for `conn_id`: `NULL` = never used, a reserved non-heap pointer `(char *)1` (`FESTINA_MAP_TOMBSTONE`) = deleted. A real key is always a `strdup` result, so neither sentinel can ever collide with one.

**Header grew from `{count, entries}` to `{count, entries, capacity, tombstones}` -- a single universal shape, not a plain/amortized pair.** `count` is live entries, `capacity` the bucket array's length (a power of two, 0 until first insert), `tombstones` the count of deleted-but-not-yet-reclaimed buckets (tracked so grow-on-tombstone-buildup works without needing a full rebuild-to-count-live-entries pass). `{0, null, 0, 0}` is still exactly "empty, nothing allocated yet," so every existing zero-init assumption (a global map's own immortal static header, `_zero_value`, struct-field auto-vivify) kept working unchanged with no representation-specific edits needed at any of those three sites.

**`amor map[T]` (claude.md #156) is removed entirely, not kept as a deprecated alias.** Asked directly and confirmed with the user before starting: once plain `map[T]` itself grows geometrically as an intrinsic part of being a hash table, `amor map[T]` does nothing a plain `map[T]` doesn't already do -- keeping it around would mean a second type whose only distinguishing behavior (doubling instead of grow-by-one) no longer distinguishes anything. `MapType.amortized`/`MapTypeExpr.amortized` are gone outright (back to a single `value` field, as before #156); `amor` immediately followed by `map` is now a clear parse error ("map[T] is a hash table now and grows the same way 'amor map[T]' used to; drop the 'amor'") rather than silently parsing and quietly dropping its own meaning. `amor arr[T]` (claude.md #174) is completely untouched -- this round never touches array code at all. `festina_amap_set` is deleted from the runtime; every runtime/codegen touchpoint that used to branch on `is_amap`/`type_.amortized` for maps lost that branch, a real simplification on top of the hash-table rewrite itself (fewer call shapes, fewer generated-IR variants, one map struct-field auto-vivify branch instead of two). One second-order consequence, decided as clearly correct rather than asked about separately: a non-escaping local `map[T]` is now eligible for the same stack-header optimization claude.md #81 already gives arrays -- the old `amor map[T]` exclusion in `_is_stack_allocatable_array_or_map_decl` existed only because amortized maps never got that treatment, and there's no amortized map left to exclude; nothing about hashing itself disqualifies keeping the 4-field header on the stack while only the bucket array is heap.

**The one place that broke map[T]'s opacity to codegen, and the highest-risk single edit in the whole round: JSON rendering.** `_json_fn_for`'s `MapType` branch bypassed every map runtime function and did raw pointer arithmetic directly on `entries` -- `off = iv * 16`, walking `[0, count)` as if it were a dense array. A hash table's buckets are sparse and unordered, so this could not survive unchanged. Kept the same 16-byte stride math (bucket layout/size didn't change) but: loop bound became `capacity`, not `count`; each iteration loads the slot's key first and branches to skip it (NULL or the tombstone sentinel) before treating it as live; the "comma iff not the first entry" test -- previously `iv > 0`, which assumed index 0 was always emitted first -- became an `alloca i8` "emitted anything yet" flag set right after each real append, since the first LIVE bucket is no longer reliably index 0. Every other map-value-touching codegen function (`_emit_map_get`/`_emit_map_set`/`_emit_delete`/`.forEach()`/`_release_fn_for_map`/`_emit_free_active_locals`'s stack-map cleanup/`_from_json_map_value`) never needed this kind of surgery at all -- they already only ever passed `count`/`entries`(/`capacity`) through as opaque scalars into a runtime function, so only their GEP sequences and the runtime signatures on the other end needed updating, not their own logic.

**`festina_map_get`/`_for_each`/`_free_entries` all dropped their `count` parameter entirely, not just changed its meaning.** A bucket scan is driven by `capacity` (how many slots exist), never by `count` (how many are live) -- `count` was only ever needed by `festina_map_set`'s own growth check and `festina_map_delete`'s own bookkeeping, both of which still take it by address. This is a real simplification, not just a rename: fewer GEPs at several call sites (the `.forEach()` dispatch and `_release_fn_for_map`'s generated wrapper, for instance, no longer need to load `count` at all).

**Two C-side `map[text]` builders that predate codegen entirely -- `FestinaMapBlockCore` (`festina_runtime.c`, `url.searchParams`) and `FestinaMapBlock` (`festina_runtime_http.c`, `req.headers`/`.headers`/`socket.state`) -- needed their struct layout updated to match, plus every call site threading the two new out-parameters through.** These are exactly the four call sites claude.md #167 found leaking through the wrong (value-blind) release function; this round didn't touch that fix, only widened the header shape it and every other C-side map[text] construction site already depended on.

**Verified directly, not just by inspection.** Both runtime files compile clean (`gcc -Wall -Wextra`, no warnings, no errors) after the rewrite. Manually compiled and ran: basic get/set/delete/missing-key/JSON round-trip; a 30-insert/15-delete/30-insert churn program whose `.forEach()` output was checked for exactly 45 unique keys with zero duplicates (the direct proof `festina_map_grow`'s rehash correctly skips tombstones and moves only live entries); `map[text]`/`map[Box]` (struct-valued) literal, delete, and `free` -- all under Valgrind, both runs reporting 0 definitely/indirectly/possibly-lost bytes and 0 errors. `amor map[int] m = {}` confirmed to fail to parse with the new error message; `amor arr[int]` confirmed completely unaffected (push/length/indexing all still work).

**Tests:** `tests/test_maps.py` -- `TestAmorPrefix`'s six `amor map[T]` semantic tests replaced with one (`test_amor_map_is_a_parse_error`, confirming the new parse-time rejection); its `amor arr[T]` tests and their own comments left as-is (untouched feature) -- file total 46 -> 41. `tests/test_codegen.py` -- `TestAmorMap` (7 tests) removed outright, its literal/get/set/forEach/delete/JSON coverage already duplicated in `TestMaps`; its 200-insert capacity-growth test migrated into `TestMaps` itself (now the proof that plain `map[T]` really rehashes under growth, not an amor-only claim); `TestMaps` gained three genuinely new tests a linear scan could never have needed: interleaved insert/delete forcing a rehash while tombstones are present, JSON rendering skipping a tombstoned bucket (the direct test of `_json_fn_for`'s rewritten skip/comma logic), and a multi-key JSON test compared via `json.loads` rather than exact string equality (bucket order is a function of each key's hash now, not insertion order, so multi-key JSON output is genuinely unordered where it incidentally wasn't before) -- file net -3 tests despite the three additions, since removing `TestAmorMap` costs more than they add back. Full suite: 1785 passed, 9 skipped, 1 deselected (the same pre-existing, timing-sensitive `test_graceful_shutdown.py` flake claude.md #174 already documented, confirmed still unrelated and still passing in isolation) -- `test_wasm.py` (excluded from that run, run separately) all 24 green, including its own `map[int]` regression test. Documented in api.md (the Maps section's own "not a hash table... O(n)" paragraph replaced with the real description; the `amor` section narrowed to arrays only, with a closing note on why `map[T]` has no `amor` variant left) and this entry; todo.md had no open "map[T] should hash" item to close (confirmed directly), so nothing to remove there.

176. `enum` + `typeof` -- A TAGGED UNION OVER ANY TYPE, AND FESTINA'S FIRST GENUINE RUNTIME TYPE IDENTITY

Asked for directly, with a worked example (`struct Circle`/`struct Square`, `enum Shape = Circle, Square`, `extractShapeMetric(shape:Shape)` dispatching on `typeof shape == 'Circle'`). Genuinely new territory: every type this compiler had ever resolved was fixed entirely at compile time, and every existing "run the right code for this type" mechanism (`_release_fn_for`'s own dispatch, the cycle collector's gray/scan/black/white functions) was 100% `isinstance`-on-a-known-`Type`, never a runtime tag read off a value. A `shape:Shape` parameter can hold a `Circle` *or* a `Square`, and `typeof`/field access both need to know which, at runtime, from a bare pointer with no other context.

**The tag, uniformly: a `ptr` directly to the type's own interned name string, not a small integer needing a lookup table.** `self.string_const(type_name)` -- the exact global-constant interning every text literal already uses -- so reading a tag back out *is* reading a valid `text` value already, and `typeof` never needs a separate type-id -> name table anywhere.

**Two representations, decided by whether every member is a struct, chosen after the real cost difference was traced through rather than picking one uniformly:**
- **Pure-struct** (`enum Shape = Circle, Square`): zero overhead. A `Shape`-typed value simply IS whichever member struct's own pointer it currently holds -- self-tagged in that struct's own per-instance heap header, widened from `{refcount}` to `{tag, refcount}` (tag first at `payload-16`, refcount staying at the fixed `payload-8` every existing `festina_retain`/`festina_release_check` already assumes, so neither needed a single change). Only a struct that's actually a member of at least one pure-struct enum gets the wider header (`self._tagged_structs`, computed once from `AnalyzedProgram.enums`); every other struct is byte-for-byte unaffected.
- **Mixed** (any non-struct member, e.g. `enum Json = int, text, User`): a real, independently heap-allocated `{ptr tag, i64 value}` box, refcounted the ordinary way, `value` marshaled through the exact `_map_value_to_i64`/`_i64_to_map_value` conversions `map[T]` values already use.

**Field access (`shape.radius`) is scoped to pure-struct enums only, and resolves to a single, unambiguous owning member at compile time** -- `analyze_enum` rejects an enum outright if two member structs declare the same field name, which is what lets codegen skip any per-access-site disambiguation. At runtime it's a tag read + `icmp eq ptr` against the owning struct's own constant + branch, `festina_fail`-ing on mismatch rather than silently reading whatever bytes happen to sit at that offset in a different member's layout -- the documented safety net for a missing or wrong `typeof` guard.

**Coercion is one addition to `check_assignable`/`_coerce`, covering every position that already goes through them** (var decl, function param/return, struct field, array/map element) -- a member type coerces into its enum exactly the same one-directional way `text` already coerces into `blob`/`color`/`font`/`aud`/`img`.

**Six real bugs found and fixed while getting the worked example to actually run, none of them caught by writing the feature itself -- every one only surfaced by compiling and running real programs, confirming again that "the IR looks right" and "the program behaves right" are different claims:**
1. Three call-site argument checks (`_infer_call`'s bare-Identifier direct-function-call path, its func-typed-local path, and its Member-callee indirect-call path in semantic.py) compared `arg_type != param_type` directly instead of going through `check_assignable` -- so `extractShapeMetric(c)` (a `Circle` argument against a `Shape` parameter) rejected with "expects Shape, found Circle" even though the coercion rule existed. All three now call `check_assignable`, which also means an enum-typed value can be passed through a func-typed field/array element/map value indirect call, not just a direct one -- one gap, not three coincidentally identical ones.
2. `CodeGen._resolve` (codegen.py) called `semantic_mod.resolve_type_name` with five positional arguments, omitting `self.enums` entirely -- shifting every later argument down one slot (the AST node meant for `node` landed in `filename`, and `node` itself silently defaulted to `None`). The result was a real, working-as-designed `enums` fallback in `resolve_type_name` that codegen's own only caller of it could never reach, surfacing as `unknown type 'Shape'` with a mangled error location (the file field literally printing a `<festina.ast.FuncDecl object at 0x...>`, since a Python object landed where a filename string belongs) the instant any function declared an enum-typed parameter.
3. `escape_analysis.py` raises on any expression node kind it doesn't recognize, by design (its own module docstring) -- `ast.TypeofExpr` had no branch, so the very first `typeof` inside a function body crashed escape analysis outright. Given the identical conservative treatment `UnaryOp`/`PostfixOp` already get (walk the operand; typeof reads a value without ever storing or retaining it, so treating it as "escaping" anyway costs nothing worse than one avoidable retain/release pair, never a soundness gap).
4. `CodeGen._toplevel` had no `ast.EnumDecl` branch (unlike `StructDecl`/`TableDecl`, which correctly no-op since their real data already lives in `self.structs`/`self.enums`) -- an enum declaration fell through to the generic "any other top-level statement" branch and was appended to `entry_stmts`, reaching `_emit_stmt` (which has no idea what to do with a declaration) and raising `cannot generate code for statement EnumDecl`.
5. **The most serious of the six, a real segfault, not a compile-time error:** `_release_fn_for_enum`'s pure-struct branch read the tag at `payload-16` completely unconditionally, with no null check -- unlike every other release path in the compiler, which always calls `festina_release_check(payload)` FIRST (itself null-safe, `if (!payload) return 0;`) before ever dereferencing near the pointer. An enum-typed value legitimately starts out `null` (no auto-vivify, spelled out as a deliberate scope cut below), so the very FIRST reassignment of ANY enum-typed global/local -- `Shape shape = someCircle` reached before `shape` was ever otherwise assigned -- read 16 bytes before address zero and crashed. Caught immediately by actually running the worked example's own natural next step (assigning through an as-yet-unset `Shape` variable), not found by inspection. Fixed with an explicit `icmp eq ptr %payload, null` guard before the tag GEP, mirroring `festina_release_check`'s own null-first discipline.
6. Once (5) surfaced the null case, the same unguarded `payload-16`/box-field-0 read existed in both `typeof` and the field-access tag check themselves -- neither is only ever reached through the release path, so both got the identical null guard, failing loudly (`festina_fail`, "typeof applied to a null Shape value" / "field 'radius' accessed on a null Shape value") instead of crashing. This keeps `typeof shape == 'Circle'` -- the documented safe-guard idiom the worked example itself uses before field access -- genuinely safe to write against a not-yet-assigned enum value, not merely safe against a wrongly-tagged one.

**Explicit scope cuts, stated rather than silently dropped:** no enum-of-enum members (checked in `analyze_enum`); no duplicate members in one enum; an enum-typed value (variable, field, parameter) reads `null` until assigned, like any other reference-typed value -- there is no canonical "empty" variant for a tagged union the way `{count:0, entries:null}` is a canonical empty map, so no auto-vivify; an enum-typed edge is not walked by the cycle collector (`_managed_type_children` has no `EnumType` case) -- a genuine reference cycle routed through an enum-typed field would leak rather than being collected, the same category of accepted gap the table-row-off-an-array leak already is, not a new kind of risk.

**Verified directly, not just by inspection:** the exact worked example, compiled and run, for both a `Circle` and a `Square` argument; `typeof` on every non-enum type (`int`/`float`/`bool`/`text`/`arr[int]`/a plain struct) and on both enum representations; the field-mismatch case, confirmed to `festina_fail` cleanly (nonzero exit, the exact message on stderr) rather than misread memory; the null-enum case for both `typeof` and field access, confirmed to fail the same clean way instead of segfaulting; a mixed enum (`enum Json = int, text, User`) round-tripping each member type through `typeof`; two enum-typed variables aliasing the same struct pointer (mutating through one is visible through the other, proving the pure-struct representation really is identity, not a copy); repeated reassignment of both a pure-struct and a mixed enum-typed local starting from `null` (the direct regression test for bug 5/6 above) staying correct across every iteration.

**Tests:** `tests/test_enums.py` (new, mirroring `tests/test_maps.py`'s lexer/parser/semantic-only discipline) -- 21 tests: declaration (pure-struct and mixed, forward references in both directions, unknown/duplicate/enum-of-enum/field-collision/duplicate-name rejections), `typeof` (parses on any expression, infers as `text`, works on an enum-typed value), coercion (member -> enum through var decl/param/struct field, the reverse and an unrelated struct both rejected), field access (type-checks on a pure-struct enum, rejected on a mixed one, rejected for a field no member declares). `tests/test_codegen.py`'s new `TestEnums` -- 11 end-to-end tests covering the worked example (both branches), `typeof` on every non-enum type and on a pure-struct enum, the field-mismatch `festina_fail`, the null-`typeof`/null-field-access `festina_fail` cases (bug 6's own regression coverage), a mixed-enum round trip, struct-pointer aliasing, and reassignment-from-null for both representations (bug 5's own regression coverage). 32 new tests total. Fixing bug 1 also fixed three existing tests' own error-message assertions that had been asserting the OLD (bypassed-check_assignable) wording -- `test_syntax_declarations.py`'s two func-typed-call-argument-type tests now match `check_assignable`'s own "cannot assign argument N ... to ..." phrasing instead of the retired "argument N expects ... found ..." one. Fixing the earlier struct-header-widening groundwork (claude.md #176's own codegen prerequisite, landed just before this entry) had already changed an escaping struct local's own generated temp names from a stable `%name.raw.<uid>` to the shared `_emit_fresh_heap_header`'s anonymous `%tN` ones -- one pre-existing `TestAutomaticMemoryReclamation` test in `test_codegen.py` still asserted the old naming and was updated to check the same underlying claim (exactly one `@calloc` call backs the escaping local, none backs the stack-allocated safe one) without depending on temp-naming internals. Full suite: 1830 passed, 9 skipped, 1 failed -- `TestScreenSizeAndSetClientSize::test_screen_size_matches_the_real_display_resolution`, a pre-existing Xvfb-timing flake unrelated to any of this round's changes (nothing here touches graphics/display code), confirmed passing cleanly in isolation immediately afterward. Documented in api.md (a new "Enums" section between Structs and Arrays, with the worked example, the coercion/typeof/field-access rules, the null-and-fails-loudly behavior, and a short representation/cost note) and this entry.

177. `exec(args, callback)` -- A NON-BLOCKING COUNTERPART TO `exec(args)`

Asked for directly, alongside a separate design question about `.callback()`'s own named-variable form (answered in prose, no code change). The request's own example (`exec('echo "hello world!"', callback)`, a single shell-command string) does not match `exec()`'s real, existing signature (`exec(args:arr[text]):int` -- a PATH-searched argv array, never run through a shell; see claude.md #150). Parsing a shell string is a materially different, riskier feature (quoting/escaping, an injection surface this design deliberately has none of) and was explicitly out of scope; this instead extends the *existing* `arr[text]` signature with a trailing optional callback, keeping the request's own argument order: `exec(['echo', 'hello world!'], onDone)`.

**Reuses the async-io worker pool wholesale** -- the exact mechanism `blob`/`img`/`aud`'s own `.callback()` (#165/#171) and `req.send()`'s callback (#163) already share (`festina_async_io_dispatch`, `runtime/festina_runtime_async.c`). `fork()`/`execvp()`/`waitpid()` (and Windows's `_spawnvp`) are ordinary blocking calls with no main-thread-only OS resource involved (unlike graphics/audio) -- safe to run on a pool worker exactly like a blob's file read already is.

**The one real wrinkle blob/img/aud never had: the result is a scalar `int`, not a pointer-shaped value.** `festina_async_io_dispatch`'s callback ABI is fixed at `void(*)(void*)`; blob/img/aud's own callback is already `func[T]:void` for a pointer-shaped `T`, so it passes straight through with no adapter. `exec`'s callback is `func[int]:void` -- a genuinely different shape, needing a real bridge.

**That bridge is a single, generic, lazily-cached codegen-generated trampoline (`_emit_exec_callback_trampoline`), not a per-call-site one.** The obvious first design -- one fresh trampoline per call site hardcoding which Festina function to call, the shape `_emit_map_value_release_trampoline` already uses for a release function -- doesn't work here: `exec(args, callback)`'s own `callback` is checked the same permissive, structural way blob/img/aud's `.callback()` already is (any `func[int]:void`-typed *expression*, not restricted to a bare declared-function name the way `setTimeout`'s older rule is), so the real callback can be an ordinary runtime SSA value -- a variable, a struct field -- that a separately-emitted top-level LLVM function can never reference directly. The fix: route the callback pointer through the payload as plain data, exactly like the exit code itself. `FestinaExecPayload` (`runtime/festina_runtime.c`) starts with a fixed two-field prefix both sides agree on -- `{ int64_t exit_code; void (*user_callback)(int64_t); ... }` -- and the ONE generated trampoline reads both fields back out of `%payload` (`load i64` for the exit code, `getelementptr {i64,ptr}, ptr %payload, i32 0, i32 1` for the callback) and makes an indirect call through the pointer it just loaded. That means every `exec(args, callback)` call site in a program shares the identical trampoline, compile-time-constant callback or not -- generated once, cached in `self._exec_callback_trampoline`.

**Return type: `void`, not an int placeholder.** Unlike a `blob` (a shared, mutable handle another binding can alias and read through once populated), Festina's `int` is a plain value type -- `int status = exec(args, callback)` could never observably update once the job finishes, since assignment copies the value, not a reference. There is also no cancel/kill mechanism to hand a caller an id for (unlike `setTimeout`'s real, `clearTimeout`-able timer id). So the 2-argument form is a plain statement, with the real exit code delivered only through `callback(code:int)`.

**`festina_process_exec` was refactored, not duplicated, to share its actual spawn logic** with the new async path: the tricky, platform-specific "run this NULL-terminated argv, return the real exit code" core (POSIX's self-pipe fork/exec/waitpid dance in particular) was extracted into a static `festina_run_argv(char *const *argv_c)` helper, used unchanged by both the existing synchronous `festina_process_exec` (which still borrows the caller's own `arr[text]` strings, safe since it returns before the array could be released) and the new `festina_process_exec_dispatch` (which must deep-copy every argv string with `strdup`, since the actual spawn happens later on a worker thread, quite possibly after codegen has already released the caller's array -- the same release timing the existing synchronous path's own codegen already uses).

**semantic.py** gives `exec` one dedicated `_infer_call` branch handling both arities (removing its old `_BUILTIN_RETURN_TYPES`/`_BUILTIN_SIGNATURES` entries, which could express neither the arity-dependent return type nor a structurally-checked callback argument) -- 1 argument keeps `arr[text] -> int`; 2 arguments additionally checks the second argument structurally against `func[int]:void`, `check_assignable`-free since a func's exact signature match is already the identical strict rule blob/img/aud's own `.callback()` uses.

**codegen.py** splits the existing `exec` `_emit_call` branch on `len(expr.args)`: 1 argument is completely unchanged (`festina_process_exec`); 2 arguments sets `self.uses_exec` (unchanged wasm32-wasi compile-time rejection) *and* `self.uses_async_io` (links `festina_runtime_async.c`, keeps the event loop alive until the callback fires -- the identical flag/mechanism blob/img/aud's own `.callback()` already sets), emits/reuses the cached trampoline, and calls `@festina_process_exec_dispatch(ptr args, ptr callback, ptr trampoline)`, releasing `args` right after -- identical release logic and timing to the existing 1-argument branch.

**Verified directly:** a worked example (`sleep 1 && exit 7` in the background) -- the dispatch-site log line prints immediately, `sleep 1`'s own delay elapses, and the callback then receives the real exit code (`7`); a missing-executable case delivered `-1` through the callback, matching the synchronous form's own contract exactly; several concurrent callback-carrying execs (`5` at once, summed inside their shared callback) all completed; `--target=wasm32-wasi` still rejects the 2-argument form at compile time with the existing "no process model" error (`gen.uses_exec` unchanged as the signal); a new `tests/stress/exec_callback_churn.f` (40 passes * 4 dispatches, mixing real quick children and missing-executable cases, argv length varying pass to pass) run under `scripts/leak_stress.sh` -- clean, no leak or memory error in the new argv-deep-copy/payload/trampoline path.

**Tests:** `tests/test_async_io.py`'s new `TestExecCallbackSemantics` -- 8 tests covering both arities, a stored (non-bare-identifier) `func[int]:void` value as the callback, wrong arity, the first argument's `arr[text]` check unchanged, and the callback's own arity/param-type/return-type structural rejections. `tests/test_codegen.py`'s new `TestExecCallback` -- 7 end-to-end tests: does-not-block ordering, clean exit with no other loop-driving construct, the real exit code delivered, a missing executable delivering `-1`, 5 concurrent execs all completing, a callback passed as a stored value (not a bare identifier, exercising the trampoline's own data-carried design), and the wasm32-wasi rejection. 15 new tests total, all passing, alongside every pre-existing `exec`/async-io test (unaffected by the refactor); `tests/test_leak_stress.py`'s own coverage-completeness test updated for the new `exec_callback_churn.f` stress file. Full suite: 1860 passed, 9 skipped. Documented in api.md (a new "Running without blocking: `exec(args, callback)`" subsection under "Running other programs", styled after `.callback()`'s own worked example) and this entry.

178. THREE FIELD REPORTS -- A MISSING `cairo_surface_flush()`, A TABLE-ROW SEGFAULT, AND A DOCUMENTED-NOT-FIXED HOISTING SURPRISE

A user bug report, not self-discovered: three items, two real defects and one flagged-but-not-a-bug behavior asked to be documented. All three investigated by actually reproducing (or, for the first, tracing the exact mechanism when reproduction wasn't possible in this container), not by inspection alone.

**`img.clip()` materializing pixel data only on its first call in a process.** The report: every call after the first reports correct dimensions but reads back blank unless something else happens to draw onto the result first -- exactly the `saveCanvas().clip(...)` idiom `layers.f` itself recommends, so it silently broke every chunk background after the first one built that way. Reproduced several shapes headlessly against this container's own Xlib/Cairo (multiple `clip()`s from one `saveCanvas()` snapshot, with and without an extra draw call in between, composited via `drawImage` and read back both via `.save()`'s PNG encoding and a real on-screen `render()`) without success -- Cairo's plain software image backend applies paint operations synchronously here, masking the bug. Traced instead by auditing every raw (non-Cairo-API) read of a Cairo image surface's own pixel buffer: both the macOS and Windows windowing backends (`festina_runtime_window_mac.m`'s `drawRect:`, `festina_runtime_window_win32.c`'s `festina_win32_paint`) call `cairo_image_surface_get_data(g_last_backing)` directly, entirely outside Cairo's own drawing API -- unlike the X11 backend, whose `festina_window_present` reads `g_backing_surface` only through `cairo_set_source_surface`+`cairo_paint`, Cairo mediating the read the same way it mediates every write. Cairo's own documented contract for `cairo_image_surface_get_data()` requires a `cairo_surface_flush()` first, "to ensure that all pending drawing operations are finished" -- and neither backend's own paint callback (dispatched asynchronously, `WM_PAINT`/`drawRect:`, an arbitrary amount of further Cairo drawing after whatever last touched that exact surface) ever called one. Missing this precisely explains "correct dimensions, blank pixels" (the header fields Cairo always keeps current regardless of a flush; the buffer isn't) and precisely explains "works if something else draws onto it first" (an unrelated later Cairo operation happening to trigger a flush of its own is not something any caller could rely on). Fixed by adding `cairo_surface_flush(g_last_backing)` immediately before each raw read, in both backends -- at the point of the read rather than back in `festina_window_present` at present-time, since the paint callback can fire an arbitrary amount of time (and drawing) later. `.save()`/blob-column encoding needed no equivalent fix -- `cairo_surface_write_to_png[_stream]` is Cairo's own API and already flushes internally, which is also why every earlier repro attempt through that path came back clean.

Verified structurally rather than on real hardware (no macOS/Windows box in this session, the same constraint macos.md/windows.md's own "shared work, tested from every platform" pattern already exists for) -- a new `tests/test_platform.py::TestNativeWindowPresentFlushesBeforeRawRead`, reading each backend's own source and asserting every `cairo_image_surface_get_data(g_last_backing)` call is preceded, in the same function, by a `cairo_surface_flush(g_last_backing)` -- confirmed to fail cleanly (not error out) against the pre-fix source via `git stash`, then pass against the fix.

**A manually-built table row segfaulting on its first field assignment.** The report: `Table t` (declared with no query anywhere) then `t.field = value` crashed outright; worked around by using a plain `struct` for anything built by hand, converting at the query boundary. Reproduced immediately -- a real SIGSEGV (`run()`'s own exit code, `-11` through the shell), not a hang or a clean failure. Root cause: `codegen.py`'s `_member_ptr_from` computes a table row's field-write pointer as a flat `getelementptr i8, ptr %obj, i64 idx*8` with NO null check at all -- unlike a struct field (which auto-vivifies, `_load_field_value`'s own comment) and unlike an enum value (which fails loudly, claude.md #176's own null guard). `codegen.py`'s own VarDecl handling explains why: `StructType` gets a dedicated branch that ALWAYS allocates real, zeroed storage immediately, with or without an initializer -- `TableType` has no equivalent branch at all, so it falls through to the generic "store null if uninitialized" path every other bare pointer-shaped type uses, and nothing downstream ever taught it to auto-vivify the way a struct field does. This isn't an oversight worth patching with auto-vivify, though -- `codegen.py`'s own `_emit_free` already documents TableType as "a borrowed query row": it is never retained, released, or independently allocated anywhere else in this compiler (freeing one only ever nulls the binding). Giving it real standalone ownership semantics just for this would be a materially bigger change than the report calls for, and `struct` -- api.md's own "Structs as query targets" section -- already exists as exactly the sanctioned hand-built alternative, which is also the workaround the report itself landed on independently. Fixed at the root instead: `semantic.py`'s `analyze_var_decl` now rejects a `TableType`-typed declaration with no initializer at compile time (the identical shape `amor arr[T] xs` with no initializer already gets), pointing at both the fix (assign an existing row) and the alternative (`struct`) in one message. Assigning from a real row (`People p = rows[0]`), a table-typed function parameter, and every other legitimate use are all unaffected -- confirmed directly, not just by the check's own placement.

Verified: the exact reproduction now fails at compile time with a clear message instead of crashing at run time; a real `sqlite()`-round-trip assignment (`arr[People] rows = sqlite(...); People p = rows[0]; p.name = 'Updated'`) still compiles and runs correctly, both through `semantic.analyze()` directly and through the real compiler end to end. `tests/test_sqlite_schema.py`'s new `TestTableRowRequiresAnInitializer` (6 tests: bare local and global declarations rejected, the error names `struct` as the alternative, assignment-from-a-real-row/parameter/for-loop-init all correctly unaffected or still enforced) and `TestTableRowSegfaultEndToEnd` (2 tests: the exact reproduction rejected through the real `compile_file`, and the real round trip compiling and running correctly) -- 8 new tests total.

**Event handlers active as soon as declared, regardless of source position -- flagged as a real time cost, not requested as a bug fix.** Confirmed directly: `setClientWidth`/`setClientHeight` fire `on resize` synchronously, inline, at the call site -- a call written ABOVE an `on resize` declaration still triggers it, and any global the handler reads that hasn't been initialized yet (because ITS OWN top-level initializing statement sits below the trigger) reads its zero/default, not the value the source implies it should already have by then. Root cause, traced rather than assumed: `codegen.py`'s `_emit_main_and_entry` registers every declared handler (`festina_register_*_handler`) in one fixed block, unconditionally, before `call void @__festina_main()` ever runs -- i.e. before any of the entry file's own top-level code, regardless of where in the file each `on ...` is textually written. This is the identical hoisting api.md's own "Functions are hoisted" note already documents for `func` declarations (and the identical mechanism, both ultimately "every declaration exists everywhere in the program") -- just far less obviously surprising for a `func`, which only ever runs when something calls it, versus a handler, which an ordinary top-level statement can trigger before ever reaching its own declaration. Not a bug: nothing here contradicts hoisting's own existing, intentional design, and the "fix" is the same one hoisting-adjacent gotchas always have -- declare handlers, and initialize whatever global state they read, before any call that could plausibly trigger them. Documented in api.md, directly where the seven event handlers are introduced, with the exact `setClientWidth`/`on resize`/uninitialized-`arr[int]` reproduction as the worked example. Pinned with a new `tests/test_codegen.py::TestEventHandlersAreHoistedLikeFunctions` (1 test, the exact reproduction, confirming both the hoisted firing order and the not-yet-initialized read) -- not a bug fix, but this exact ordering is exactly the kind of thing that could regress silently without something asserting it stays true.

Nothing here changed `festina_image_clip`/`festina_canvas_to_image`/`festina_image_resize` themselves, or any codegen path other than `analyze_var_decl` -- audited for other raw (non-Cairo-API) reads of a surface's pixel buffer first (only the two windowing backends do this; `.save()`/blob-column encoding already goes through Cairo's own flushing API), and audited for other TableType call sites that might need the identical null-check (function parameters and array elements both already carry a real row from their own origin, needing nothing new). 10 new tests total across all three items (1 + 8 + 1). Full suite: 1870 passed, 9 skipped.

179. GRAPHICS WINDOW OPENED AT A HARDCODED 800x600 BEFORE THE PROGRAM'S OWN `setClientWidth`/`setClientHeight` EVER RAN

A user bug report (uraikus/festina#79), filed with the root cause already correctly diagnosed and a suggested fix. A program that calls `setClientWidth`/`setClientHeight` near the top of its own boot sequence -- the documented, `on resize`-safe pattern claude.md #178 itself covers -- briefly opened a real, on-screen window at the wrong size before correcting itself: harmless under Xvfb (the correction is instant, no window manager to race), but a real desktop WM's own reflow/repaint lag around a just-resized window meant this could be visibly perceptible (a stale/blank strip along one edge on first launch, gone after any later real resize) in `festina-game`, which is exactly where it was found.

**Root cause, confirmed by reading both sides of the same bug.** `codegen.py`'s `main()` prologue called `festina_graphics_init()` unconditionally whenever `self.uses_graphics` was set, *before* `call void @__festina_main()` -- i.e. before any of the entry file's own top-level code, including whatever `setClientWidth`/`setClientHeight` calls it makes. `festina_graphics_init()` (`festina_runtime_graphics.c`) opened the real window at the hardcoded `FESTINA_CANVAS_WIDTH`/`_HEIGHT` (800x600) and then unconditionally reset `g_canvas_width`/`g_canvas_height` back to those same constants -- clobbering them even if a call that ran earlier (impossible under the OLD ordering, but this reset alone would have defeated fixing just the ordering) had already changed them. By the time the program's own `setClientWidth(1024)` finally ran, the window was already open at 800x600, so `festina_set_client_size` took its real, `g_window_open`-gated branch: an actual `XResizeWindow` plus a genuine `on resize` firing -- confirmed directly against the issue's own repro (`on resize` logging `clientWidth`/`clientHeight`): two resize events fired for two `setClientWidth`/`setClientHeight` calls that never asked to see an intermediate size at all, with `clientHeight=600` (exactly the hardcoded default, never requested anywhere in the script) showing up as the first event's own reported size.

**Fix: stop opening the window before the entry file's own code runs, and stop clobbering the canvas size when it finally does open.** `festina_graphics_init()` no longer resets `g_canvas_width`/`g_canvas_height` -- it opens the platform window (`festina_window_open`, the one shared, portable seam every platform backend implements) at whatever those globals already hold, and is now self-guarding (`if (g_window_open) return;`) rather than relying on every caller to check first, since it now has more than one legitimate caller. `codegen.py`'s `main()` prologue no longer calls it at all before `__festina_main()` -- only event-handler registration still happens there (`festina_register_resize_handler` and friends), which has no window dependency at all (each one just stores a function pointer). The window itself now opens lazily, from whichever of two places reaches for it first: `festina_render()`'s own pre-existing `if (!g_window_open) festina_graphics_init();` guard (unchanged), or a matching new guard added to the top of `festina_run_event_loop()` (the loop `main()` still unconditionally enters after `__festina_main()` returns, whenever `self.uses_graphics` is set) -- covering the case a program declares a handler or sets its client size but never itself calls `render()`/draws anything, which still needs a real window to exist before the loop can service its events. Either lazy-init site reads `g_canvas_width`/`g_canvas_height` at the moment it actually runs -- by which point any `setClientWidth`/`setClientHeight` call the entry file's own top-level code already made (harmless to run against no window at all, since `festina_set_client_size` only touches the live window/backing store inside its own `if (g_window_open)` branch) has already taken effect. One fix point, `festina_graphics_init()`, covers all three platforms uniformly -- X11, macOS, and Windows's own `festina_window_open` implementations all take an explicit width/height argument already; none of them reference the hardcoded constants directly.

**Verified directly, both the fix and its absence of regressions.** The issue's own exact repro, compiled and run under Xvfb: no `on resize` firing at all (previously two), and the real window (`xdotool getwindowgeometry`) opening directly at 1024x700 -- not 800x600, and not the 1024x600 intermediate size the bug produced. A program using no graphics at all, and one using the plain, untouched `render()`-first pattern (no pre-window `setClientWidth`), both still open at the standard 800x600 default, confirming no regression to the common case. A real, `g_window_open`-gated resize (`setClientWidth` called AFTER `render()` already opened the window) still fires `on resize` exactly as before -- unaffected, since that branch of `festina_set_client_size` was never touched.

**Tests:** five pre-existing `tests/test_codegen.py` IR-pattern tests asserted `"call void @festina_graphics_init()"` present or absent in generated IR to distinguish "opens a window" from "doesn't" -- now vacuous (the call is never emitted by codegen at all any more, window-opening or not), so all five were updated to check for `@festina_render()`/`@festina_run_event_loop()` instead, the actual new observable boundary. New `TestScreenSizeAndSetClientSize::test_setting_client_size_before_the_window_opens_is_honored_as_its_initial_size` -- the real, end-to-end regression test: compiles and runs the issue's own repro under Xvfb, asserts the real window's geometry via `xdotool getwindowgeometry` and that no `on resize` fired. 1 new test. Full suite: 1871 passed, 9 skipped. Documented in api.md, both in the "Drawing is offscreen" note (the window's lazy-open timing) and directly under `setClientWidth`/`setClientHeight` (a new worked example matching this entry's own fix). Version bumped to 0.2.2 (CHANGELOG.md, `festina/__init__.py`).

180. A DECORATED WINDOW (MINIMIZE/MAXIMIZE/CLOSE, LIKE ANY OTHER WINDOW) PLUS `enterFullscreen()`/`exitFullscreen()`

Requested directly, alongside PR #80 (claude.md #179) still in flight: the window has been deliberately undecorated -- borderless, "canvas, nothing else" -- since claude.md #95 first opened one, on the reasoning that claude.md's own examples describe a canvas, not a desktop app chrome. Asked to make it look and behave like a normal OS window instead (title bar, minimize/maximize/close), plus give a program its own way to go fullscreen on top of that.

**Decorations: one line changed per platform, since every backend already treated "how is this window decorated" as a property of how it's created, not something added on afterward.** X11's Motif WM hints flip from `decorations=0` to `decorations=1` (MWM_DECOR_ALL) -- still set explicitly, not simply omitted, since some window managers default a borderless-hint-free window to undecorated too, matching this window's own existing convention of stating what it wants rather than assuming a WM's default. macOS's `styleMask` grows from bare `NSWindowStyleMaskBorderless` to `NSWindowStyleMaskTitled | NSWindowStyleMaskClosable | NSWindowStyleMaskMiniaturizable | NSWindowStyleMaskResizable`. Windows' `CreateWindowExW` style grows from `WS_POPUP` to `WS_OVERLAPPEDWINDOW`. `windowShouldClose:`/`WM_CLOSE`/`WM_DELETE_WINDOW` already routed every platform's real close button through the same `on close` + `festina_window_close()` path *before* this change (there was no borderless-window-specific close handling to remove) -- a real title-bar close button just means that path is reachable by mouse now, not that it needed rewiring.

**Two adjustments the decoration change itself forced, on two different platforms, for two different reasons.** (1) Cocoa: `NSWindowStyleMaskResizable` means a user can now drag-resize the window for the first time -- previously, the view's own frame only ever changed via `festina_window_resize`'s explicit `setContentSize:` call, so nothing kept it in sync with a resize the WINDOW gained on its own (dragging an edge, clicking zoom). `[g_view setAutoresizingMask:NSViewWidthSizable | NSViewHeightSizable]` fixes this -- without it, `windowDidResize:` (which reports whatever `[g_view frame]` happens to be) would report a stale size after any user-driven resize, since AppKit doesn't auto-track a view's frame to its window's content size without being told to. (2) Win32: `WS_POPUP`'s outer window size and client size were always identical (no border to account for), which `festina_window_open`'s `CreateWindowExW` call and `festina_window_resize`'s `SetWindowPos` call both relied on directly. `WS_OVERLAPPEDWINDOW` breaks that equivalence -- both call sites now run the requested CONTENT size through `AdjustWindowRect` first, converting it to the outer size those two Win32 calls actually need, so `width`/`height` keep meaning what every caller already expects (the canvas's own content size) exactly like X11/Cocoa's own conventions, where the window manager/AppKit already does this same content-vs-frame translation invisibly. `festina_window_resize` reads the window's CURRENT style (`GetWindowLongW`) rather than hardcoding `WS_OVERLAPPEDWINDOW`, so it also stays correct if called while fullscreen's own temporary `WS_POPUP` state (see below) happens to be active. Neither X11 nor macOS needed an equivalent fix: a WM-driven X11 ConfigureNotify was already routed through the identical `cairo_xlib_surface_set_size` update any other resize gets (`festina_window_events_drain`'s own ConfigureNotify case, unconditional on WHO triggered it), and `initWithContentRect:`/`setContentSize:` already both operate purely in content-size terms regardless of `styleMask` -- Cocoa does its own frame-vs-content translation on every call, not just window creation.

**`enterFullscreen()`/`exitFullscreen()`: one new portable seam function (`festina_window_set_fullscreen`, alongside `festina_window_open`/`_close`/`_present`/`_resize`/... in `festina_runtime_window.h`), three genuinely different platform implementations.** X11 sends a `_NET_WM_STATE` ClientMessage to the ROOT window (not the client window -- that distinction is what tells an EWMH-compliant WM this is a state-change REQUEST, not a property to just record) asking it to add/remove `_NET_WM_STATE_FULLSCREEN` -- the WM does the actual resizing/repositioning, the same as every other window's fullscreen already works on that desktop. macOS calls `[window toggleFullScreen:nil]` -- AppKit's ENTIRE API for this, no separate enter/exit selector pair exists -- guarded by checking `[window styleMask] & NSWindowStyleMaskFullScreen` against the requested state first (querying AppKit's own live truth rather than trusting a separately-tracked flag that could drift, e.g. if the user exits via Escape or the Full Screen menu item rather than through Festina's own `exitFullscreen()`); the window also has to opt into this via `NSWindowCollectionBehaviorFullScreenPrimary` at creation time, or `toggleFullScreen:` does nothing.
