Windows has no single native fullscreen API at all -- `festina_window_set_fullscreen` fakes it the well-known way (Raymond Chen's "borderless popup sized to the monitor" recipe): entering saves the CURRENT style and `GetWindowPlacement` (not just a rect -- that also captures whether the window was maximized, which a plain rect can't), switches to `WS_POPUP`, and `SetWindowPos`s to exactly cover `GetMonitorInfoW`'s own monitor rect; exiting restores the saved style first, then `SetWindowPlacement`, in that order, since `SetWindowPlacement`'s own restore behavior depends on the window already being a normal, decorated kind again. `g_win32_is_fullscreen`/`g_prev_style`/`g_prev_placement` are reset in `festina_window_close()` -- otherwise stale bookkeeping from a closed window could desync a same-process reopen's own state.

**Portable layer: one flag doing exactly the double duty claude.md #178's `g_canvas_width`/`g_canvas_height` already established for canvas size.** `g_is_fullscreen` (`festina_runtime_graphics.c`) is both "what was requested before a window existed" and "what's true now that one does" -- `festina_enter_fullscreen()`/`festina_exit_fullscreen()` set it and, if a window is already open, call `festina_window_set_fullscreen` immediately; if not, `festina_graphics_init()` (already self-guarding since #178) applies it right after opening the window. This is what makes `enterFullscreen()` called before the first `render()` open DIRECTLY in fullscreen -- no flash of a normal window first, the identical fix #178 already made for a pre-window `setClientWidth`/`setClientHeight` call. Both functions no-op if already in the requested state, the same guard `festina_set_client_size` already has for a same-value call. `enterFullscreen`/`exitFullscreen` join `render()` as the only two `_CANVAS_OPS` builtins that set `self.uses_graphics` (`codegen.py`) -- meaningless without a real OS window, unlike every other canvas operation, which paints an offscreen surface that needs no display at all (claude.md #95).

**The resulting size change is asynchronous, unlike `setClientWidth`/`setClientHeight`'s own synchronous update -- documented as a real behavioral difference, not glossed over.** Entering/exiting fullscreen is a real negotiation with the window manager/OS (X11's ClientMessage protocol; AppKit's own animated transition; Win32's own message pump), not something Festina does to itself the way `festina_set_client_size` directly manipulates `g_canvas_width`/`g_canvas_height` inline. `clientWidth`/`clientHeight` and any `on resize` handler only update once that negotiation's own resize notification (ConfigureNotify/`windowDidResize:`/`WM_SIZE`) actually arrives, on a later pump through the event loop -- covered by no NEW code on any platform, since all three already routed a WM-driven resize (dragging an edge, clicking zoom, now this) through the identical `cairo_xlib_surface_set_size`/`windowDidResize:`/`WM_SIZE`-pushes-a-RESIZE-event path any other native resize already used.

**Verified directly against a real window manager, not just Xvfb.** `x_display_with_wm` (openbox, already existing test infrastructure from claude.md #123's own BadMatch regression) confirmed: real decorations (`_NET_FRAME_EXTENTS` reporting a nonzero title bar/border, not just the Motif property being set), a title bar reading "Festina" with visible minimize/maximize/close buttons (captured via `xwd`, inspected visually), `enterFullscreen()` growing the real window to exactly the display's own resolution (`xdotool getwindowgeometry`/`xwininfo`) with zero decoration offset, `on resize` firing with the new size, `exitFullscreen()` restoring the EXACT prior geometry (800x600, decoration offset back to (1, 20)) and firing `on resize` again, and that redundant calls (`enterFullscreen()` twice, an `exitFullscreen()` that was never entered) produce no spurious extra `on resize` firing. macOS and Windows verified structurally only (compiled/type-checked by CI, the same real-hardware-verification gap #39/windows.md's own Phase 2 sections already flag and gate behind `FESTINA_ENABLE_MACOS_GRAPHICS`/`FESTINA_ENABLE_WINDOWS_GRAPHICS`) -- no hardware available in this session, consistent with every other windowing change to those two backends so far.

**Tests:** new `tests/test_codegen.py::TestFullscreenAndDecorations` -- 6 tests: real decorations confirmed via `_NET_FRAME_EXTENTS` under `x_display_with_wm`, `enterFullscreen`/`exitFullscreen` arity rejection, both alone (no `render()`/handler) still forcing `self.uses_graphics` (a `festina_run_event_loop()` IR check), the full enter-then-exit round trip's real window geometry and `on resize` sequence, entering fullscreen before the window ever opens skipping the windowed flash, and redundant calls producing no extra `on resize`. 6 new tests. Documented in api.md (retired the "undecorated" language throughout, and a new `enterFullscreen()`/`exitFullscreen()` subsection right after `setClientWidth`/`setClientHeight`'s own, matching its worked-example style) and `festina_runtime.h`'s own Graphics doc comment.

181. `on mouseWheelUp`/`on mouseWheelDown` AND `devicePixelRatio`

Requested directly, alongside PR #80 (claude.md #179/#180) still in flight. Two independent additions, sharing only the general "a new graphics event"/"a new read-only display global" shape claude.md #40/#139 already established.

**The scroll wheel, split by direction the same way `on mouseDown`/`on mouseUp` are split by press/release rather than one combined event** (claude.md #106's own reasoning applies identically: a program that only cares about one direction shouldn't have to filter the other out itself). Both take `(x:int, y:int)` -- the pointer's position at the moment of the scroll, the same convention every other mouse event already has; there is no delta/magnitude to report, only direction, since how far one "notch" is is entirely up to the OS/input device.

**X11 has no dedicated scroll-wheel event in its core protocol at all** -- by long-standing, universal convention (older than XInput2's real smooth-scroll events, but still what every application/toolkit still honors for a simple wheel), a wheel notch is reported as an ordinary `ButtonPress` immediately followed by its own `ButtonRelease`, on button 4 (up) or button 5 (down). Firing the new wheel event on the PRESS half only, and swallowing the paired release entirely (`continue`, never reaching `mouseDown`/`mouseUp` at all), is what makes this "one wheel event per notch" rather than two -- and incidentally uncovered and fixed a real pre-existing bug: every button's press/release used to reach `mouseDown`/`mouseUp` completely unfiltered, so scrolling over the canvas already silently fired a spurious `mouseDown`+`mouseUp` pair at the wheel's own position, before this entry's fix. Confirmed directly, both the bug (via `git stash`, reproduced: an `on mouseDown`/`on mouseUp`-only program logging a click for every wheel notch) and the fix (the same program, post-fix, logging nothing for a wheel scroll). macOS's `scrollWheel:` and Windows' `WM_MOUSEWHEEL` never had this problem -- both platforms already deliver the wheel as an entirely separate message/NSEvent from any mouse button, so those two backends' own wheel handling is purely additive, no equivalent fix needed.

**`devicePixelRatio:float`** -- a new read-only global, the identical registration shape `screenWidth`/`screenHeight` (claude.md #139) already have (a physical-display property, answerable with or without a window open), except FLOAT-typed rather than int, kept in its own `_DEVICE_PIXEL_RATIO_GLOBALS` tuple in semantic.py precisely because of that type difference (the existing `_SIZE_GLOBALS` registration loop is int-only) while still sharing the same read-only-assignment check via a `_READONLY_SCALAR_GLOBALS` combination. Purely informational -- this runtime does no actual backing-pixel-resolution rendering anywhere, so reading a non-1.0 ratio doesn't change how anything drawn appears; it just tells a program what's true about the display it's running on. Per-platform: X11 has no single canonical API for this at all (the obvious-looking `DisplayWidthMM`-based DPI heuristic is well known to be unreliable -- many real monitors report inaccurate EDID physical dimensions, which is why GTK/Qt/every serious X11 toolkit instead reads the `Xft.dpi` X resource, the actual standard mechanism a desktop environment writes when a user picks a scale factor) -- reads `Xft.dpi` via `XGetDefault`, falling back to `1.0` (also the CORRECT answer for the common case: a plain X11 setup with no HiDPi configuration at all) if unset. macOS reads `[NSScreen backingScaleFactor]` directly (exactly this ratio already -- 2.0 on Retina, 1.0 otherwise). Windows reads `GetDeviceCaps(..., LOGPIXELSX) / 96.0` off the screen DC -- the broadly compatible way to ask, working back to any Windows version with no per-monitor-DPI-awareness manifest declaration required (which the newer `GetDpiForWindow`/`GetDpiForSystem` APIs need to report anything but the system default, and this program declares no such manifest).

**Verified directly on X11.** The scroll-wheel fix/feature: real `xdotool click <wid> 4`/`5` against a compiled program declaring `on mouseDown`/`on mouseUp`/`on mouseWheelUp`/`on mouseWheelDown` together -- two wheel-up clicks produced exactly two `wheelUp` lines (not four), one wheel-down produced exactly one `wheelDown` line, and neither ever also fired `mouseDown`/`mouseUp`; an ordinary left/middle/right click still fires `mouseDown`+`mouseUp` normally, confirming the button-4/5 filter doesn't touch real buttons. `devicePixelRatio`: read successfully headlessly and under Xvfb, reporting `1.0` (the correct answer -- Xvfb sets no `Xft.dpi` resource). macOS/Windows verified structurally only, the same real-hardware-verification gap every other windowing change to those two backends already has (gated behind `FESTINA_ENABLE_MACOS_GRAPHICS`/`FESTINA_ENABLE_WINDOWS_GRAPHICS`, claude.md #123/#128).

**Tests:** new `TestMouseWheelButtonAndCursor`/`TestDevicePixelRatio` classes (the former shared with claude.md #182's own work, landed together) plus `TestEventHandlers`' own new `mouseWheelUp`/`mouseWheelDown` parse/arity cases in `tests/test_graphics.py`. Documented in api.md (a new "on mouseWheelUp/on mouseWheelDown" note under "Mouse events", and a new `devicePixelRatio` paragraph alongside `screenWidth`/`screenHeight`'s own).

182. `button:int` ON `on mouseDown`/`on mouseUp`, AND `showCursor()`/`hideCursor()`

Requested directly, immediately after #181 above, along with confirmation that the wheel-triggers-click bug #181 already fixed stays fixed. Two more additions to the same graphics surface.

**`button:int`, a required third argument on `on mouseDown`/`on mouseUp` specifically** (`on mouse`, continuous movement, keeps its plain `(x:int, y:int)` -- a move has no button of its own to report). A real, deliberate BREAKING CHANGE to those two handlers' own fixed signature (claude.md #40's own `_EVENT_SIGNATURES` enforcement) -- every existing 2-argument `on mouseDown(x:int, y:int)`/`on mouseUp(x:int, y:int)` in this repo's own examples/tests/README/api.md was updated to the new 3-argument form as part of this entry, confirmed via a dedicated regression test (`test_mouse_button_handler_now_requires_button_argument`) that the OLD 2-argument form is now correctly REJECTED.

**One canonical numbering, X11's own, adopted specifically because X11 already produces it natively with zero translation needed** -- `FestinaWindowEvent` gained a `button` field (documented once, in its own struct comment in `festina_runtime_window.h`, rather than duplicated per backend): `1` = left, `2` = middle, `3` = right, `8` = back, `9` = forward; anything else reports its own platform-raw number, best-effort. X11's `ButtonPress`/`ButtonRelease` already reports every button through `ev.xbutton.button` uniformly (the same field #181's own wheel filter already reads) -- no new code needed beyond passing it through.

**macOS and Windows previously only ever implemented the LEFT button at all** -- `mouseDown:`/`mouseUp:` (Cocoa) and `WM_LBUTTONDOWN`/`WM_LBUTTONUP` (Win32) were the only button messages either backend handled, discovered while implementing this: right-click and middle-click did *nothing* on either platform before this entry, since a `button` argument would have been meaningless with only ever one possible value. Both gained real support for the other buttons as part of adding the argument that reports them, not as an unrelated scope increase:
- **Cocoa**: added `rightMouseDown:`/`rightMouseUp:` (button 3) and `otherMouseDown:`/`otherMouseUp:` (buttonNumber 2 and up, translated via a new `festina_mac_other_button_number` -- AppKit's own buttonNumber is 0-indexed and ordered left/right/middle, 0/1/2, a genuinely different numbering AND ordering than X11's 1/2/3 left/middle/right; buttonNumber 3/4, empirically "back"/"forward" on most multi-button mice though Apple documents no fixed meaning past 0/1/2, map to 8/9 to match). All four new methods and the existing `mouseDown:`/`mouseUp:` route through one new shared `festinaMouseButtonEvent:kind:button:` helper rather than duplicating the coordinate-flip logic five times.
- **Win32**: added `WM_RBUTTONDOWN`/`WM_RBUTTONUP` (button 3), `WM_MBUTTONDOWN`/`WM_MBUTTONUP` (button 2), and `WM_XBUTTONDOWN`/`WM_XBUTTONUP` (back/forward, read from the HIGH word of `wParam` -- the same field `GET_XBUTTON_WPARAM` extracts, read directly rather than pulling in `<windowsx.h>` for that one macro, matching `WM_MOUSEWHEEL`'s own existing choice). `WM_XBUTTONDOWN`/`WM_XBUTTONUP` are the one real exception to every other message here returning 0 -- MSDN documents that a window MUST return `TRUE` for this specific pair if it handled them, gotten right by reading the actual Win32 documentation rather than assuming symmetry with every other message.

**`showCursor()`/`hideCursor()`** toggle the mouse cursor's visibility over the canvas -- useful for a program drawing its own cursor/reticle. Unlike `render()`/`enterFullscreen()`/`exitFullscreen()` (claude.md #95/#180), neither forces a window open: a cursor is meaningless with none, so calling either before the window exists is a harmless no-op that just records the desired state (`g_cursor_visible`, the identical double-duty desired/current-state flag `g_is_fullscreen` (#180) and `g_canvas_width`/`g_canvas_height` (#178) already established) for `festina_graphics_init` to apply once a window actually opens. Each call also no-ops if already in the requested state, the same guard every other toggle in this family already has -- load-bearing here specifically because BOTH platform primitives underneath are counter-based (`[NSCursor hide]`/`unhide` on macOS, `ShowCursor` on Windows both maintain their own internal display counter, needing a balanced hide-then-show or the counter drifts), so a redundant call reaching the seam would leave it imbalanced; the portable guard means the seam is only ever reached on a genuine transition, one hide matched by one show. X11 has no direct "hide the cursor" call in its core protocol either (`XFixesHideCursor` exists, but pulling in `libXfixes` as a whole new link dependency for one call isn't worth it, claude.md #59's "smallest dependency that does the job") -- uses the standard, dependency-free workaround (also how SDL's own X11 backend does it): define a real cursor that's simply a fully transparent 1x1 bitmap, so nothing of it is ever drawn; `XUndefineCursor` removes the override to restore the default.

**Verified directly on X11.** Left/middle/right click (`xdotool click 1`/`2`/`3`) reported `button` 1/2/3 respectively, confirmed via a real compiled-and-run program's own log output -- not just reasoned about from the X11 numbering. `hideCursor()`/`showCursor()`, including called redundantly twice in a row each way, and called before the window ever opens: no crash, program continues normally past them either way (the one thing practically observable from an automated test -- there is no queryable X11 window property for "what does the cursor currently look like" the way `_NET_FRAME_EXTENTS` exists for decorations, claude.md #180). The wheel-doesn't-trigger-click fix (#181) re-confirmed still holds after this entry's own changes to the same button-dispatch code path. macOS/Windows verified structurally only -- no hardware available in this session, the same gap every other windowing change to those two backends already has.

**Tests:** new `tests/test_codegen.py::TestMouseWheelButtonAndCursor` -- 5 tests: wheel scrolling firing no spurious click, wheel up/down firing exactly once per notch (2 up + 1 down produces exactly that many lines), left/middle/right click reporting the right `button` number, `showCursor`/`hideCursor` (including redundant calls) never crashing, and `hideCursor()` called before the window opens not crashing. `tests/test_graphics.py`'s `TestEventHandlers` gained `test_mouse_button_handler_now_requires_button_argument` (the OLD 2-arg form now rejected) and updated its existing parse/arity/type tests for the new 3-arg signature. Every pre-existing example/test declaring the old 2-argument `on mouseDown`/`on mouseUp` (`examples/graphics.f`, `examples/tic_tac_toe.f`, `README.md`, and every occurrence across `tests/test_codegen.py`, `tests/test_graphics.py`, `tests/test_events_and_graphics.py`, `tests/test_entry_point_and_example.py`, `tests/test_http.py`) updated to the new 3-argument form. Documented in api.md's "Mouse events" section (the numbering convention, a worked `if button == ...` example) and a new `showCursor()`/`hideCursor()` paragraph alongside `enterFullscreen()`/`exitFullscreen()`'s own.

183. `fillAlpha` NOW APPLIES TO `drawImage` TOO (uraikus/festina#78)

A user bug report. The report: `fillAlpha` visibly blends a fill drawn either onto the canvas or directly onto an `img`'s own surface, but two `drawImage` calls under `fillAlpha(0.3)` and `fillAlpha(1.0)` come out pixel-for-pixel identical -- fully opaque either way. The report's own "Ask" was scoped to documentation only (a line noting the limitation); investigated further and fixed at the root instead, since the actual root cause was a small, well-precedented, one-line omission rather than an intentional scoping decision worth documenting as permanent.

**Root cause: `festina_draw_image` was the one draw path in the whole file that never read `g_fill_alpha` at all.** Every other draw operation already carries it -- `festina_set_fill_source`'s `cairo_set_source_rgba(cr, ..., g_fill_alpha)` for an ordinary fill (canvas or an `img`'s own surface, both go through the identical style-state globals, which is exactly why the report's own second repro -- a fill drawn straight onto an `img` -- already worked), and that same function's own `cairo_paint_with_alpha(cr, g_fill_alpha)` for a gradient fill (needed there for the identical underlying reason `drawImage` needed it: `cairo_set_source_surface`/`cairo_set_source` for a pattern has no alpha channel of its own the way `cairo_set_source_rgba` does, so the alpha has to be applied at PAINT time instead of source-setup time). `festina_draw_image` used plain `cairo_paint(cr)` -- unconditional full opacity, `g_fill_alpha` never consulted at all.

**Fix: the identical `cairo_paint_with_alpha` call the gradient-fill code path already uses, right next to it in the same file.** `cairo_paint_with_alpha(cr, 1.0)` is Cairo's own documented equivalent of plain `cairo_paint`, so this is a strict extension with no behavior change for the overwhelmingly common case where `fillAlpha` is never touched -- confirmed by every pre-existing `drawImage` test continuing to pass unchanged. Audited every other `cairo_paint(` call site in the file first to confirm this was the only one that needed it: the rest are all either a transparent clear (`clearCanvas`/`festina_backing_require`/a canvas resize, all deliberately alpha-independent -- clearing is not a styled draw operation), a pure image-to-image copy with no style state involved at all (`festina_image_clip`, `festina_canvas_to_image`/`saveCanvas()`'s no-path form, image resize -- none of these are "draw with the current style" operations, and applying `g_fill_alpha` to any of them would be wrong, not merely unnecessary), or the final backing-surface-to-window blit (`festina_window_present`, which must always be a faithful 1:1 copy of whatever's already been composited, or every earlier alpha blend would double-apply).

**Verified directly, not just reasoned through.** The report's own repro pattern, compiled and run against a real X11 window: a white square drawn under `fillAlpha(0.5)` onto a red background reads back as `(255, 128, 128)` -- a real 50% blend, not a flat opaque white -- while the identical square drawn under `fillAlpha(1.0)` reads back as pure `(255, 255, 255)`, confirming the fix is scoped correctly (an explicit full-opacity call still behaves exactly as before).

**Tests:** new `TestCanvasPathsRenderRealPixels::test_fill_alpha_applies_to_draw_image_too`, mirroring that class's own existing `50% red over white should blend` fill-alpha assertion (`test_paths_transforms_and_gradients_render_correctly`) but for a `drawImage` blit instead of a fill -- reads real pixels back via `xwd` against a live X11 window, not just an IR-pattern check. Documented in api.md's "Gradients and transparency" section: replaced what would have been a documented limitation with a line (and worked example) confirming `fillAlpha` now applies uniformly to every fill AND `drawImage`.

184. `arr[T].sort(cmpFn)` (uraikus/festina#76 item 2)

Requested directly: the first of four items pulled from issue #76's own grab-bag list, the one the report itself calls out as coming up constantly in real game code (depth-sorting a frame's sprites by Y position) with no way to do it short of hand-rolling insertion/selection sort against `arr[T]`'s own push/pop/splice/indexOf.

**A comparator-based sort, `xs.sort(cmpFn)` with `cmpFn:func[T,T]:int` -- JavaScript's/C `qsort()`'s own convention**: negative if the first argument belongs before the second, positive if after, `0` if equal. In place, returns nothing. Checked structurally against `T,T -> int` the same permissive "any func-typed expression" way `blob`/`img`/`aud`'s own `.callback()` already is (claude.md #165/#171) -- not restricted to a bare declared-function name the way `setTimeout`'s older convention is.

**Not plain C `qsort()` -- its comparator signature has no user-data slot at all, and the "portable" fixes aren't.** `qsort_r`/`qsort_s` exist specifically to add one, but glibc's `qsort_r` puts userdata LAST, BSD's puts it FIRST, and Windows' `qsort_s` again differs from both -- three incompatible call shapes to `#ifdef` around for one feature. `festina_array_sort` (runtime/festina_runtime.c, next to the rest of claude.md #96's array helpers) is instead a small hand-rolled bottom-up merge sort whose OWN comparator signature (`int(*)(const void*, const void*, void*)`) carries userdata as a real parameter from the start -- no portability hazard to route around, and STABLE as a free consequence of the merge-sort shape (`<=`, not `<`, in the merge step keeps a tie resolved in favor of the left/earlier run) -- unlike `qsort()`, which makes no stability promise at all. JavaScript's own `Array.prototype.sort` IS stable, and re-sorting a list by a second key after an earlier sort ("score descending, ties broken by name already in place") is exactly the kind of case where that difference would otherwise be a silent surprise.

**Bridging a compile-time-known element type to a runtime-arbitrary comparator function value, without a process-global variable.** `userdata` isn't a payload struct to read something back out of (unlike claude.md #177's `_emit_exec_callback_trampoline`) -- it IS the callback pointer itself. `.sort()`'s comparator argument is evaluated once, at the call site, into an ordinary `ptr` value (first-class function values already ARE bare pointers, claude.md #141), and `festina_array_sort` hands that same pointer to its own comparator argument on every single comparison, unchanged. codegen's new `_emit_sort_comparator_trampoline(elem_type)` generates one small function per DISTINCT element type a program calls `.sort()` on (cached in `self._sort_trampolines`, keyed by `types_mod.type_name(elem_type)` the same way `_array_release_fns` already keys its own per-type helpers) -- it loads `elem_type`'s own LLVM-typed value out of the two raw comparison-slot pointers `festina_array_sort` hands it, makes an indirect call through `userdata` with THAT signature, and truncates the `i64` result down to the `i32` a C comparator returns. One trampoline correctly serves every `.sort()` call site sharing that element type, whatever the comparator's own compile-time shape (a bare function name, a variable, a struct field, ...).

**No ownership work at all in codegen -- the first array method with none.** Unlike `push`/`unshift` (retain-or-copy an incoming element) or `splice(..., insertArr)` (retain-or-copy a whole inserted range, claude.md #130), a sort only ever repositions elements ALREADY inside the same buffer -- nothing is created, nothing changes owner, so there's nothing to retain, copy, or release. The comparator argument itself needs no release either: a `func[T,T]:int` value is a bare function pointer, not a heap-allocated, refcounted Festina value (`_is_refcounted` correctly excludes `FuncType`).

**Verified directly**, not just by construction: ascending/descending `arr[int]`, `arr[float]`, `arr[bool]` (the one-byte element stride, claude.md #97's own bool-specific coverage), a struct element type sorted by one field, empty and single-element arrays (the zero-swap edge cases), and a genuine stability check (two structs with equal sort keys, pushed in a known order, still coming out in that same order afterward) -- plus a 1200-iteration ASan/LeakSanitizer stress run (`tests/stress/sort_churn.f`) hammering both a scalar and a refcounted struct element type through the comparator trampoline repeatedly: zero leaks, zero ASan errors.

**Tests:** new `tests/test_codegen.py::TestArraySort` -- 6 tests, plus `tests/test_leak_stress.py`'s stress suite gained `sort_churn.f`. Documented in api.md's "Growing arrays" section, a new "Sorting: sort(cmpFn)" subsection with a worked struct example (depth-sorting, matching the issue's own motivating case).

185. `drawImage` DESTINATION SIZE AND SOURCE RECT (uraikus/festina#76 item 3)

Requested directly, alongside #184 above, from the same issue #76 grab-bag: the only way to draw an image at a different size than it's stored at used to be `img.resize()`, which mutates in place -- so drawing one stored sprite at two different sizes (the issue's own example: a small palette icon and a full-size stamp from the same generated sprite) meant generating or copying it twice, by hand, every time the size needed to change.

**Two new forms, picked by argument count, alongside the existing `drawImage(img, x, y)`.** `drawImage(img, x, y, w, h)` scales the WHOLE source image to fit a `w`x`h` box at `(x, y)`. `drawImage(img, sx, sy, sw, sh, dx, dy, dw, dh)` is the full canvas-style form -- a SOURCE rect cut out of the image, scaled to fit a DESTINATION rect -- the variable-size-paint-brush-from-one-fixed-size-source case the issue also named. All three share the first argument's image type and are otherwise unambiguous by length alone (3 vs. 5 vs. 9), the identical mechanism claude.md #133's `drawRect`/`drawPixel` optional-trailing-color forms already established (`_BUILTIN_SIGNATURE_ALTERNATES`, matched by `len(expr.args)`) -- `drawImage`'s own fixed 3-argument `_BUILTIN_SIGNATURES` entry moved there alongside the two new ones, the same migration `drawRect`/`drawPixel` themselves already went through.

**A plain scale-then-paint, not a resample into a fresh surface.** `festina_draw_image_scaled` (runtime/festina_runtime_graphics.c) translates to `(x, y)`, scales by `w`/`src_w` and `h`/`src_h`, then paints -- Cairo's own source-pattern filtering (`CAIRO_FILTER_GOOD`, an image pattern's default) does the interpolation, so this needs no image processing of its own, and costs nothing extra when `w`/`h` happen to already match the source size. `festina_draw_image_region` additionally clips to the DESTINATION rect first (`cairo_rectangle` + `cairo_clip`, saved/restored around the call) before translating/scaling/painting with the source offset by `(-sx, -sy)` -- clipping to the destination, not the source, is what keeps a source rect reaching past the image's own edge from spilling paint outside the intended box; that overflow instead behaves exactly like `festina_image_clip`'s own established "the overlap is copied, the rest stays transparent" rule. Both share the identical `cairo_paint_with_alpha(cr, g_fill_alpha)` claude.md #183 just gave plain `drawImage`, so `fillAlpha` applies uniformly across all three forms with no extra work.

**Verified directly against real composited pixels**, not just IR-pattern-matched: a 10x10 solid-blue image scaled to fill a 40x40 box reads back blue well inside the box and unmodified background well outside it; a two-color (blue/green) source image, with only its green half cut out via a source rect and scaled into an unrelated destination rect elsewhere on the canvas, reads back green at the destination and the original background everywhere else -- confirming the source-rect clipping is real, not merely that SOME image got drawn somewhere. Both tests explicitly pin the source image's own size with `setClientWidth`/`setClientHeight` before `saveCanvas()`, rather than relying on the window's default size -- `saveCanvas()` snapshots the WHOLE canvas, so an unconstrained size would leave the drawn shape as a small opaque corner of an otherwise much larger, mostly-transparent image, silently changing what "the whole image, scaled" actually means.

**Tests:** two new pixel-level tests in `TestCanvasPathsRenderRealPixels` (`test_draw_image_with_destination_size_scales_the_whole_image`, `test_draw_image_with_source_and_dest_rects`) plus an arity-rejection test for the three invalid argument counts in between the valid ones (4, 6, 8). Documented in api.md's "Graphics" section: the code block gained both new call forms, and a new paragraph explains all three, cross-referencing `.clip()`'s own edge behavior for the source-rect-past-the-edge case.

186. `map[T].keys()`/`.values()` (uraikus/festina#76 item 7)

Requested directly, alongside #184/#185 above, conditioned on "if no performance hit" -- the third of four items pulled from issue #76. The issue's own complaint: `.forEach()`'s callback is bare/no-closures (claude.md #72, itself an intentional consequence of this language having no closures at all), so every `forEach` call site needing to collect matching entries had to promote its own "parameters" and "results" to extra GLOBAL variables purely so the callback could reach them -- happened repeatedly in the issue's own tile-game codebase.

**Judged a genuine "no performance hit": a single O(capacity) scan, the exact same cost `.forEach()` already pays for the identical traversal, just building an array instead of invoking a callback per entry.** No new persistent overhead, no new per-map bookkeeping, nothing paid by a program that never calls either method. This is the deciding difference from item 9 (see #187 below): `.keys()`/`.values()` need no new heap-managed TYPE, no new ownership/lifetime rules, and no new call-site machinery beyond what already exists for `.forEach()`/`.push()` -- purely a new way to consume data this runtime was already computing internally.

**`festina_map_keys`/`festina_map_values` (runtime/festina_runtime.c) share `.forEach()`'s own traversal** (scan by CAPACITY, not count, a slot live when its key is neither NULL -- never used -- nor the tombstone sentinel) but write into a plain array instead of calling back into Festina code. `dst` is always a header codegen already allocated fresh via `_emit_fresh_heap_header` (refcount=1, zeroed) -- both functions only fill in its `length`/`data` fields, the exact division of labor `festina_array_splice`'s own `dst` output parameter already established, so no new allocation-ownership convention needed.

**`.keys()` is trivial -- always `arr[text]`, regardless of `T`** -- each live key is `festina_text_own`'d into a fresh, independent copy (never the map's own internal `strdup`'d pointer, which the map keeps managing on its own: deleting a key, or freeing the whole map, must not retroactively invalidate an already-returned snapshot). `.values()` is where `T` actually matters: `elem_size` (1 for bool, 8 for everything else, exactly `_elem_size`'s own domain) picks the write width for the destination array's own slot convention, and `is_refcounted`/`is_text` (both compile-time known from `T`, passed from codegen the same way `festina_array_index_of`'s own `is_text` flag already is) pick the ownership operation -- a struct/arr/map/img/aud/regex/blob value is RETAINED (the map keeps its own live reference to the identical pointer, so without this the returned array and the map would silently share ownership, and whichever released first would leave the other dangling -- confirmed directly: freeing the source map immediately after `.values()` leaves every collected struct/text value completely intact), a text value is COPIED (`festina_text_own`, text having no shared representation to retain), anything else needs neither.

**A plain, independent SNAPSHOT, not a live view** -- collected once, at the call. A `delete` or a new key on the source map afterward never retroactively changes what was already returned, confirmed directly by a dedicated test. This is the same semantics JavaScript's own `Object.keys()`/`Object.values()` have, and the natural reading of "here is an array" rather than "here is a window onto the map."

**Verified directly**, not just by construction: an int-valued map's `.keys()` (content-checked via `.indexOf()`, since bucket order is unspecified) and `.values()` (sorted afterward via #184's new `.sort()`, landed together in this same round); an empty map answering two empty arrays; a snapshot outliving a `delete` on the source; a text-valued map's `.values()` surviving `free`ing the source map; a struct-valued map's `.values()` likewise; and `arr[bool]`'s own one-byte element stride specifically (claude.md #97's own bool-specific coverage extended here) -- plus a 1200-iteration ASan/LeakSanitizer stress run (`tests/stress/map_keys_values_churn.f`) covering a scalar, a text, and a struct value type together, each iteration also freeing/deleting the source map right after collecting: zero leaks, zero ASan errors.

**Tests:** new `tests/test_codegen.py::TestMapKeysAndValues` -- 7 tests, plus `tests/test_leak_stress.py`'s stress suite gained `map_keys_values_churn.f`. Documented in api.md's map section, alongside `.forEach()`'s own worked example.

187. WHY `func`-BOUND-ARGUMENT CALLBACKS (uraikus/festina#76 item 9) WEREN'T ADDED

Requested conditionally, alongside #184/#185/#186 above: "add ... 9 (if no performance hit)". Investigated and judged NOT to clear that bar -- not implemented, on that basis specifically, not because the underlying request is unreasonable.

**What was asked: a callback type that can carry a fixed set of arguments BOUND at the point the value is created**, so a generic helper written against a fixed-arity callback type (the issue's own example: `img func generateSprite(w, h, drawFn:func[]:void)`, which calls `drawFn()` with zero arguments) could still receive a per-call-site-PARAMETERIZED function -- "the first N arguments are bound when the value is created, the rest supplied by the caller" -- explicitly scoped short of real closures, which this language deliberately doesn't have (claude.md #72's own `.forEach()` restriction is the direct consequence of that same design line).

**Why every real implementation of this needs a NEW heap-managed value, not just a new way to read an existing one.** Every `func[...]:...`-typed value in this language today (claude.md #141) is a bare, non-owning `ptr` -- literally the LLVM address of a `define`d function, no allocation, no refcount, indistinguishable in cost from calling any other function pointer. A BOUND value cannot be that: calling it with zero arguments has to somehow still reach the underlying multi-argument function WITH the bound arguments supplied, which means the bound arguments have to be stored SOMEWHERE reachable from the callback pointer at call time. Two shapes exist, and neither is free:
- **A capture box** (a small heap-allocated struct holding the bound argument values plus the real function pointer, with a codegen-generated trampoline as the actual `func[]:void`-shaped value, reading the box back out): this is a real ALLOCATION on every `.bind(...)`-like call, a genuinely new heap-managed value needing its own lifetime rules (when is a bound value freed? does passing one to `generateSprite` above transfer ownership, the same as any other refcounted argument today, or does it need to survive past the call for a LATER re-invocation? struct/arr/map fields, array elements -- is a bound callback storable in any of those, and if so what does aliasing one even mean?) -- none of which this language's existing "func values are plain pointers" model has ANY precedent for answering.
- **Compile-time-constant-only binding** (no heap allocation, a distinct trampoline generated per unique constant combination -- the identical zero-allocation approach claude.md #184's own `.sort()` comparator trampoline uses) avoids the allocation, but doesn't answer the issue's own motivating case at all: "a sprite sheet, where each cell needs its own `(row, col, offsetX, offsetY)`" is squarely a LOOP-VARYING runtime value, not a handful of distinct compile-time literals -- a constant-only version would need one freshly-generated trampoline function per sprite-sheet cell, unrolled at compile time, which isn't what "bind the current loop variable" means at all.

**The capture-box shape is the only one that actually serves the request, and it fails "no performance hit" on two separate, compounding counts: a real heap allocation per bound callback value (something a plain `func[]:void` today costs literally nothing for), and a genuinely new subsystem's worth of design and implementation risk** (a new heap-managed value kind, its own ownership/lifetime/aliasing rules threaded through every existing call site that currently assumes "a func value is a bare, non-owning pointer" -- struct fields, array/map elements, `.forEach()`'s own trampoline, every builtin callback from `setTimeout` through `.sort()`'s own brand-new one two entries above) to introduce for a single, narrower use case (reusing one generic drawing helper across parameter counts) that a caller can already work around today by writing N differently-shaped helper functions, or by threading the extra parameters through a struct argument instead of relying on binding.

See #188 below for issue #76's remaining items (1, 4, 5, 6, 8), analyzed the same way -- pros and cons written up, none implemented, matching what was actually asked for those.

188. `Math.floorDiv`, `blankImage(w,h)`, `row.rowid`, CANVAS-ALPHA DOC NOTE, AND drawRect/drawCircle BORDER-COLOR OVERRIDE (uraikus/festina#76 items 1, 4, 5, 6, 8)

Requested directly: "implement 1, 4, 5, and 8" from issue #76's own remaining grab-bag, all previously analyzed as pros/cons-only in claude.md's own prior round rather than built. Item 6 (the canvas-alpha documentation note) is included too -- it was the one item explicitly framed, in the issue itself, as a pure documentation fix with no implementation risk at all, and was done alongside these as a genuinely free addition rather than left for a future round; everything else here matches exactly what was asked.

**1 -- `Math.floorDiv(a:int, b:int):int`, floor-toward-negative-infinity integer division**, closing the gap the issue itself named: `/` always promotes to float (a deliberate, documented safety net -- claude.md's own reasoning stands unchanged), so every tile/grid calculation needed `Math.floor(a / b)` spelled out by hand. Given the choice this repo's own prior pros/cons write-up laid out (a new `//` operator vs. a `Math.*` builtin), the builtin won on risk: it fits `Math`'s own existing "(int,int)->int"/"(float,float)->float" family shape with zero grammar/lexer/parser changes, in its own new `MATH_INT2_FUNCTIONS` set (kept separate from every other `Math.*` check, which all assume FLOAT arguments). **Not built on `sdiv`/`select` alone** -- `sdiv`/`srem`'s own truncate-toward-zero disagrees with floor division exactly when the operands' signs differ and the division isn't exact (`-7 sdiv 2` is `-3`, but `floor(-7/2)` is `-4`), so `_emit_floor_div` (codegen.py) computes both, then adjusts by one exactly when the remainder is nonzero AND its sign differs from the divisor's -- Python's `//`/Java's `Math.floorDiv` use the identical rule. Shares claude.md #57's own by-zero convention (real control flow, mirroring `_emit_divmod`'s own zero-check branch, since `sdiv`/`srem` by zero is undefined behavior at the hardware level) rather than inventing a second one just for this function.

**4 -- `blankImage(w, h): img`, a fresh, fully-transparent image with nothing to derive it from.** Every existing way to get an `img` -- `.clip()`, `.resize()`, `saveCanvas()` -- copies FROM something that already exists; the issue's own workaround (bouncing through the real canvas: `clearCanvas(); ...; saveCanvas()`) was both indirect and, unlike this, touched the actual on-screen canvas along the way. `festina_blank_image` (runtime/festina_runtime_graphics.c) is two lines: `cairo_image_surface_create` already zero-initializes every byte (Cairo's own documented guarantee), which for ARGB32 IS fully transparent, so there is nothing else to paint. A plain builtin function (`blankImage(w, h)`, not an `img.blank(w, h)` static method) -- this language has no `Type.staticMethod()` syntax anywhere outside the hardcoded `Math` namespace, so the free-function shape `saveCanvas()`/the since-removed `loadImage()` already established (claude.md #37, #109) is the one that needed no new grammar at all. Composes with every other `img` operation immediately: `.clip()`, `.resize()`, `drawRect`/`drawCircle`/`drawText`/`drawImage` (both canvas-level and as `img` methods) all just work on the result, since a blank image is exactly as real an `img` as any other.

**5 -- `row.rowid`, a table row's own SQLite identity, read-only.** SQLite already computes a `rowid` for free on every ordinary (non-`WITHOUT ROWID`) table; this exposes it rather than inventing a new schema concept, closing the issue's own "upserting by key means hand-tracking the next id, or a manual DELETE-then-INSERT" complaint. **Deliberately NOT threaded through `_table_arrays`, the shared names/types globals both a query's row-collection AND `festina_sync_table`'s own CREATE TABLE/ALTER TABLE DDL read** -- appending a synthetic `rowid` column there would make schema sync try to `ALTER TABLE t ADD COLUMN rowid INTEGER`, which SQLite outright rejects (`rowid` is a reserved, already-implicit column). Instead, `festina_sqlite_collect_rows` gained one new trailing parameter, `want_rowid` (true only for a TableType row's own collection, `_emit_sqlite_collect` -- always false for a struct query target's collection, `_emit_sqlite_collect_struct`, which has no rowid concept at all): when true, one more hidden slot is allocated PAST the existing presence-mask slot, filled from a `rowid`-named RESULT column found the identical by-name way every declared column already is -- so `col_count`/`col_names`/`col_types` (and therefore `festina_row_undefined`'s own presence-mask offset) are completely untouched either way. `.rowid` only ever populates when the query's own SQL explicitly selects a column named `rowid` (`SELECT rowid, ...` -- a bare `SELECT *` does NOT implicitly include it), reading as int's own null otherwise, the identical "the query never mentioned this" signal `.undefined()` already gives an ordinary column. Read-only (assigning is a compile error, the same placement/reasoning `.length`/http's own fields/url's own fields already established) -- a row is a plain in-memory snapshot regardless, so mutating a column's VALUE in memory has never meant a live database UPDATE, and `.rowid` mutated in memory would mean even less.

**6 -- one sentence** next to api.md's existing "a fresh or cleared canvas is transparent, not white" claim, clarifying that this is only true OFF-screen: `render()` composites onto an ordinary opaque on-screen window, so a transparent region reads back as solid white once on screen, even though the identical content saved via `saveCanvas()` still carries real alpha. Distinguishes two very different bugs that otherwise look pixel-identical on screen -- "my background never drew" vs. "my background drew transparent, which paints as opaque white."

**8 -- a further optional trailing `borderColor` on `drawRect`/`drawCircle` (and their `img`-method equivalents), overriding it for that one call only.** Directly closes the "global, mutable draw style silently leaks between unrelated shapes" gap the issue reports twice happening in real code (a UI highlight color bleeding onto palette swatches; a sprite's border color bleeding between procedurally generated frames) -- `saveState()`/`restoreState()` already existed as the general fix, but nothing prompted reaching for them until a color visibly bled. `festina_fill_and_border_with_colors` (runtime/festina_runtime_graphics.c) is the direct extension of `festina_fill_and_border_with_color`'s own existing fill-only save/restore pattern (claude.md #133) to ALSO save/restore/override the border globals (`g_border_r/g/b`, `g_border_set`) around the identical `festina_fill_and_border` call both share -- `border_color < 0` means no border for this one call, matching `borderColor('none')`'s own encoding, and (matching the fill-only override's own precedent) deliberately does NOT also touch `g_line_width`: a border color given while `lineWidth()` is still 0 draws nothing, the same "nothing to stroke" case plain `borderColor()` already has. **`drawCircle` gains BOTH trailing forms here, newly** -- unlike `drawRect`/`drawPixel`, it previously had no per-call color override AT ALL (claude.md #133 only ever migrated `drawRect`/`drawPixel` into the optional-trailing-color family); giving it the identical fill-only AND fill+border shapes as `drawRect` is what makes "the same way" in the issue's own wording literally true, not merely close. `drawPixel` is deliberately UNCHANGED -- a 1x1 shape has nothing meaningful to stroke, the same reasoning that already kept it border-free.

**Every one of the six new/extended `_BUILTIN_SIGNATURE_ALTERNATES` and `_BUILTIN_SIGNATURES` entries, and both duplicated free-function/img-method dispatch dicts in codegen.py, were updated together** -- `drawRect`/`drawCircle`'s own free-function forms (semantic.py's top-level alternates dict) and their SEPARATE `img.drawRect`/`img.drawCircle` forms (a second, independently-maintained alternates dict inside the Member-call branch, claude.md #134) needed the identical new shapes in both places, the same duplication `drawPixel`'s own claude.md #133 addition already had to cross.

**Verified directly against real composited pixels for the visual ones** (`Math.floorDiv`/`blankImage`/`.rowid` verified via `log()` output and a real sqlite round trip instead, having no visual component): a border color override read back at a few pixels in from the stroke's own antialiased edge (not directly on it, which reads as a blend of both colors), confirming the override wins at the border, the fill override wins at the center, and neither leaks into a subsequent plain `drawRect()`/`drawCircle()` call reading the ordinary `fillStyle()`/`borderColor()` state instead. `blankImage`'s own transparency confirmed via a real PNG round trip (`saveCanvas`'s own alpha-preserving writer, claude.md #101), not just reasoned about from `cairo_image_surface_create`'s documented zero-initialization.

**Tests:** new `tests/test_codegen.py::TestMathFileAndTime`'s own `Math.floorDiv` section (4 tests), `TestBlankImage` (5 tests), `TestRowRowid` (5 tests), `TestDrawRectAndCircleBorderColorOverride` (5 tests) -- 19 new tests total. Documented in api.md: a new `Math.floorDiv` paragraph in the numeric-coercion section, a `blankImage`/border-color paragraph in "Graphics" (plus both in the Graphics code block's own worked example), a new "`row.rowid`" subsection under "Partial queries and `undefined()`", and the canvas-alpha clarifying sentence.

189. `getPixelColor(x,y)`, AND `img.getPixelColor(x,y)`

Requested directly, with a worked color-picker example (`on mouse` -- see below for a real mismatch the request's own example had): "Add a getPixelColor(x:int, y:int) function ... Also allow the .getPixelColor method to the img type."

**Reads a pixel back off the canvas's own offscreen backing store (or, for the `img` method, an image's own surface) as a packed `color`** -- the exact reverse of `pack_color`'s own `(r<<16)|(g<<8)|b` (claude.md #91), sharing one C helper (`festina_pixel_color_from_surface`, runtime/festina_runtime_graphics.c) between both entry points (`festina_get_pixel_color`/`festina_image_get_pixel_color`) since the only difference is which surface to read. `cairo_surface_flush` first -- direct pixel access needs every pending drawing operation actually committed to memory, the identical Cairo contract claude.md #178's own mac/Windows present-path flush already had to satisfy, just for the offscreen surface here instead of a window's.

**Cairo's ARGB32 stores PREMULTIPLIED alpha, and undoing that is the one genuinely nontrivial part.** A pixel painted at `fillAlpha(0.5)` stores roughly half-brightness R/G/B, not the real paint color scaled down -- reading it back raw would answer a darkened color, not the one `fillStyle`/`fillAlpha` actually asked for. Dividing back out by alpha (rounding to nearest, not truncating) is what makes `getPixelColor` answer the color that was PAINTED. A fully transparent pixel (alpha 0 -- nothing ever painted there, or painted then cleared) has no real color to recover at all: premultiplied R/G/B are always 0/0/0 regardless of what was last set there, so this reads it as `color`'s own `null`/'none' sentinel (`-1`) rather than a meaningless black. Out-of-bounds coordinates (and a `null`/never-assigned `img` receiver) answer the same `-1`.

**Reusing `-1` for `null` here (rather than inventing a second reserved value) uncovered and fixed a REAL, pre-existing gap: `color == null` was never actually valid IR before this.** `_emit_value_for`'s own `ColorType`/`FontType` branch intercepts EVERY node reaching it when the expected type is `color` -- including a bare `ast.NullLit` -- and, having no case for one, fell through to `_emit_expr(node, ...)` on the raw `NullLit`, which (like every other position that's never given `color` as its expected type) produces the generic LLVM `null` keyword. `null` is only valid IR for a POINTER type, and `color` is `i64` (claude.md #91) -- so `x == null` on any `color`-typed value was **already broken, unconditionally**, for any color-typed program that tried it, entirely independent of this feature. `getPixelColor`'s own documented "reads as `null` where there's nothing painted" contract is what actually exercised the path and surfaced it. Fixed at the source: a `NullLit` reaching the `ColorType` branch now short-circuits to `-1` immediately, ahead of the "must come from a literal" check that branch otherwise applies (a bare `null` was never a text literal to resolve in the first place). `-1` specifically because it's not a second, newly-invented sentinel -- it's the SAME value `_zero_value` already gives an uninitialized `color` global/field (claude.md #91's own "an unset colour is 'none', not 0 -- 0 is a real colour, opaque black" reasoning), so `color == null` and `color == none` are now simply the same comparison, with nothing new to keep in sync.

**The request's own worked example named a non-existent event, `on mouseMove` -- the real continuous-movement handler is `on mouse(x:int, y:int)` (claude.md #40).** An unrecognized event name is not a compile error in this language (`analyze_event_handler` leaves it unconstrained, so a program can freely name a handler for planned-but-not-yet-real future events) -- so `on mouseMove(...)` would have compiled cleanly and then never fired, a genuinely nasty silent-dead-code trap for exactly the reason this is worth flagging rather than quietly "fixing" the request's own example without saying so. Verified end-to-end under a real X11 window with the CORRECT event name (`on mouse`) instead: moving the pointer over a red-filled canvas fires the handler, and `getPixelColor(x, y) == red` inside it reads back true.

**Tests:** new `tests/test_codegen.py::TestGetPixelColor` -- 5 tests (a painted pixel, unpainted/out-of-bounds reading as null, premultiplied-alpha unpacking under `fillAlpha`, the `img` method, and arity/type rejection), needing no display (reads the offscreen backing store directly, the same `DISPLAY=''` reasoning `saveCanvas()`'s own tests already establish) -- plus a real X11 end-to-end check (moving the mouse over a filled canvas, confirming `on mouse` + `getPixelColor` together read back the right color) run manually during this round, not left in the suite (redundant with the `DISPLAY`-free coverage once the feature itself was confirmed working end to end). Documented in api.md's Graphics section, with the color-picker worked example spelled using the real `on mouse` event name.

190. `.toText()` JSON-RENDERING PERFORMANCE (two optimizations, no behavior change)

Requested directly, as a question first ("Are there optimizations that can be made for .toText() for json serialized types") -- answered with two concrete candidates and their expected win, then implemented on confirmation. Pure internal optimization: `_json_fn_for`'s generated IR walks the identical struct/table/array/map shapes it always has, in the identical order, producing byte-for-byte identical output -- every existing JSON-rendering test (claude.md #114/#115) passes unchanged, confirming this.

**1 -- `festina_sb_append_n`, a length-aware string-builder append, replacing the runtime `strlen()` rescan on every codegen-emitted literal.** Every JSON-punctuation and field-key append `_json_fn_for` generates (`{"`, `,"`, `":`, `}`, `[`, `]`, a struct field's own baked `"name":` prefix -- 15 call sites total) comes from a compile-time `string_const()`, whose exact byte length is already known in Python at codegen time -- the SAME count `_encode_c_string` computes for the global's own storage. The plain `festina_sb_append(sb, s)` runtime function has no way to know that; it calls `strlen(s)` itself, rescanning a string the compiler had already measured and then thrown the answer away. New codegen helper `_emit_sb_append_const(self, body, sb, text)` computes `n = len(text.encode("utf-8"))` in Python and emits a call to the new `festina_sb_append_n(sb, s, len)` instead, skipping the rescan entirely. `festina_sb_append` itself is now a thin wrapper over a shared `festina_sb_append_bytes(sb, s, n)` helper (grow-then-`memcpy`-then-NUL-terminate) that both it and the new `_n` form call -- no behavior change to any EXISTING caller of plain `festina_sb_append` (dynamic strings whose length genuinely isn't known ahead of time, e.g. a field's own text VALUE, still call it exactly as before).

**2 -- run-scanning JSON string escaping, replacing a byte-at-a-time switch/`snprintf`/`strlen`/`memcpy` sequence run unconditionally for every byte of every text field, regardless of whether that byte needed escaping at all.** `festina_sb_append_json_text` now scans FORWARD for a "safe run" -- consecutive bytes that are all `>= 0x20` and neither `"` nor `\` (a run happily spans valid UTF-8 multi-byte sequences too, since every continuation byte is `>= 0x20` by construction) -- and bulk-copies the whole run via `festina_sb_append_bytes` in one call, falling back to the original per-character escape logic (`\"`, `\\`, `\n`, `\r`, `\t`, `\uXXXX` for any other control byte) only at an actual escape-needing byte. Most real text (names, sentences, UTF-8 prose) is almost entirely safe bytes with the occasional escape, so this turns what used to be N small appends (one function-call's worth of overhead each) into a handful of large ones.

**Why `-O2` doesn't already give you this for free.** The generated program and `runtime/festina_runtime.c` are compiled as SEPARATE translation units with no `-flto` (`festina/cli.py`'s own actual build invocation) -- so the compiler can never see, across that boundary, that a given `festina_sb_append` call site's `s` argument is a global whose length it could fold `strlen()` down to at compile time. `-O2` optimizes each translation unit well on its own terms; it cannot optimize across a boundary it never gets to see through.

**Measured, not just reasoned about: a controlled before/after benchmark, `git stash`-isolated so both runs compiled the identical benchmark program against only the runtime changing.** A struct (`id:int, name:text` [template literal], `description:text` [containing real JSON-escape-needing content -- quotes, a newline, a tab], `price:float`, `inStock:bool`, `tags:arr[text]`) rendered via `.toText()` in a tight loop (freeing the result each iteration), timed with `now()`. At 100,000 iterations, median of 5 runs: **~215ms before, ~85ms after -- roughly a 2.5x speedup** for this text-heavy struct-rendering workload (a number-heavy struct with little text to escape would see a smaller win, dominated more by #1 than #2).

**A genuine, unrelated, pre-existing bug turned up while benchmarking at higher iteration counts, deliberately NOT investigated or fixed here.** Above roughly 150,000-300,000 loop iterations, a program allocating a fresh struct (with an `arr[text]` field and template-literal text fields) every iteration segfaults -- confirmed independent of this round's changes both ways: it reproduces identically with `.toText()` removed from the loop entirely, and a plain int-arithmetic-only loop at 300,000 iterations does not crash at all, isolating it to struct/array allocation-at-scale rather than anything JSON-rendering touches. Left as a known issue rather than chased down here, to avoid scope creep into a separate, likely allocator/lifetime bug this optimization task didn't ask for.

**Verified:** the full existing JSON-rendering suite (`TestJsonRendering`, now 10 tests -- a new `test_escape_run_boundaries_render_correctly` added specifically for the run-scanning rewrite's own edge cases: a string starting AND ending on an escape-needing byte with no leading/trailing safe run, a string of NOTHING but escape-needing bytes back-to-back so every "run" the scanner finds is zero-length, and an empty string) all pass unchanged -- byte-for-byte identical output before and after. A new 800-iteration ASan/LeakSanitizer stress test (`tests/stress/json_render_churn.f`) covers every shape `_json_fn_for` generates a walker for (struct, nested struct, empty struct, `arr[T]`, `map[T]`, a table row) with text needing real escaping, including multi-byte UTF-8 straddling run boundaries: zero leaks, zero ASan errors.

**Tests:** `tests/test_codegen.py::TestJsonRendering::test_escape_run_boundaries_render_correctly` (new), plus `tests/test_leak_stress.py`'s stress suite gained `json_render_churn.f`. No `api.md` changes -- `.toText()`'s documented behavior is unchanged, only its cost.

191. LOOP-BODY ALLOCAS GREW THE STACK EVERY ITERATION -- THE #190 SEGFAULT, ROOT-CAUSED AND FIXED

The bug #190 flagged-but-deferred (a loop allocating a struct with an `arr[text]` field and template-literal text fields segfaulting at ~150,000-300,000 iterations, with completely FLAT heap usage) fell squarely into this round's "full code review, fix bugs" request, and its cause turned out to be foundational: **codegen emitted `alloca` instructions at their declaration sites -- including inside loop bodies -- on the belief, written down twice (the module docstring and the VarDecl stack-allocation comment), that "LLVM's alloca reserves a single fixed address for the whole enclosing function regardless of which basic block textually contains it." That belief is false.** Only entry-block allocas behave that way. An alloca whose instruction EXECUTES inside a loop body allocates NEW stack space on every execution, reclaimed only at function return -- so every iteration of `while ... { Item it ... }` pushed the struct's storage (~56 bytes), its pointer slot, and every per-statement scratch temporary, forever. ~64+ bytes/iteration against an 8MB stack lands the crash exactly in the observed 150k-300k window. Confirmed three independent ways: ASan pinpointed `stack-overflow` (not any heap error) in `__festina_main`; the runtime-reviewer's minimal 48-byte-alloca IR loop crashed at 300k and not 170k (8388608/48 = ~175k); and RSS sampling showed flat ~4.6MB heap right up to the crash.

**The fix is a final IR pass, `_hoist_allocas_to_entry` (codegen.py), applied to the whole joined module in `generate()`:** every static `alloca` line in every emitted function moves to the top of that function's entry block -- one slot per declaration site per CALL, genuinely reused each iteration, which is exactly what clang itself emits for a C local declared inside a loop. A single application point (the final module text) rather than edits at the ~30 individual alloca-emitting call sites, so no future site can reintroduce the bug by forgetting a convention. Dynamic allocas (a runtime element-count operand -- none are emitted today) are deliberately left in place by the pass's own guard, since moving one would change how much stack a single execution reserves.

**Why hoisting is semantics-preserving here, specifically:** every slot this generator emits is explicitly stored before it is read AT ITS DECLARATION SITE (the `store %struct.Item zeroinitializer` and friends stay exactly where they were, so a loop-body struct is still re-zeroed every iteration -- LLVM allocas are undef-initialized anyway, so no code could ever have soundly relied on a fresh alloca's contents), and no slot's address outlives its scope (escape_analysis is precisely what decides stack-vs-heap storage for struct/arr/map locals; an address that escaped its iteration would already have been dangling after the function returned). It also HARDENS the sjlj try/catch path as a side effect: `llvm.eh.sjlj.setjmp` records the stack pointer at try entry and an unwind restores it, so a slot alloca'd INSIDE a try body used to sit below the restored SP after a catch; now every slot predates the save.

**One existing test had asserted the bug as intended behavior** -- `test_loop_local_struct_is_stack_allocated_and_reused_across_iterations` required the alloca to sit inside the loop body, its comment citing the same false one-fixed-address belief. Its INTENT (one reused slot, re-zeroed per iteration) is exactly what the fix delivers, so the test was corrected to assert the alloca in the entry block, no alloca in the loop body, and the zeroinitializer store still inside it.

**Tests:** the corrected IR-shape test above, plus a new end-to-end regression (`test_a_long_running_loop_declaring_locals_does_not_grow_the_stack`) running the original crashing shape for 500,000 iterations -- previously dead by ~300k, now completing in a fixed-size frame (verified separately to 3,000,000 iterations at ~2.3MB peak RSS during diagnosis). Full suite green; the ASan/LeakSanitizer stress suite unchanged and clean.

**One behavior shift worth naming:** an uninitialized scalar local declared inside a loop body (`int x` with no initializer, used before assignment) now reads the PREVIOUS iteration's value rather than fresh stack garbage, because the slot is reused. Reading an uninitialized local is undefined either way -- nothing defined changed -- but the specific garbage differs. (A struct/arr/map local is unaffected: its zeroinitializer store stays at the declaration site and re-runs every iteration.)

192. CODE-REVIEW ROUND, PART 1: RUNTIME MEMORY-SAFETY AND SECURITY FIXES

A full-codebase review (the same "look for and fix bugs" request that produced #191) run as several parallel focused passes over the C runtime, the compiler frontend, and codegen. This entry collects the CONFIRMED **runtime C** fixes; #193 collects the frontend type-checking holes and #194 the codegen ownership bugs found in the same round. Each was traced to a concrete failure, not pattern-matched.

**Two remotely-triggerable denial-of-service bugs in the HTTP server, both from an unchecked attacker-controlled length feeding size arithmetic (`runtime/festina_runtime_http.c`):**
- **Chunked `chunk-size` overflow → infinite loop.** `festina_chunk_decode_step` accepted a chunk-size line of up to 16 hex digits (nearly 2^64) with no cap. A value like `fffffffffffffffe` made `data_start + chunk_size + 2` wrap below `len` (passing the "wait for the rest" guard) and drove the buffer-growth loop's `new_cap *= 2` to overflow to 0 -- an infinite loop that hangs the whole single-threaded server on ONE unauthenticated request. The identical decoder runs client-side (`req.send()` parsing a response), so a malicious server could hang a fetching client too. Fixed by rejecting `chunk_size > FESTINA_HTTP_MAX_BUFFER` (the 8MB cap every other body path already enforces) the moment it's parsed.
- **WebSocket 64-bit frame-length overflow → process abort.** `festina_ws_try_parse_frame` read an attacker's 64-bit payload length and used it in `pos + len` (wraps below `buf_len`, bypassing the "payload not fully arrived" guard) and then `malloc((size_t)len)` -- a ~16-exabyte request that fails and `festina_fail`s the process. One crafted frame killed any server accepting WebSocket upgrades. Fixed by rejecting `len > FESTINA_HTTP_MAX_BUFFER` before either use, tearing the connection down the same way every other malformed-frame path already does.

**A stack-overflow-via-recursion in the JSON parser (`runtime/festina_runtime.c`).** `festina_json_skip_value` -- used to skip an unknown struct field's value during `.toStruct()` -- recurses one C frame per `{`/`[` with no depth limit, so hostile input like `{"x":[[[[...` (reachable through `req.toStruct()` on a network body) overflowed the stack and SIGSEGV'd instead of throwing the catchable error this parser otherwise guarantees. Fixed with a depth counter on the cursor, capped at `FESTINA_JSON_MAX_DEPTH` (1000, far past any real document, well short of the stack) -- past it, the same catchable throw every other malformed input gets.

**A silent integer-precision bug in JSON int parsing (`runtime/festina_runtime.c`).** `festina_json_read_int` routed every integer field through the `double` `festina_json_parse_number` returns, so any `|n| > 2^53` silently lost low bits -- and the specific value `INT64_MAX` rounds to 2^63, whose `double`->`int64` conversion is UB landing on `INT64_MIN`, which is exactly `festina_null_int()`: a valid max-int field read back as **null**. Fixed by re-parsing an integer-shaped token (no `.`/`e`/`E`) directly with `strtoll`, falling back to the double only for genuinely fractional/exponent tokens. Verified: `9223372036854775807`, `-9223372036854775808`, and `9007199254740993` (2^53+1) all now round-trip exactly.

**A finite-double render bug (`runtime/festina_runtime.c`).** `festina_sb_append_json_float`'s NaN/Infinity guard was `v > 1.7e308`, a hand-typed literal SHORT of `DBL_MAX` (~1.7977e308), so a legitimate finite double in `(1.7e308, DBL_MAX]` rendered as `null`. Fixed to `v > DBL_MAX` (via a new `<float.h>` include -- header-only, no link cost); infinity is the only value strictly past `DBL_MAX`, so NaN and the two infinities still render `null` and every finite double renders as itself.

**A per-failed-request leak of up to 8MB in the fetch client (`runtime/festina_runtime_http.c`).** `festina_parse_http_response` throws (catchably) on a short or malformed response -- a realistic dropped-connection case a program catches and retries -- and that throw unwound past the caller's `free(resp_data)`, leaking the entire read buffer every time; in the async callback path, once per failed background fetch in a polling loop. Fixed by transferring ownership of the buffer into the parse function, which now frees it on every exit path (all three throws, the chunked early return, and the normal end -- bodies are always copied out first).

**A leak of the half-built URL value on parseURL's invalid-port throw (`runtime/festina_runtime.c`).** `festina_parse_url` throws (catchably) on a bad port after allocating `protocol`/`username`/`password`/`hostname` and the value itself -- leaking ~5 allocations per bad port, unbounded in a `try`-wrapped validation loop. Fixed by freeing the partial value before the throw (pathname/hash/search-params are still NULL from `calloc`, so `free(NULL)` covers them).

**Two graphics/audio robustness fixes:**
- **`img.getPixelColor()` on a JPEG always returned `none` (`runtime/festina_runtime_graphics.c`).** A JPEG loads as a `CAIRO_FORMAT_RGB24` surface -- a 32-bit pixel whose top byte is unused and stored as 0, NOT alpha. `festina_pixel_color_from_surface` read that top byte as alpha, saw 0, and returned the `-1`/'none' sentinel for every pixel of any JPEG. Fixed by checking the surface format and treating RGB24 as fully opaque; only ARGB32 (canvas, PNG, clips, resizes) carries the real premultiplied alpha to unpack (claude.md #189).
- **A libjpeg `setjmp`-clobber UB leak (`runtime/festina_runtime_graphics.c`).** `festina_decode_jpeg`'s `surface`/`scanline` locals are modified between `setjmp` and the error `longjmp` and read in the cleanup path, but weren't `volatile` -- C11 leaves them indeterminate after `longjmp`, and at -O2 clang restored the pre-decode NULLs, leaking the decoded surface and scanline on a corrupt/truncated JPEG (the graceful corrupt-image `.callback()` path, claude.md #172). Fixed by declaring both `volatile`, the standard libjpeg-example pattern.
- **A malformed WAV with sample-rate 0 took down all audio with a wrong diagnosis (`runtime/festina_runtime_audio.c`).** The WAV decoder never validated the sample rate, so a `rate: 0` file "loaded" fine and then failed at device-open time -- where the EBUSY-retry loop misreads every open failure as device contention, halting every other playing channel one by one before dying with a misleading "is any audio device available?" fatal. Fixed by rejecting `sample_rate < 1` (and an absurd channel count) at decode time, alongside the existing bits-per-sample/channels checks -- one malformed asset is now a normal load failure, not a cascading audio shutdown.

**Tests:** `tests/test_json_parse.py` gained `test_large_int_fields_keep_full_64_bit_precision` and `test_deeply_nested_unknown_field_throws_instead_of_crashing`. The DoS/leak fixes are guarded structurally (the caps and ownership transfers are unconditional) and covered end-to-end by the existing http/url/json suites plus the ASan/LeakSanitizer stress suite, all still clean.

193. CODE-REVIEW ROUND, PART 2: FRONTEND TYPE-SAFETY HOLES, A TRY/CATCH USE-AFTER-FREE, AND A THROW DOUBLE-FREE

The frontend half of the #192 review. Three of these are memory-unsafety or type-confusion bugs that let an ill-typed or ordinary program produce garbage, a crash, or invalid IR; the last is a serious pre-existing double-free the review surfaced.

**A use-after-free from escape analysis never walking `try`/`throw` bodies (`festina/escape_analysis.py`).** `find_escaping_names` decides which locals are heap-refcounted (escaping) vs. stack-allocated (non-escaping, freed at scope exit); `_walk_stmt` handled every statement kind EXCEPT `TryStmt` and `ThrowStmt`, which are ordinary function-body statements (claude.md #157) whose bodies codegen emits under the same escaping set. So a value that escaped only inside a try or catch body -- `try { g = xs }`, `g` a global -- was judged non-escaping, stack-allocated, and freed at scope exit while `g` still pointed into the returned function's reclaimed frame: a real use-after-free (verified crashing, then ASan-clean after the fix). `_walk_stmt` now walks both `try_body` and `catch_body`, and a `throw`'s expression (`throw f(xs)`). Walking can only ADD names to the escaping set, so the conservative direction (claude.md #74) is preserved.

**Ternary branches were never checked against each other (`festina/semantic.py`).** The alt branch's type was inferred and DISCARDED, the whole `?:` typed from the cons branch alone -- so `c ? 'yes' : someBlob` silently compiled and rendered a blob handle's bytes AS text (garbage), and `c ? xs : someMap` walked a map header as an array. The two branches must now have the same type (the same rule `==`/`!=` already applied for the same #2 "no implicit coercion" reason), with `null` valid against either branch (#25) and the result taken as the OTHER, concrete branch's type. An int/float mix is rejected with a message naming the fix (`.toFloat()` on the int branch) rather than silently truncating -- a `?:` is one phi of one type, so unlike a binary operator (#143) its branches must already match.

**`&&`/`||` operands were never checked for bool (`festina/semantic.py`).** Both operand types were inferred and discarded, the result hardcoded to bool -- so `1 && 2` compiled and printed the raw i8 (2 is the bool-null sentinel, so it rendered as `null`), and `i && true` on an int operand reached codegen's `icmp ne i8` on an i64 value (invalid IR). Both operands are now required to be bool, the same check an `if`/`while` condition gets (claude.md #17: values like 0/1/-1 must not silently become booleans).

**A bare `null` ternary branch emitted invalid IR or crashed the compiler (`festina/codegen.py`).** The exact sibling of the `color == null` bug (#189): `_emit_ternary` used the cons branch's type for the phi and for the alt branch, so `c ? 1 : null` phi'd a raw `"null"` against `i64` (invalid IR) and `c ? null : 7` crashed on a `None` cons type. A `null` branch is now emitted via `_emit_value_for` AS the other branch's type -- the pointer `"null"` keyword for a pointer-shaped type, the reserved sentinel constant for int/float/bool/color -- with the null branch emitted second (or the whole expression driven off the alt branch when cons is the null one).

**A serious PRE-EXISTING double-free of any refcounted local declared before a throwing try (`festina/codegen.py`), surfaced by the review.** A `throw` freed every active local down to the function frame base (`_current_func_frame_base`), on the reasoning that the longjmp skips the normal scope-exit cleanup. That's correct only when the throw propagates OUT of the function. When it's CAUGHT by a try in the SAME function, the catch (and the code after the try/catch) keeps running, and a local declared BEFORE that try is still live -- its ordinary scope-exit release runs after the catch. Freeing it in the throw too was a double-free: `arr[int] xs = [1,2,3]; try { throw 'x' } catch(e){...}; log(xs[0])` aborted with glibc's "double free detected". The throw now frees only down to the NEAREST enclosing `_TryFrameMarker` in this function (the locals genuinely unwound between that try and the throw); with no enclosing try it still frees the whole frame, exactly as a Return does. This double-free predated the whole review -- the try/catch escape fix above merely gave the review a reason to exercise the shape.

**A note on ASan and `throw`:** the throw path uses `llvm.eh.sjlj.setjmp`/`longjmp`, which SIGILLs under this project's ASan harness (confirmed: a pre-existing throwing program SIGILLs identically), so the stress suite carries no throwing program and these fixes are verified by correct output + glibc's own double-free detector (which caught the original bug and reports clean after the fix) rather than by ASan.

**Tests:** `tests/test_semantic_errors.py` gained ternary-branch-mismatch (text/blob, arr/map, int/float), ternary-null-allowed, and logical-operand-must-be-bool cases; `tests/test_codegen.py` gained `test_ternary_with_a_null_branch`; `tests/test_try_catch.py` gained the try-body escape, catch-body escape, and refcounted-local-before-a-throwing-try (double-free) regressions. Full suite green.

**Not fixed this round (flagged for follow-up):** the review also found a batch of lower-severity frontend robustness gaps where an ill-formed or unusual program produces an internal LLVM error or a raw Python traceback instead of a clean `CompileError` -- a lexer `SyntaxError` escaping unconverted, deep parenthesis nesting hitting Python's `RecursionError`, `==` between two structs, a void call used as a value, a duplicate `on <event>` handler, an `arr`/`map`/`func`-typed table column, int literals past the i64 range wrapping silently, and template/`${}` error positions pointing at line 1. These are UX/robustness issues (wrong error shape), not miscompilations of valid code, and are left for a dedicated round rather than bundled here.

194. CODE-REVIEW ROUND, PART 3: CODEGEN OWNERSHIP BUGS FOR HANDLE-TYPED ARGUMENTS AND ARRAYS

The codegen half of the #192 review, all in `festina/codegen.py`. Every one is an ownership/refcount mistake specific to a HANDLE type (`img`/`blob`/`aud`, and the `arr[T]` of them) reached through a coercion the older ownership predicates predated; each was traced to emitted IR and verified with a real ASan run (`tests/stress/handle_arg_and_arr_churn.f`, new).

**A text literal/template passed to an `img`/`blob`/`aud` PARAMETER was a heap corruption or a leak.** All three call paths (a direct call, a call through a func-typed variable, a call through a member-callee) coerced each argument with `_coerce(val, vtype, ptype, lines)` -- WITHOUT `source_expr` -- then recorded the PRE-coercion `vtype` next to the POST-coercion `val` for cleanup. For `show(`sprite${n}.png`)` where `show` takes an `img`: `_coerce` mints a fresh img handle (and, lacking `source_expr`, leaks the argument's own text temp), then post-call cleanup took the `_free_text_temp` branch with `vtype=TEXT` and emitted `free()` on `val` -- which is now the img PAYLOAD, not text: an invalid free / heap corruption (glibc abort). For a `show('plain.png')` literal it instead never released the freshly loaded handle, leaking a decoded image per call. Fixed by threading `source_expr=arg_expr` into `_coerce` at all three sites (so the coercion frees the arg's text temp) and gating the post-call release on `_refcounted_source_is_fresh(arg_expr, vtype, ptype)` -- the exact test (`text` in, handle out) that already distinguishes a `blob b = 'path'` fresh handle elsewhere (claude.md #109/#118) -- instead of the node-only `_is_owning_refcounted_source`, which a StringLit/template never satisfies.

**A heap-released `arr[blob]`/`arr[img]`/`arr[aud]`/`arr[regex]`/... leaked every element.** `_release_fn_for_array`'s predicate for "does an element need releasing" listed only struct/arr/map/table/text -- MISSING every refcounted HANDLE element type.
