**Verified:** a real compile-and-run of the worked example (`int? count = 1`) and a manually-managed struct (declare, mutate a field, `free`, confirm the freed binding reads `null` exactly like an ordinary `free`); `Circle?`/`Circle` confirmed non-interchangeable via a real `check_assignable` rejection; `?` confirmed accepted-and-inert on every scalar/`text`/`color`/`font`/`table`; all three "no nesting" restrictions (`arr[Circle?]`, a `Circle?` struct field, a `Circle?` return type) confirmed as real parse errors; `on message(p:Circle?)` and a manually-managed `postMessage` argument both confirmed rejected with the new, accurate message. ASan/LeakSanitizer, both directions: a new `"manually_managed"` entry in `tests/test_leak_stress.py`'s own `_PER_TYPE_PROGRAMS` (struct/arr[T]/map[T] together, all freed explicitly every iteration, leak-free) and a new, dedicated `test_manually_managed_value_leaks_when_never_freed` canary (the opposite-direction proof every other per-type program in that suite does NOT make: a manually-managed struct that's never freed MUST show up as a real, reported leak -- 199 of 200 iterations, the 200th still reachable through the global `sink` binding at exit, exactly the expected count). A new `tests/test_manually_managed.py` (mirroring `tests/test_threads.py`'s own grammar/semantic split, plus a `TestRuntime` class for real compile-and-run coverage -- 31 tests) covers the grammar/semantic/no-nesting/runtime checks above directly, including every bug this phase found and fixed, so a regression in any of them fails with a name rather than needing this changelog entry re-read. Full suite green: 2052 passed, 9 skipped confirmed before this new file was added (up from 2050/9 at claude.md #201, the two new leak-stress tests accounting for the difference); `test_manually_managed.py` itself green standalone (31 passed) and `test_leak_stress.py` green standalone (38 passed, both directions) after every fix above landed.

203. `T?` -- MANUALLY-MANAGED (NON-GARBAGE-COLLECTED) VALUES, PHASE 2: THREAD REFERENCE-SHARING

The second half of the original request, deferred at claude.md #202: "if postMessage to and from a thread, if it has a manually managed variable as an argument, then don't copy it (unless it's a primitive or a string) but instead pass the reference." `postMessage`/`on message` deep-clone every other value type (claude.md #195-#198) -- that design's whole safety argument is that this runtime's `festina_retain`/`festina_release_check` are non-atomic, correct only because exactly one thread ever touches a given value's refcount. A manually-managed value's refcount is never touched by EITHER side's automatic bookkeeping at all, so sharing its raw pointer across threads cannot race on that mechanism specifically -- what remains is exactly what "manually managed" already means, now spanning two threads: no unsynchronized concurrent read/write, and exactly one `free`/`delete` call from whichever side is provably done with it.

**Phase 1's own explicit rejection guards (in `analyze_thread`'s `on message` handling and `_merge_thread_outbound_type`) are removed outright, not merely relaxed** -- replaced by a single early `return True` at the very top of `_is_thread_sendable_type` (semantic.py) for a manually-managed type, ahead of even the scalar cases. One dispatch point, not two duplicated guards, matching the rest of this function's own single-source-of-truth shape.

**Codegen: four early-return checks, each at the single dispatch point the design doc named, all reading `_is_manually_managed(type_)` off `info.inbound_type`/`outbound_type` -- semantic-level resolved types that already legitimately carry the flag, unlike the BARE types codegen keeps everywhere else (claude.md #202's own deliberate reversal).** `_emit_thread_clone_value` returns `val` unchanged instead of dispatching to any clone mechanism -- the payload IS the sender's own raw pointer, no independent allocation at all. `_thread_payload_release_fn` returns a new `@festina_noop_release` (declared once, defined as a genuine no-op in festina_runtime.c/.h) instead of a real release cascade -- the receiving side must never touch this payload's refcount, since it owns no independent reference to release. `_is_thread_clonable_type` returns True unconditionally, checked before even the cyclic-type rejection -- there is no clone recursion left to loop forever on a cyclic value when nothing is ever cloned, a genuine, correctly-reasoned side effect (though in practice UNREACHABLE today: forming an actual self-reference would require assigning a `T?` value into a plain-`T`-typed field, which the "no nesting" restriction -- claude.md #202's own struct-field rule -- already blocks by construction; the check is still correct for whatever future escape hatch might one day allow it). `_thread_payload_is_passthrough`/`_emit_thread_unbox`/`_emit_param_bindings` needed zero changes, exactly as designed -- all three are already flag-agnostic `isinstance` checks or already gated on `p.manually_managed` since claude.md #202's own Phase 1 wiring.

**A fifth real bug found by this phase's own stress test, not anticipated by the design doc: `_emit_thread_postmessage_cleanup` -- the function that releases `postMessage(x)`'s own argument once a clone has been made -- needed its own gate too.** Since a manually-managed value is never cloned, its own `val` becomes the payload directly; if this cleanup then released `val` anyway (believing a clone had made it safe to), it would drop the program's own single shared reference out from under the payload that now also points at it -- a real, silent correctness bug this phase's own design reasoning missed until the code was actually traced through. Fixed with the identical early-return-on-manually-managed pattern as the other four sites.

**A sixth real bug, found only once ASan stress testing actually tried to `free` a received value: a manually-managed thread-handler PARAMETER could not be freed at all.** `free`'s own semantic check (claude.md #111) blanket-rejects freeing ANY parameter ("a parameter borrows its caller's value; free it in the caller") -- sound for an ordinary parameter, where the caller genuinely does still hold and will release its own copy, but categorically wrong for a manually-managed one: nothing auto-releases it on either side, ever, so `on message(p:T?)`'s own parameter is not merely allowed to free it, it is frequently the ONE place that legitimately should. This gap existed since Phase 1 (an ordinary, non-thread manually-managed parameter -- `void func consume(c:Circle?) { free c }` -- was equally broken) but went unnoticed until Phase 2's own stress test tried the shape a thread handler needs. Fixed with a `not getattr(sym.type, "manually_managed", False)` exemption on the existing check.

**New `tests/stress/thread_manually_managed_churn.f`** (5000 iterations) -- deliberately race-free BY DESIGN, not by luck: each iteration constructs a brand-new `Item?`, posts it to `reader`, and never touches it again -- ownership passes to `reader` exclusively at that point. `reader` reads the field it needs and explicitly frees the value itself (required -- nothing auto-manages a `T?` value on either side), simultaneously the ASan leak check (miss the `free` and every one of these leaks) and a real ThreadSanitizer proof that the SHARING mechanism itself introduces no race -- not that concurrent access to a manually-managed value is somehow safe (it categorically is not, and this file does not attempt to prove otherwise). Named `thread_*.f` (not `manually_managed_*.f`) specifically so `scripts/thread_tsan_stress.sh`'s own default glob picks it up automatically, alongside `thread_churn.f`/`thread_db_churn.f`. `tests/test_leak_stress.py`'s own coverage-completeness manifest gains its entry.

**Verified with a direct, positive proof no clone ever happened, in either direction -- not merely "no clone function appeared in codegen's own dispatch."** A real compile-and-run: main constructs `Circle? c`, posts it to a thread that mutates the field it received THROUGH its own `on message` parameter and echoes it back unmodified (the thread -> main direction, exercising the identical no-clone path); main's own callback reads BOTH the echo's own field (`x.x`, unsurprising even under a clone) AND `c`'s own ORIGINAL binding (`c.x`, never itself touched by main again after the initial `postMessage` call) -- both read 99, which is only possible if the thread's own mutation landed on the exact same underlying memory `c` still points to. ASan/LeakSanitizer: the new stress file, plus the FULL existing `thread_churn.f`/`thread_db_churn.f` suite re-run clean (confirming no regression to the ordinary deep-clone paths). ThreadSanitizer: the new stress file plus the full existing `thread_*.f` suite, via `scripts/thread_tsan_stress.sh` with no arguments (its own default glob), all clean. `tests/test_manually_managed.py` gains three new semantic tests (message-type acceptance, `postMessage` acceptance, and confirming a genuine `Circle?`/`Circle` TYPE mismatch across a thread boundary is still correctly rejected as an ordinary type error, unrelated to sendability) and one real round-trip runtime test (the direct-proof scenario above) -- replacing two Phase-1 tests that asserted the now-superseded rejection behavior. Full suite green: 2086 passed, 9 skipped (up from 2083/9 at claude.md #202).

204. `T?` -- THE FRESH-CONSTRUCTION ESCAPE HATCH, CLOSING A GAP claude.md #202 LEFT DOCUMENTED

claude.md #202's own documented, accepted gap: `regex?` had no way to be populated from a fresh `/pattern/` literal at all, since a literal always infers as plain `regex` and `regex`/`regex?` are genuinely non-interchangeable types (by design -- "no implicit decay either direction"). Asked to fix it directly. Investigating turned up a materially BIGGER gap than the one that was documented: the identical problem hits `arr[T]`/`map[T]` literals (`arr[int]? xs = [1, 2, 3]` was ALSO a compile error) and, more surprisingly, a STRUCT built by an ordinary factory FUNCTION rather than field-by-field (`Circle? c = makeCircle()` too) -- struct's own "no literal syntax" escape hatch only ever covered the no-initializer case, never a function returning one. Every eligible type except blob/img/aud (which already have their own text-coercion escape hatch) and struct's no-init case turned out to have no way to become manually-managed from a fresh value at all.

**The fix: a new `_is_fresh_construction(expr)` (semantic.py), checked at exactly one place -- a manually-managed VarDecl's own initializer, right before the ordinary `check_assignable` call.** True for `ast.Call`/`ast.ArrayLit`/`ast.MapLit`/`ast.RegexLit` -- the identical shape set `codegen._is_owning_refcounted_source` already recognizes as "owning" (nothing else could already reference a value that was just constructed), reused here for a parallel but distinct purpose: not deciding whether to skip a retain (codegen's own job, already unconditional on manually_managed regardless of freshness -- see claude.md #202's own codegen section), but deciding whether semantic.py's type check should ACCEPT the combination at all. When true, `check_assignable` runs against the BARE (unflagged) counterpart of the declared type rather than the manually-managed one -- exactly what a fresh literal/call naturally infers as -- while the SYMBOL actually bound afterward still carries the real, manually-managed `declared_type`, identical to every other branch in `analyze_var_decl`.

**Why this is sound, not a relaxation of "no implicit decay":** the restriction exists to stop an ALREADY-referenced ordinary value from being aliased into a manually-managed binding without anything tracking that the ordinary side might still auto-release it out from under the new one. A value that was JUST constructed at this exact declaration has no such "already referenced elsewhere" history to worry about -- this scope is provably its first and only reference, the identical reasoning that already lets every other with-initializer declaration in this compiler skip a retain for a Call/literal source. Confirmed the boundary is still enforced correctly: reading an EXISTING plain binding (`Circle plain; Circle? c = plain`) is still rejected, and a genuine type mismatch through a fresh construction (`Square? s = makeCircle()`) still raises the ordinary error -- neither test was a given without actually writing them and watching them fail before the fix landed.

**Placement matters: this new branch sits in `analyze_var_decl`'s own existing bypass elif-chain (the `arr[img]`/`amor arr[T]`/`http {...}` literal-shape bypasses, claude.md #137/#162/#174), immediately before the final generic `else`.** The three existing bypasses above it never call `check_assignable` on the whole container type at all (they validate elements/fields directly), so they already worked correctly for a manually-managed declaration regardless of this fix -- confirmed directly (`amor arr[int]? xs = [1, 2, 3]`, `http? h = {...}` both already compiled before this change). This new branch only ever fires for the shapes none of those already cover.

**Verified:** all four originally-broken shapes (`regex? r = /pattern/`, `regex? r = regex(...)`, `arr[int]? xs = [...]`, `map[int]? m = {...}`) plus the struct-factory-function case, real compile-and-run, correct values, correct `free` behavior, no crash. `tests/test_manually_managed.py` gains a parametrized fresh-construction acceptance test (4 shapes), a dedicated struct-factory-function test, a still-enforces-the-bare-type-match rejection test, a still-rejects-an-existing-plain-binding test (the boundary check), and one real compile-and-run test exercising all four shapes together -- replacing the now-stale `test_regex_literal_cannot_initialize_a_manually_managed_regex`. `todo.md`'s own `regex?` gap entry removed outright (fully closed, not narrowed). Full suite green: 2093 passed, 9 skipped (up from 2086/9 at claude.md #203). Also confirmed directly with ASan/LeakSanitizer, both directions, outside the pytest suite: a fresh-construction manually-managed struct that's correctly `free`d is clean, and the identical program with the `free` removed is a real, reported leak (199 of 200 iterations, matching the exact pattern claude.md #202's own opposite-direction canary already established) -- proving the fresh-construction escape hatch didn't accidentally weaken the "never auto-managed" guarantee for the values it now accepts.

205. `T?` -- PER-TYPE THREAD REFERENCE-SHARING TEST COVERAGE, AND THREE REAL BUGS IT FOUND

Requested directly: make sure there is real test coverage for manual memory management, testing each eligible type SEPARATELY crossing a thread boundary. Phase 2 (claude.md #203) shipped the reference-sharing mechanism itself with exactly one round-trip proof -- struct. Every other manually-manageable, thread-sendable type (`arr[T]`/`map[T]`/`enum`/`img`/`blob`/`aud`/`regex`/`url`, `http`/`socket` semantically but not practically) had never actually been SENT across a thread at all. Writing that coverage found three real, previously-latent bugs -- one a genuine heap-use-after-free, unrelated to threads at all, and two real gaps in the reference-sharing codegen itself.

**Bug 1 (found first, while designing the enum test): a real, ASan-confirmed heap-use-after-free, with no thread involved.** `check_assignable`'s own EnumType member-coercion bypass (claude.md #176 -- `Circle -> Shape` for `enum Shape = Circle`) fired regardless of whether the DECLARED enum was manually-managed, letting an ORDINARY, automatically-managed member value flow straight into a manually-managed binding with no retain (codegen's own retain-skip for a manually-managed declaration is unconditional on the declaration's own flag, exactly as designed for every other eligible type -- claude.md #202's own codegen section). Once the source value went out of scope and its own automatic release dropped the last reference, the manually-managed binding was left pointing at freed memory -- reproduced directly with a real `AddressSanitizer heap-use-after-free` report (`scripts/leak_stress.sh` against a hand-written 4-line repro), not just reasoned about. **Fixed by gating the bypass on `not declared.manually_managed`** -- when the declared enum IS manually-managed, execution now falls through to the ordinary strict `declared != actual` check, which correctly rejects a plain member value the same way it already rejects a plain `Circle` flowing into `Circle?`. `analyze_var_decl`'s own fresh-construction escape hatch (claude.md #204) is unaffected and remains the one legitimate way in: it checks against the BARE enum type, which reaches this exact branch un-flagged.

**Bug 2 (found writing the blob test): a manually-managed thread-message PARAMETER's own body_env binding carried the FLAGGED type, unlike every other declaration/parameter site in this file.** `_emit_thread_on_message` passes `info.inbound_type` (deliberately flagged, per claude.md #203's own design, so the four clone-decision call sites can read `_is_manually_managed` off it directly) straight into `_emit_param_bindings`'s own `param_types` tuple -- which then stores that SAME flagged type into the handler's own `body_env`, unlike an ordinary function/local declaration (which always resolves independently via `self._resolve()`, kept deliberately bare -- claude.md #202's own reversal). Concretely: `on message(p:blob?) { p.write(...) }` raised a genuine "cannot access field 'write' on blob?" CodegenError -- blob's own exact-equality (`== BLOB`) method dispatch, and `_is_thread_handle_type`'s identical `type_ == BLOB` check (used by `_thread_payload_is_passthrough`, reached while unboxing the handler's own parameter), both stopped recognizing a flagged blob as blob at all. **Fixed two ways, addressing two distinct exposure points:** a new `_bare_type(t)` strips the flag specifically before it reaches `body_env` (so the handler's own body sees the ordinary bare type for every OTHER dispatch, matching the rest of this file); `_is_thread_handle_type` itself also switched from `type_ == BLOB` to an isinstance-safe check (`isinstance(t, PrimitiveType) and t.name == "blob"`, mirroring semantic.py's own `_is_blob_type`), since the flagged type legitimately still reaches `_thread_payload_is_passthrough` via the unboxing step (which has no early `_is_manually_managed` gate of its own -- unboxing a pointer-shaped payload correctly is unrelated to whether it's manually managed) even after the `body_env` fix.

**Bug 3 (found writing the regex test, immediately after fixing Bug 2): `_thread_payload_is_passthrough` never had an answer for regex/http/socket AT ALL.** Not a regression -- a genuinely unreached code path until now: semantic.py's own `_is_thread_sendable_type` rejects an ORDINARY regex/http/socket outright (claude.md #195's own list -- "an escaping regex has no retained pattern text to recompile from"; "http/socket are tied to the single main-thread connection table"), so this predicate was never asked about any of the three before claude.md #202 Phase 2's own early `manually_managed` return opened the door for a manually-managed one to reach it. `on message(p:regex?)` compiled fine (semantic analysis correctly allows it, per design) but produced invalid LLVM IR (`add ptr %t1, 0` -- `add` requires an integer operand) at the identical unboxing step Bug 2 touched, since answering False routed a pointer-shaped payload down the scalar-unboxing path instead of the plain pointer-alias GEP a passthrough type needs. **Fixed by widening `_thread_payload_is_passthrough` to also recognize `RegexType`/`HttpType`/`SocketType` directly** (not folded into `_is_thread_handle_type`, whose own name and doc comment promise a real `festina_*_clone` function exists for each of its members -- none of these three has one, and none ever needs one: an ordinary instance still can never reach here at all, and a manually-managed one is never cloned in the first place, per `_emit_thread_clone_value`'s own early return).

**A fourth thing found, not a bug: `.play()` is the wrong tool for an aud identity proof.** `festina_audio_is_playing` genuinely compares the queried value's own pointer against each channel's `clip` field (festina_runtime_audio.c) -- a real, reliable per-VALUE identity check, exactly what a "shared, not cloned" proof needs. But `beep.wav` is short enough that a one-shot `.play()` had already finished by the time a full round trip through the thread's own message queue completed, observed directly as a false-negative `isPlaying()` read on both sides before switching the test to `.playLoop()` (which keeps the channel active until explicitly `.stop()`-ped) fixed it. Documented in the test's own comment so the next person extending this coverage doesn't rediscover it.

**Coverage added, `tests/test_manually_managed.py`:** a new `TestThreadReferenceSharingPerType` class with one real compile-and-run round-trip test per type -- `arr[int]?`/`map[int]?` (push/key-set, observed via `.length`/index-read), `enum?` (a struct-payload member's own field, via the fresh-construction escape hatch), `img?` (`drawPixel`/`getPixelColor`, an in-place pixel-buffer mutation), `blob?` (`.write()`/`.toText()`), `aud?` (the `.playLoop()`/`isPlaying()` pointer-identity proof above), `regex?` and `url?` (round-trip-and-no-crash proofs -- both types are immutable from Festina's own perspective, so a same-address proof isn't behaviorally writable in this language, only in C). `http?`/`socket?` get semantic-only acceptance tests (`TestSemantic`) rather than a runtime round trip -- neither is practically constructible as a fresh, standalone value outside a live request/connection context. Every test follows the identical shape claude.md #203's own struct proof established: the handler mutates/reads the value it received through its own parameter, echoes it back via a bare `postMessage`, and the receiving callback checks BOTH the echo's own property and the SENDER's untouched original binding -- the echo doubling as the synchronization barrier that makes reading the sender's own binding race-free, not just an implementation convenience. `TestSemantic` also gains three regression tests for Bug 1 (the UAF itself now rejected, the fresh-construction path proven unaffected, ordinary non-manually-managed enum coercion proven unaffected).

**Verified:** every new test passes; the original UAF repro confirmed rejected at compile time (not just "doesn't crash" -- a real `CompileError`) and, separately, confirmed via `scripts/leak_stress.sh` that the exploit no longer even compiles, so there is nothing left for AddressSanitizer to catch. Full suite green: 2106 passed, 9 skipped (up from 2093/9 at claude.md #204).

206. `.toStruct(T)`/`.toArr(T)` -- `\uXXXX` UNICODE ESCAPE DECODING, CLOSING A GAP claude.md #159 LEFT DOCUMENTED

todo.md's own "Language & standard library" section carried this as an open gap since claude.md #159 first shipped JSON parsing: every other JSON string escape (`\n \t \r \" \\ \/ \b \f`) decoded correctly, but `\uXXXX` hit a hardcoded `festina_json_throwf("... not yet supported")` inside `festina_json_parse_string`'s escape switch (runtime/festina_runtime.c) -- meaning any JSON payload containing a non-ASCII character escaped the standard way (as virtually every real-world JSON producer does for anything outside Basic Latin) threw instead of parsing. Fixed by giving `'u'` a real `case` instead of falling through to `default`.

**Implementation:** a new `festina_json_read_hex4` helper reads exactly four hex digits (throwing on anything else -- running past the end of input, or a non-hex character -- the same "malformed input is a real error" convention every other JSON parsing helper here already follows) and returns the 16-bit value they encode. The new `case 'u':` block reads one, and if it lands in the high-surrogate range (0xD800-0xDBFF) requires an immediately-following `\uXXXX` low surrogate (0xDC00-0xDFFF), combining the pair into one astral-plane codepoint (`cp = 0x10000 + ((high - 0xD800) << 10) + (low - 0xDC00)`) exactly per the UTF-16 spec; a bare high surrogate with no follow-up, or a low surrogate encountered on its own, both throw a distinct `"unpaired UTF-16 surrogate \uXXXX"` rather than silently guessing. The resulting codepoint (BMP or astral) is then UTF-8-encoded inline (1-4 bytes depending on range, the same branching every UTF-8 encoder uses) directly into `out`, growing the buffer first if the encoded bytes don't fit -- reusing the exact same `realloc`-and-double growth pattern every other append into `out` in this function already uses, so this path participates in the function's own existing buffer-management invariants rather than adding a second one. Writes `out` itself and `continue`s the outer loop, rather than falling through to the ordinary single-byte-append path every other escape uses, since a `\u` escape can produce zero to four output bytes from one source token instead of exactly one.

**What this does NOT touch:** `festina_json_render`'s own JSON-producing direction (`.toText()` on a struct/map) -- that side already emits non-ASCII text as raw UTF-8 bytes rather than escaping it to `\uXXXX` in the first place (valid per the JSON spec, and was never the gap todo.md described), so there was nothing to change there, and round-tripping a struct through `.toText()` then back through `.toStruct()` was never affected by this bug at all -- only INCOMING JSON that used the escape form (hand-written, or produced by a stricter JSON serializer than Festina's own) ever hit the old "not yet supported" throw.

**Coverage added:** `tests/test_json_parse.py::TestRuntimeBehavior` gained seven tests -- a plain BMP codepoint (`café`), a real astral-plane surrogate pair (U+1F600, the four-byte UTF-8 case), and five distinct error cases (unpaired high surrogate, lone low surrogate, a high surrogate followed by a non-surrogate escape, a truncated escape, an invalid hex digit) each asserting a distinct, catchable `caught:` message rather than a crash. `tests/stress/json_parse_churn.f` (the existing JSON-parsing leak/ASan coverage, extended rather than duplicated into a new file) gained a `Note{msg:text}` struct-field case mixing a BMP escape and a surrogate pair in the same string, run for real under `scripts/leak_stress.sh` to confirm the new UTF-8-encode-and-possibly-grow-the-buffer path doesn't leak or corrupt memory across 150 repeated iterations -- ASan clean.

**A genuinely easy-to-get-wrong mechanical note, left here because it cost real time twice while writing this fix's own tests:** getting a literal `\uXXXX` sequence in front of the JSON parser requires writing TWO literal backslashes in Festina source (`'\\u00e9'`), not one -- the lexer's own `_unescape` (festina/lexer.py) treats a single `\` followed by any character NOT in its `_ESCAPES` table (`n t r \ ' " `` 0`) as that character with the backslash silently DROPPED, so a naive single-backslash `'é'` in Festina source becomes the literal text `u00e9` (no backslash at all) by the time the runtime string exists, and the JSON parser never sees an escape to decode. Two backslashes (`\\`) IS in `_ESCAPES` (maps to one literal `\`), so `'\\u00e9'` unescapes to one real backslash immediately followed by `u00e9` -- which is the actual six-character `é` JSON escape sequence this fix decodes. The equivalent trap exists one layer further out when generating Festina source FROM Python (as every test in `compile_and_run`-based files does): a non-raw Python string's own `é` is itself a Python unicode escape (silently producing the literal character `é`, not the six characters `\`,`u`,`0`,`0`,`e`,`9`), so producing the correct two-backslash Festina source from a Python string literal needs either a raw string (`r"""..."""`, where every backslash is kept literally) or four literal backslashes in a non-raw one. This is the same trap claude.md #159's original test-writing session hit and worked around by hand each time; a `r"""..."""` source block, used consistently here, is the actually-durable fix.

Full suite green: 2113 passed, 9 skipped (up from 2106/9 at claude.md #205).

207. `thread`'S OWN PRIVATE SQLITE HANDLE -- CLOSED ON `kill()`, CLOSING A GAP todo.md LEFT DOCUMENTED

todo.md carried this since claude.md #199 Phase 5 first gave a `thread` its own `DatabaseURL`: `on_load` unconditionally opens a fresh `sqlite3*` every time a thread's worker starts (both the initial spawn and any later `NAME.live()` after a `kill()`), but nothing ever closed the PREVIOUS one first -- a real, small, per-cycle leak (one `sqlite3*` plus an open fd) on every `kill()`/`live()` cycle, simply reclaimed by the OS at actual process exit like every other still-open handle.

**Why this isn't just "call `festina_db_close` from the thread's own exit path" -- the one real subtlety here.** `festina_db_close` (claude.md #126) exists to run exactly ONCE, at true process shutdown: its own finalize loop walks `g_cached_stmts`, the ENTIRE process-wide prepared-statement registry (claude.md #113/#199 Phase 5 -- shared across main and every thread's own connection, guarded by `g_stmt_cache_lock`), finalizing every entry unconditionally before closing. Calling that from a thread that's merely being `kill()`ed -- while another thread, or main, is still alive and has its OWN cached statements sitting in that same registry, against a DIFFERENT connection -- would finalize those out from under whichever thread is still using them, a real, if narrow, cross-thread correctness bug the fix could easily have introduced instead of the leak it was closing.

**Fixed with a second, SCOPED close path instead of reusing the first.** `g_cached_stmts` (`festina_runtime.c`) gained a parallel `g_cached_stmt_dbs` array (same index, same count/cap, populated alongside every `festina_sqlite_prepare_cached` insert) recording which `sqlite3*` each cached statement was actually prepared against -- previously nothing tracked this at all, since the one existing consumer never needed to distinguish. A new `festina_thread_db_close(sqlite3 *db)` locks the same `g_stmt_cache_lock`, finalizes and compacts out only the entries whose own `db` matches the one being closed (leaving every other connection's own cached statements untouched), then closes. `festina_db_close` itself is completely unchanged -- still the one true "finalize everything, then close" function, still called exactly once, at real process shutdown, for main's own database.

**Wired to the actual moment a thread's worker stops, not to `NAME.kill()` codegen directly.** A per-thread `void(*)(void)` closure (`FestinaThreadHandle.db_close`, registered once via a new `festina_thread_set_db_close`, mirroring `festina_thread_set_out_callback`'s own shape exactly) is called from `festina_thread_main` itself, right after `on_exit(0)` and right before `alive` flips to 0 -- the one guaranteed point this thread's own worker is genuinely done, whether that's an explicit `NAME.kill()` or `festina_thread_kill_all()` at process teardown, either path running the identical worker-loop code. Codegen (`_emit_thread_db_close_trampoline`) emits a tiny zero-argument trampoline per thread that DOES declare its own `DatabaseURL` (never for one that doesn't -- `db_global` stays `None` there, and the whole registration is skipped, so `db_close` stays `NULL` and costs nothing, the identical "accepted-but-inert absence" shape `on_load`/`on_message`/`on_exit` already have for an undeclared handler): loads `@__festina_thread_NAME_db`, calls `festina_thread_db_close` on it, stores `null` back. Registered right after `festina_thread_register`, before `festina_thread_spawn` -- the same ordering `in_release`/`out_release` already use, so there is no window after the OS thread actually starts where `db_close` could still be unset.

**A genuinely correct side effect, not a scope creep:** because this hooks the worker's own actual stop point rather than something keyed to a USER-visible `kill()` call specifically, a thread's own database now also gets closed during `festina_thread_kill_all()` at real process exit -- slightly MORE thorough than main's own database (still left open at exit, per todo.md's own separate, deliberate note), but harmless either way: nothing runs after `festina_thread_kill_all()` in `festina_program_exit` except the real `exit()` call, and closing a connection nothing will touch again has no downside.

**Coverage added:** `tests/test_codegen.py::TestThreads::test_kill_then_live_reopens_a_genuinely_working_database_handle` -- five real, blocking `kill()`/`live()` cycles (deterministic, no message-passing race, mirroring `test_kill_then_isalive_is_false_then_live_revives_it`'s own shape exactly) followed by a genuine `on message()` round trip against the thread's own database, proving the handle the LAST `live()` reopened is actually usable, not just that the process didn't crash. `tests/stress/thread_db_kill_live_churn.f` -- 500 real kill()/live() cycles, run under `scripts/leak_stress.sh`: confirmed to genuinely catch the leak (temporarily disabling the `db_close()` call reproduced a real ~70MB LeakSanitizer report, 500 objects each, tracing straight into `sqlite3_open`/`festina_db_open`) before confirming the actual fix is clean. Also re-verified `scripts/thread_tsan_stress.sh` clean across every `thread_*.f` stress program, `thread_db_churn.f` included -- the one file that already exercises real concurrent sqlite traffic between two threads against the shared statement-cache registry this fix's own new `g_cached_stmt_dbs` array touches.

Full suite green: 2114 passed, 9 skipped (up from 2113/9 at claude.md #206).

208. `thread` EXTENSIONS, PHASE 0: UNIFIED MESSAGING MODEL

Requested directly, as the first of six related `thread` extensions (thread pools, thread-private helper functions, wider builtin access inside a thread, a thread's own private HTTP/WebSocket context, and live HTTP-request handoff from main -- Phases 1-5, not yet started). The original request specified per-thread `NAME.onMessage(callback)` registration; a follow-up, delivered mid-plan-review, replaced it outright: **"let's remove the compile time error on give message... Change socket on message namespace to on socketMessage so there is no conflict for on message from the main thread. Instead of using worker.onMessage, use a global on message (worker:thread, msg:<any, defined on postMessage>)... use the same format in threads, however if the worker:thread is the main thread, then it == null... also allow threads to reference each other."** This entry covers exactly that replacement -- the foundation every later phase's own messaging touches, so it went first.

**The naming collision the plan found before writing any code: `on message` was already taken at the top level.** `_EVENT_SIGNATURES["message"]` (claude.md #151) is the existing, shipped WebSocket frame handler, `on message(s:socket, msg:blob)` -- exactly the conflict the follow-up's own "so there is no conflict for on message from the main thread" refers to. **Renamed to `on socketMessage(s:socket, msg:blob)`** -- `_EVENT_SIGNATURES` key, codegen's handler-name dispatch, and every example/test using the old top-level name, all updated together; WebSocket fragmentation behavior itself is completely unchanged, only the name.

**Design refinement found while working through the details, simpler than the original plan: every message receiver -- main, or a specific thread -- now gets exactly ONE `on message(worker:thread, msg:T)` handler that DECLARES its own `T` directly, via its own second parameter.** A thread's own inbound handler already worked this way (`info.inbound_type` was always read directly off `on message(p:T)`'s own declared parameter, never inferred) -- this generalizes the identical mechanism to main's own receiving side, which previously had none at all (the outbound direction was inferred from scattered `postMessage(x)` call sites via `_merge_thread_outbound_type`, and delivered through a dynamically-registered `NAME.onMessage(callback)` trampoline). **Because both ends of every send are now always DECLARED, the entire inference/merge/registration mechanism becomes obsolete outright, not merely widened** -- `_merge_thread_outbound_type`, the `onmessage_cb_global`/`_emit_thread_out_trampoline`/`festina_thread_set_out_callback` runtime-callback-registration path, and the end-of-`analyze()` "no dead sends" loop are all removed. Every send -- `NAME.postMessage(x)` to a specific thread, or a bare `postMessage(x)` to main -- is checked with an ordinary `check_assignable` against the receiver's own declared type, exactly the way a function argument already is against its parameter's declared type. Sending more than one shape to the same receiver still needs a pre-declared `enum`, exactly as the inbound direction already required -- now true symmetrically in both directions, for the identical reason (`check_assignable`'s own enum-member-coercion, claude.md #176, has no way to spell a compiler-invented anonymous type either direction).

**`thread` is a new, real value type -- `worker:thread`'s own type -- deliberately minimal.** `types.ThreadType.name` widens from `str` to `str | None`: `None` is the new GENERIC variant (what the bare `thread` keyword spells in a parameter position), kept a distinct dataclass value from any specific declared thread's own `ThreadType("someName")` even though ordinary code never constructs the named variant as a value -- only the generic one is ever used for a `worker:thread` parameter, and its only runtime value ever arrives via message delivery (a boxed sender handle), never via an ordinary expression. `thread` is a new reserved type keyword in `parse_type()`. Codegen: `_llvm_type` returns bare `ptr` for both variants; **not refcounted** -- a thread handle is an immortal, process-lifetime singleton, the identical treatment `FuncType`/`FontType` already get, not the retain/release treatment every other cross-thread-sendable type needs. `worker`'s own runtime value is bound with the same "pointer-alias, no boxing" GEP trick `_emit_thread_unbox_into` already uses for passthrough types (`{dest} = getelementptr i8, ptr %sender, i64 0`), reused directly since `%sender` itself is never boxed.

**`worker == null` works; `worker == otherWorker` does not, on purpose.** The null case routes through the existing, already-correct generic ptr-vs-null fast path in `_emit_binop` (works for any type whose `_llvm_type` is `"ptr"`, unrelated to this change). Comparing two REAL thread values would reach the SAME invalid-LLVM-IR hazard `struct == struct` already has (confirmed directly: `Circle == Circle` compiles at the semantic layer and crashes LLVM object emission with a confusing internal-error-shaped message) -- rather than ship a second instance of that pre-existing, out-of-scope bug, semantic.py's own `==`/`!=` compatibility check gains an explicit `ThreadType`-vs-`ThreadType` guard raising a clear Festina-level error instead. `worker` also deliberately has no methods at all (`worker.postMessage(x)` to "reply to sender" is out of scope -- a real reply is already expressible via `NAME.postMessage(x)` using the sender's own compile-time-known name, now that inter-thread messaging is unblocked; a runtime-dispatched call on `worker` itself would need dynamic dispatch machinery this codebase has never built, and was never asked for).

**Threads may now message each other directly, not just main -- "messaging only," per explicit follow-up.** `NAME.postMessage(x)` is unblocked from inside another thread's own body: the ThreadType Member-call dispatch's rejection (`_current_thread[0] is not None`) is now conditioned on `callee.prop != "postMessage"`, so `postMessage` alone is exempted while `kill()`/`live()`/`isAlive()` keep rejecting unconditionally from any thread body -- a thread may message a sibling, but still may not control its lifecycle.

**Sender identification: every message now carries its sender.** `FestinaThreadMsg` (`festina_runtime_thread.c`) gains a `void *sender` field -- `NULL` for a send from main, or the sending thread's own `FestinaThreadHandle*` otherwise -- populated at post time by a new explicit `sender` argument to `festina_thread_post` (the `NAME.postMessage(x)` codegen path: `"null"` from main, or a `load` of the calling thread's own handle global from inside another thread's body) and set implicitly to `h` by `festina_thread_post_outbound` (a thread's own outbound queue can only ever be filled by itself, so no argument is needed there). Delivered straight to the receiving handler's `worker:thread` parameter via the same GEP-alias trick described above.

**Hook-seam convention, mirrored exactly for main's own new handler:** a single, statically-known top-level `on message` (unconditionally registered, mirroring how `on request` already works) needed a new `festina_set_global_message_handler` setter plus a NULL-by-default function-pointer global in the runtime, replacing the old per-thread dynamic-registration path; `festina_thread_drain_impl` now just calls the one global handler if set, dropping the delivery on the floor (matching every other "declared but nothing listens" case in this codebase) if not.

**A real runtime crash found and fixed purely by testing all the way through codegen+the C runtime, not stopping at semantic analysis.** `_current_thread_ctx` shrank from a 4-tuple `(thread_name, handle_global, outbound_type, db_global)` to a 3-tuple (dropping `outbound_type`, no longer per-thread -- replaced by one program-wide `self.analyzed.main_message_type`) -- one read site (`_emit_thread_on_load`'s own `thread_ctx[3]` for `db_global`) was missed in the renumbering and produced a genuine `IndexError: tuple index out of range` on a real compile-and-run, never surfaced by semantic-only tests. Fixed (`thread_ctx[2]`), then grepped the whole file for any other stale `[3]` index to confirm no second instance existed. Verified end to end afterward with three distinct real compile-and-run scenarios: a simple thread<->main round trip with correct non-null sender identification, main->thread with correct null sender identification, and genuine thread-to-thread relaying (thread A forwarding to thread B directly) with correct payload propagation all the way through to main's own final receipt.

**Full regression rewrite, not just new coverage -- ~30 existing test call sites across four files, per the follow-up's own explicit acceptance that this is a full replacement, not an addition.** `tests/test_threads.py`: every `on message(p:T)`/`.onMessage(...)` call site updated to `on message(worker:thread, msg:T)`; the old "no dead sends"/outbound-inference tests replaced with their new equivalents (a bare `postMessage(x)` with no top-level handler declared is still a clear compile error, now naming the top-level handler specifically; declaration-order now matters for the top-level handler exactly the way it already did for a thread's own declaration, since analysis runs in strict textual program order); new coverage for `worker == null`, the `ThreadType`-vs-`ThreadType` rejection, and a thread messaging another thread directly. `tests/test_codegen.py::TestThreads`: every real compile-and-run round-trip test (int/text/float/bool/struct/array/map/enum/blob/img/aud/url, the DatabaseURL-private-handle test, the enum-coercion-leak regression) updated to declare a real top-level `on message` handler ahead of the relevant `thread` declaration instead of registering `.onMessage(...)` afterward; `test_two_independent_threads_do_not_collide` needed a genuine redesign, not just a rename -- with only one global handler, which of two real, independently-scheduled OS threads posts its reply FIRST is genuine unordered concurrency (confirmed directly: an initial draft asserting a fixed arrival order failed intermittently), so it now sorts by the reply's own value instead of by arrival order. `tests/test_manually_managed.py`: every `T?` thread-message test (struct/arr/map/enum/img/blob/aud/regex/url) updated identically. `tests/test_http.py`/`tests/test_graceful_shutdown.py`: the pre-existing top-level WebSocket tests updated to `on socketMessage`.

**`tests/stress/thread_churn.f` needed a real design change, not a mechanical rename.** Its ten worker threads each used to reply to main with a DIFFERENT shape (int/text/`Item`/`arr[int]`/`map[int]`/`DataPacket`/blob/img/aud/url), kept apart by ten separate `.onMessage(callback)` registrations -- impossible to express directly now that main has exactly one declared inbound type. Fixed by wrapping each reply shape in its own single-field struct (`IntMsg`/`TextMsg`/...), unioned into one `ChurnMsg` enum (all-distinct field names, so the pure-struct-enum field-ambiguity check claude.md #176 already has doesn't fire), and dispatching in the one top-level handler via `typeof msg` to the same ten `onXReply` functions the old callbacks used to call directly -- the identical "more than one type -> a real, pre-declared enum" convention this phase's own design doc already established, just at ten members instead of two. `tests/stress/thread_db_churn.f`/`thread_manually_managed_churn.f` needed only the declaration-order/parameter-rename mechanical update. Verified directly with real reduced-volume compiles+runs of all three before relying on the full-volume ASan/TSan stress scripts.

**Verified:** full suite green, 2120 passed, 9 skipped (up from 2114/9 at claude.md #207) -- a net +6 from the new `worker == null`/thread-comparison-rejection/inter-thread-messaging coverage, after the full rewrite above landed with zero net test-count regression elsewhere. `scripts/leak_stress.sh` and `scripts/thread_tsan_stress.sh`, both against all four updated `thread_*.f` stress programs (`thread_churn.f`'s own new `ChurnMsg`-enum dispatch included), both clean -- the sender-boxing field on every `FestinaThreadMsg` and, for the first time, genuine thread-to-thread `postMessage` traffic (not just main<->worker) are both exercised at real volume with no leak and no data race reported.

209. `thread` EXTENSIONS, PHASE 1: THREAD POOLS

`thread NAME[N] { ... }` -- N fully independent instances of one thread body, each its own OS thread, private state, and inbound queue, addressed via `NAME[i]`. Closes the "threads are singletons" gap todo.md carried since claude.md #195 first shipped the feature.

**Verified low-risk before writing any code, exactly as the approved plan's own research predicted.** `pool[i].postMessage(x)` needs zero parser changes -- `pool[i]` already parses as an ordinary computed `Member` through the fully generic postfix loop, identical to indexing an `arr[T]`; only the DECLARATION itself (`thread NAME[N] { ... }`) needed new grammar. And a full read of `runtime/festina_runtime_thread.c` confirmed `FestinaThreadHandle`/`festina_thread_register`/the global registry store no name or index anywhere -- N independent registrations already work today, so this phase needed **zero runtime C changes**, only parser/semantic.py/codegen.py.

**Grammar: an optional `[<INT_LITERAL>]` after a thread's name (`parse_thread_decl`), a plain compile-time-literal integer only -- never a general expression, the identical "must be a literal" precedent `DatabaseURL` already set (claude.md #199), for the same reason: the size has to be known without running the program.** `ast.ThreadDecl`/`_ThreadInfo` both gain `pool_size` (`None` for an ordinary singleton). `semantic.py`'s own thread-body ANALYSIS needed no pool-awareness at all -- a pool's body is analyzed exactly ONCE, producing one `_ThreadInfo` shared by every future index, since every instance runs the textually identical code.

**Semantic dispatch: `pool[i].postMessage/kill/live/isAlive` peels the one extra `Member` layer off before falling into the identical by-name lookup a singleton thread's own bare-Identifier receiver already used** -- every check underneath (method name, the main-only lifecycle-method guard, `postMessage`'s own inbound-type check) runs completely unchanged for a pool instance; the index expression itself is separately type-checked as `int`. Two new, deliberately specific rejections round out the receiver shape: a pool referenced with NO index (`pool.kill()`) is rejected naming the actual fix ("must be indexed... e.g. `pool[0].kill(...)`"), and an ORDINARY (non-pool) thread indexed like one (`worker[0].kill()`) is rejected the other direction ("is an ordinary thread, not a pool").

**Codegen: N independent instances, each through the ordinary, completely unchanged per-thread emission path.** `_emit_thread_pool_decl` loops `_emit_thread_decl` N times over a synthesized per-instance `ThreadDecl` whose own `.name` is mangled (`NAME$0`...`NAME$N-1` -- `$` is a valid unquoted LLVM identifier character), each producing its own real, separately namespaced handle/state/on_load/on_message/on_exit globals and symbols, with zero changes needed to any of that machinery. The one thing those functions read OUTSIDE `decl.name` itself is `self.analyzed.threads[thread_name]` (the `info` lookup, and the `DatabaseURL` read inside `_emit_thread_on_load`) -- aliased once per mangled name to the SAME shared `_ThreadInfo` semantic.py already built, so every instance sees the pool's one declared `on message`/`DatabaseURL` correctly. **A new parallel `self.thread_pools` dict, not a polymorphic `self.threads`** -- the approved plan's own explicit recommendation, confirmed sound directly: since every pool instance still gets a REAL entry in `self.threads` (under its own mangled name), the existing startup registration loop (`for tname, tinfo in self.threads.items(): ...register/spawn...`) needed literally zero changes to pick up and spawn every pool instance -- it was already generic enough.

**A use site resolves the runtime index through one small piece of genuinely new machinery: a constant `[N x ptr]` array whose N elements are each the compile-time ADDRESS of one instance's own `handle_global`.** `pool[i].postMessage(...)` computes `i` once, bounds-checks it (`icmp ult i64 i, N` -- unsigned comparison rejects a negative index for free, wrapping it to a huge unsigned value), and only inside that bounds-checked block does the real op run at all: GEP into the array at the runtime index to find WHICH handle_global that slot names, then a second load to read that instance's own actual (runtime-registered) `FestinaThreadHandle*` -- one extra indirection versus a singleton's own direct single load, in exchange for never needing an emitted N-way switch/branch-chain at every call site. **An out-of-range index is a genuine, silent no-op at the LLVM level, not just a semantic-analysis-time claim** -- `postMessage`/`kill`/`live` skip their entire body (including argument evaluation -- the message/callback argument is never even evaluated when the index doesn't resolve to a real instance) and fall straight through; `isAlive` phi's between the real result and a hardcoded `false`, matching this language's own established "test, don't fail" convention (`NAME.isAlive()` already never raises).

**Coverage added:** `tests/test_threads.py` gains a new `TestThreadPools` (11 tests) -- grammar/literal/positive-size checks, indexed postMessage accepted (both a literal and a runtime-expression index), the index-must-be-int rejection, both new receiver-shape rejections (unindexed pool, indexed non-pool), lifecycle methods accepted when indexed, still-rejected-from-inside-a-thread-body, and a pool instance receiving `NAME.postMessage` from inside ANOTHER thread's own body (claude.md #208's inter-thread capability, confirmed to apply identically to a pool instance). `tests/test_codegen.py` gains a new `TestThreadPools` (3 real compile-and-run tests) -- two pool instances proven to have genuinely INDEPENDENT private state (not aliasing the same global), a real runtime out-of-range-index no-op proof (`postMessage`/`kill` silently do nothing, `isAlive` reads `false`, the process still reaches `close(0)` normally), and `kill()`ing one specific instance confirmed NOT to disturb another's own `isAlive()`. New `tests/stress/thread_pool_churn.f` -- the shape none of the existing `thread_*.f` files cover: N genuinely independent OS threads all running the IDENTICAL generated body concurrently (as opposed to `thread_churn.f`'s own ten DIFFERENT bodies, one instance each), the shape most likely to expose a bug where per-instance codegen accidentally shared something. `tests/test_leak_stress.py`'s own coverage-completeness manifest gains its entry (caught immediately by that manifest test's own "the suite quietly shrinking" guard, exactly as designed). api.md gains a "Thread pools" subsection; todo.md's own "threads are singletons" gap removed outright.

**Verified:** full suite green (2135 passed, 9 skipped, up from 2120/9 at claude.md #208). `scripts/leak_stress.sh`/`scripts/thread_tsan_stress.sh` against the new `thread_pool_churn.f`, both clean -- confirming N concurrent instances of the identical body share no accidental state and the new bounds-checked array-indirection codegen introduces no leak or race.

210. `thread` EXTENSIONS, PHASE 2: THREAD-PRIVATE HELPER FUNCTIONS

`func` declared directly inside a `thread { }` body (a sibling of its state vars/on load/on message/on exit, not nested inside one of those) -- callable only from that one thread's own handlers and other private funcs, with read/write access to that thread's own state. Closes the "thread-private helper function... isn't supported" gap todo.md carried since claude.md #195, and the last remaining item the request's own "also allow threads to own functions" line named.

**Two rejection points needed to change, both confirmed by reading first, not assumed.** `analyze_thread`'s statement loop only recognized `VarDecl`/`EventHandler`, rejecting a `FuncDecl` outright; `_infer_call`'s blanket thread-body call check rejected any call to any function-kind symbol unconditionally, with a literal "aren't supported yet" message. Both narrowed rather than removed -- an ordinary TOP-LEVEL function stays exactly as uncallable from inside a thread body as claude.md #195 originally made it; only a func declared INSIDE that same thread's own body is now allowed.

**Two-pass hoisting, scoped to one thread -- the identical "hoist every signature before any call checks" shape `register_func_signature`'s own whole-program pre-pass already uses, deliberately NOT `_iter_func_decls` itself (that recurses into the GLOBAL `functions_scope`, which would leak every private func into every OTHER thread and into main).** A new `thread_functions_scope = Scope(thread_state_scope)` -- parented on the thread's own state scope (so a private func's own body sees thread state directly, the "closes over this thread's own state" the request itself asked for), never on the top-level `functions_scope`. Pass 1 (right after the `DatabaseURL` detection, before `_current_thread[0]` is set) registers every direct-child `FuncDecl`'s signature into it as a NEW, distinct `Symbol.kind` -- `"thread_function"`, not `"function"` -- with the same builtin-name/duplicate-declaration guards `register_func_signature` already has. Pass 2 (the ordinary per-statement loop) analyzes each private func's own BODY at its own textual position, exactly like a handler's -- so two private funcs may call each other in either declaration order (signatures are hoisted), but a private func reading a state var still needs that var declared BEFORE it, textually (confirmed directly: the identical "declared before referenced" rule a handler already had). `handler_scope` itself is reparented from `thread_state_scope` to `thread_functions_scope`, so a handler can call a private func too.

**Distinguished by `Symbol.kind`, not scope-chain walking -- the blanket call-site rejection becomes an allow-list of two kinds instead of one.** `_infer_call`'s own generic "is this a real declared function" check (`sym.kind not in ("function", "thread_function")`) needed the identical widening -- both read `sym.node` (a plain `FuncDecl` either way) completely generically afterward, no further branching needed. Privacy itself falls out of ordinary lexical scoping for free: a private func's name was only ever defined in ITS OWN thread's own `thread_functions_scope`, so a call site anywhere else (another thread, main) never finds the symbol to reach either check in the first place -- confirmed directly (calling from a sibling thread or from main both fail with a plain "unknown function", not a privacy-specific error). One deliberate NON-extension: a bare, uncalled reference to a private func's own name (`func[int]:int f = helper`) is rejected outright with a dedicated message -- unlike an ordinary function, a private func has no first-class VALUE form in this phase; never requested, and "hand a function pointer closing over one thread's own private state to code outside that thread" is a can of worms claude.md #195's own isolation model doesn't need opened here.

**Codegen: a real, separately mangled LLVM function per private func (`@__festina_thread_NAME_func_fname`), emitted through the ordinary `_emit_func` -- parameterized, not duplicated.** `_emit_func` gained three optional parameters (`symbol`/`outer_env`/`thread_ctx`, all `None` for its original top-level-function caller, unchanged behavior): `symbol` overrides the emitted function's own name; `outer_env` overrides what its body_env is built on top of (`state_env` for a private func, giving direct access to this thread's own namespaced state globals, exactly the way a handler's own body_env already does); `thread_ctx` is set as `self._current_thread_ctx` around the BODY only (mirroring `_emit_thread_on_load`/`_on_message`/`_on_exit`'s own identical save/set/restore pattern exactly), so a private func's own body may call bare `postMessage(x)` or another thread's `NAME.postMessage(x)` exactly like a handler already can -- confirmed directly, no extra plumbing needed (`_current_thread_ctx`'s own existing scope already covers it). Two-pass in `_emit_thread_decl` too: every direct-child `FuncDecl`'s mangled symbol/decl/return-type is registered into a new `self.threads[NAME]["funcs"]` dict FIRST, then each body is emitted -- so a call from a handler or another private func resolves regardless of textual order, matching semantic.py's own hoisting.

**Call-site dispatch: a new branch in `_emit_call`'s Identifier-callee path, checked ONLY when `self._current_thread_ctx is not None`, BEFORE the flat global `self.func_decls` lookup -- mirroring semantic.py's own identical shadowing precedence exactly** (a thread's own `thread_functions_scope` is a CHILD of the top-level `functions_scope`, so a same-named private func always wins for a call site inside that thread's own body). Reuses the ordinary direct-call argument-marshaling/cleanup logic verbatim, just calling the mangled `symbol` instead of `@name`.

**Pools needed zero special-casing -- confirmed, not assumed.** `_emit_thread_pool_decl` already loops the ordinary, unchanged `_emit_thread_decl` once per mangled instance name (`NAME$0`...`NAME$N-1`, claude.md #209) -- since private-func registration/emission lives INSIDE `_emit_thread_decl` itself, keyed off `decl.name` (already the per-instance mangled name for a pool), every pool instance automatically gets its own independently-mangled private func symbols and its own independent closure over ITS OWN state, with no changes needed to the pool machinery at all.

**A real bug found while writing `tests/stress/thread_private_func_churn.f`, NOT a compiler bug -- a test-design one, but instructive enough to document.** An early draft tried to keep the plain thread's own replies and the pool's own replies apart in the ONE shared top-level handler using a value-range tag (`msg >= 1000000` meaning "from the pool"), the same trick `tests/test_codegen.py::TestThreads::test_two_independent_threads_do_not_collide` already uses successfully -- but at THIS file's real volume (thousands of messages), the plain thread's own `total` (accumulated through two chained private funcs, `triple`→`helper`) grows UNBOUNDED and silently crosses the 1000000 tag threshold itself partway through the run, misrouting later replies into the wrong counter and making the "done" condition permanently unreachable -- observed directly as a genuine process hang (near-zero CPU, blocked on a condvar waiting for a reply count that could now never arrive), not a crash, which is what made it look at first like a real concurrency bug in the new codegen. Confirmed the actual mechanism by bisecting down to a minimal repro (two ordinary singleton threads, no pools or private funcs at all, one with unbounded cumulative state) and watching the same hang reproduce -- proving the value-tag trick itself, not anything Phase 2 added, was the fragile part. **Fixed by dropping value-based routing entirely** for this file -- a single combined reply counter across both the plain thread and the pool, matching `thread_pool_churn.f`'s own already-successful, simpler convention.

**Coverage added:** `tests/test_threads.py` gains a new `TestThreadPrivateFunctions` (14 tests) -- accepted/callable, ordinary top-level functions still rejected, invisible from another thread, not callable from main, a same-named top-level and private function coexisting without collision, reading/writing state declared before it, the "declared after" rejection, two private funcs calling each other in either textual order, postMessage to another thread and bare postMessage to main from inside a private func, duplicate-name rejection, the builtin-name guard, the bare-reference-as-value rejection, and a private func working identically inside a thread pool. `tests/test_codegen.py` gains a new `TestThreadPrivateFunctions` (4 real compile-and-run tests) -- correct computation through a private func calling another, a private func actually mutating the thread state it closes over, a private func calling `NAME.postMessage` on another thread, and two pool instances' own private funcs mutating genuinely independent state. New `tests/stress/thread_private_func_churn.f` (5,000 messages, a plain thread AND a pool, both routing every message through two chained private funcs) -- the one file that actually exercises the new codegen path (mangled symbols, `outer_env`/`thread_ctx`, the per-thread `funcs` table lookup) under real, sustained concurrent load; `tests/test_leak_stress.py`'s own coverage-completeness manifest gains its entry. api.md's Threads section gains coverage of the new capability; todo.md's own private-helper-function gap removed outright.

**Verified:** full suite green (2153 passed, 9 skipped, up from 2135/9 at claude.md #209) -- two unrelated, pre-existing flaky tests (an X11 window-decoration timing test, the same graceful-shutdown HTTP timing test claude.md #208's own session already saw flake once) confirmed to pass individually, not a regression. `scripts/leak_stress.sh`/`scripts/thread_tsan_stress.sh` against the new `thread_private_func_churn.f`, both clean.

211. `thread` EXTENSIONS, PHASE 3: WIDER BUILTIN ACCESS -- `regex()`/`mkdir()`/`ls()`/`exec(args)`

Widens what a thread body may call: `regex()`, `mkdir()`, `ls()` come off `_THREAD_DISALLOWED_BUILTINS` outright; `exec` gets an arity split rather than a flat removal, since only ONE of its two forms is actually safe. Canvas/timer/audio builtins and `openPort`/`closePort`/`openSecurePort`/`close` stay blocked -- unchanged, Phase 4's job.

**Every claim verified by reading the actual runtime C first, exactly as the approved plan called for -- not assumed from the names alone.** `exec(args)` (the blocking, 1-argument form): `festina_run_argv`'s own fork()/execvp()/waitpid() touches no shared state at all -- fork() in a multithreaded process only duplicates the CALLING thread into the child, which execvp()'s immediately after (the standard safe pattern), and waitpid() always targets that exact child's own pid, never a wildcard. `exec(args, callback)` (the non-blocking, 2-argument form) -- a genuine finding, NOT safe: `festina_process_exec_dispatch` queues the actual argv-running step onto a background worker (confirmed: `festina_exec_worker` "Runs on a background worker thread"), but the callback itself is invoked by a trampoline read back out of the SAME payload on a completely different pass -- confirmed by reading `festina_async_io_dispatch`'s own drain step, which the payload's own doc comment names directly ("release_fn, called on the main thread right after the callback"): the callback ALWAYS runs on MAIN's own OS thread, regardless of which thread dispatched it. A thread handing it a closure over its own private state would be exactly the kind of cross-thread violation claude.md #195's own isolation model exists to prevent. `regex()`: its own memoization slot (`festina_regex_compile_memo`'s own `void **slot` parameter) is populated by a per-CALL-SITE codegen-generated LLVM global (confirmed in codegen.py: `self._regex_memo_slots`, keyed by `id(Call node)`, one `@.regex.memo.N` global per distinct call site) -- lexically private to whichever one thread's generated code contains that call site, never shared, the identical reasoning `festina_sqlite_prepare_cached`'s own per-call-site fast-path slot already relies on. `mkdir()`/`ls()`: thin, purely local POSIX wrappers (`mkdir()`; `opendir()`/`readdir()`/`closedir()`) -- no shared global anywhere in either.

**The arity split lives in `_infer_call`, ahead of the flat `_THREAD_DISALLOWED_BUILTINS` check (which no longer even lists `exec` at all) -- checked by NAME AND `len(expr.args)` together, mirroring the sqlite gate's own shape** (that one branches on `_current_thread[0].database_url is None` instead of an arg count, but the same "this builtin's safety here depends on something the flat set can't represent" reasoning). `exec(args, callback)` inside a thread body gets its own specific message naming the actual reason (the callback's own main-thread-only delivery), not the generic "touches state shared with the main program" one every other disallowed builtin gets -- `exec(args)` falls through completely unaffected.

**Coverage added:** `tests/test_threads.py` gains a new `TestThreadWiderBuiltinAccess` (6 tests) -- `regex()`/`mkdir()`/`ls()`/`exec(args)` all accepted, `exec(args, callback)` still rejected with the new specific message, and a canvas builtin confirmed still rejected (this is a widening, not a blanket amnesty). `exec(['ls'])` removed from the existing disallowed-builtins parametrize list (now accepted, no longer belongs there). `tests/test_codegen.py` gains a new `TestThreadWiderBuiltinAccess` (1 real compile-and-run test) -- `mkdir()`/`ls()`/`regex()`/`exec(args)` all actually exercised together from inside a real thread's own `on load()`, not just accepted at the semantic level, with the directory's real presence confirmed on disk afterward too. New `tests/stress/thread_wider_builtins_churn.f` -- two threads (not just one) each calling `regex()`/`mkdir()`/`ls()`/`exec(args)` at their OWN call sites CONCURRENTLY, at real volume (1000 combined messages, 20 real forked child processes), with a distinct pattern/directory per thread and a `failures` counter that fails the whole run loudly (`close(1)`) if a cross-thread mix-up ever produces a wrong regex match or directory listing -- the actual "prove the per-call-site-privacy claim under real concurrency, not just cite the doc comment" verification the approved plan called for, not merely asserted. `tests/test_leak_stress.py`'s own coverage-completeness manifest gains its entry. api.md's Threads Isolation paragraph updated to name the four newly-allowed builtins and explain the `exec(args, callback)` gap specifically, rather than silently vanishing four names from the old list.

**Verified:** `scripts/leak_stress.sh`/`scripts/thread_tsan_stress.sh` against the new `thread_wider_builtins_churn.f`, both clean -- the TSan run specifically is what actually proves two threads' own regex call sites and concurrent fork()/exec() calls don't interfere with each other, under real concurrency rather than by inspection alone.

212. `thread` EXTENSIONS, PHASE 4: PRIVATE PER-THREAD HTTP CONTEXT -- `openPort()`/`on request`/`on upgrade`/`on socketMessage`/`on socketClose`

A thread may now declare the identical four HTTP/WebSocket handlers the main program's own top-level already has (`on request(req:http)`/`on upgrade(s:socket)`/`on socketMessage(s:socket, msg:blob)`/`on socketClose(s:socket)`), and, having declared at least one, call `openPort()`/`closePort()`/`openSecurePort()` -- getting a fully private connection table and listener set, never shared with main's own context or any other thread's.

**Design: `__thread`, not a hand-threaded context struct -- the approved plan's own recommendation, taken exactly as written.** Converted every piece of `festina_runtime_http.c`'s own module-level server state to `__thread` storage (the SAME storage class this file's own `g_http_send_header_buf`/core's own catch-frame stack already used, claude.md #163) -- `g_conns`/`g_conn_count`/`g_conn_capacity`, `g_conn_free_slots`/`_count`/`_capacity`, `g_conn_index`/`_capacity`/`_used`, `g_listeners`/`_count`/`_capacity`, the four handler pointers (`g_request_handler`/`g_upgrade_handler`/`g_message_handler`/`g_socketclose_handler`), the poll-set buffers (`g_poll_fds`/`g_poll_conn_ids`/`g_poll_cap`), and `g_http_draining`/`g_http_drain_deadline`. This gives every calling OS thread -- main included -- its own independent copy automatically, with **zero function-signature changes anywhere in the file**: every function keeps reading "the one global" and it correctly becomes "this calling thread's own private copy," exactly the plan's own stated goal. The ONE deliberate exception, also called out explicitly in the plan: `g_next_conn_id` stays a genuine process-wide global (ids must never repeat across the WHOLE process, not just within one context -- the anti-use-after-free design in festina_runtime.h relies on it), now guarded by a real `pthread_mutex_t` (`festina_next_conn_id`) since more than one OS thread can legitimately allocate a connection id concurrently once more than one HTTP context exists. This file's own client-side async-request pool (`g_async_outstanding`/`g_async_pool_started`/`g_async_wake_fds`/the job queues) is DELIBERATELY left untouched, genuinely process-wide -- a thread's own context never submits work into it; see the client-form paragraph below for why.

**The combined loop: a bounded-timeout poll, matching the plan's own recommendation -- not the message queue's own condvar-wait.** `festina_thread_main` (festina_runtime_thread.c) now has two shapes: unchanged (block on the inbound condvar forever) for a thread with no HTTP context, or -- for one that declared a handler -- a loop that dispatches anything already queued, then calls a new `festina_thread_http_service_pass(timeout_ms)` (festina_runtime_http.c) with a short, fixed bound (`FESTINA_THREAD_HTTP_POLL_MS` = 20ms, matching this project's own established `FESTINA_ASYNC_IO_POLL_SECONDS` granularity), then loops back to check messages again -- the identical "poll each source per-iteration with a short bound" shape `festina_run_timer_loop`/`festina_run_http_loop` already use for main's own combined graphics+http+timers loop, applied here to one thread's own private pair of sources. `festina_thread_post`'s own `pthread_cond_signal` is simply never waited on while in this mode (a thread blocked inside `poll()` can't be woken by a condvar signal) -- worst-case latency for a newly posted message is one 20ms poll cycle, an accepted, documented tradeoff, not an oversight. `festina_thread_http_service_pass` is a deliberately SEPARATE, smaller implementation from `festina_http_service_once` (the existing graphics+http combined-loop pass) rather than a shared/refactored one -- same "don't refactor stable, tested code just to save a few lines" call claude.md #165 already made -- with two real differences: it may genuinely BLOCK for its own timeout (it IS this thread's whole loop, not a top-up alongside something else already bounding its own wait) and it deliberately does NOT drain the client-side async-request pool (main-only, as above). Its own `poll()` call is never early-returned when there is nothing to poll (no listener, no connection) -- `poll()` with an EMPTY fd set and a positive timeout is a portable, correct sleep (confirmed against POSIX's own text), which is exactly the bounded, non-busy-spinning idle wait a **receive-only** context (one that declared a handler but never called `openPort()`, needed by Phase 5's `giveRequest`) needs.

**Registration: mirrors main's own prologue exactly, just running on the thread's own OS thread instead.** `_emit_thread_http_handler` (codegen.py) emits each declared handler as an ordinary void function taking plain parameters (no thread-queue unboxing -- these fire from `festina_runtime_http.c`'s own dispatch calling straight into the generated function, exactly like main's own four do), but with `body_env = Env(state_env)` and `_current_thread_ctx` set for the duration (so bare `postMessage(x)`/a private-func call works from inside one, the identical wiring `on_load`/`on_message`/`on_exit` already get). `_emit_thread_on_load` gained a new prologue block, emitted FIRST (before even the db_open block) -- `festina_register_request_handler`/`_upgrade_handler`/`_message_handler`/`_socketclose_handler`, one call per handler this thread actually declared -- so `__thread` `g_request_handler`/etc are never NULL for even a moment this thread's own combined loop could conceivably run. A new `festina_thread_set_http_context(h, service_pass, teardown)` (mirroring `festina_thread_set_db_close`'s own shape exactly) wires `festina_thread_http_service_pass`/`_teardown`'s real addresses onto this thread's own `FestinaThreadHandle`, called once from the startup registration loop, only for a thread whose `has_http_context` (set in `_emit_thread_decl`, gated on whether it emitted any of the four handlers) is true -- codegen never references either symbol by name anywhere else, so a program with threads but no http at all never even links `festina_runtime_http.c`'s object file, let alone calls into it.

**The gate: legal only after declaring a handler -- a real runtime necessity, not just a style rule, confirmed by reasoning through what would otherwise happen.** `_THREAD_HTTP_HANDLER_NAMES` (semantic.py) tracks which of the four a thread declares; `info.has_http_handler` is set by a HOISTING pre-scan (all four names checked across the whole thread body BEFORE the per-statement loop runs), deliberately not inline as each handler is encountered in textual order -- unlike the bare-postMessage-needs-an-earlier-top-level-handler rule (a genuine whole-program ordering constraint), there is no reason to force `on request` to appear before `on load()` just because `openPort()` happens to be called from inside it, and an early draft that DID gate inline broke on exactly the most natural way to write this (`on load()` first, `on request` below it) -- caught immediately by the very first hand-compiled test program, not by the automated suite. `openPort()`/`closePort()`/`openSecurePort()` come off `_THREAD_DISALLOWED_BUILTINS` outright and get a new dedicated `_infer_call` gate instead (mirroring the `DatabaseURL`-gates-sqlite() shape exactly): without at least one declared handler, `festina_thread_main`'s own loop-mode decision stays the plain, no-HTTP-awareness-at-all shape, so an accepted connection would simply sit forever with nothing ever polling for it -- a real, confusing runtime gap the gate exists specifically to make impossible to reach, not a redundant compile-time nicety layered on top of something codegen would have handled correctly anyway.

**A real leak, found by the sanitizer this phase's own verification discipline exists to run -- not theoretical.** `scripts/leak_stress.sh` on a first hand-written kill()-cycle test caught a genuine 64-byte leak in `festina_open_port_impl`'s own `g_listeners` realloc every single time an HTTP-context thread was killed. Root cause: every OTHER teardown path in this runtime (main's own "no GC yet, process exit tears everything down" convention, `festina_conn_teardown`'s own per-connection cleanup, which recycles a connection SLOT but never frees the table backing it) correctly leaves these top-level tables allocated FOR REUSE -- exactly wrong for a table that's `__thread`-local to an OS thread about to exit for good: nothing else will EVER free it once that specific pthread is gone (a later `NAME.live()` spawns a genuinely FRESH OS thread with its own freshly zero-initialized `__thread` storage, never reusing the dead one's). **Fixed** with a new `festina_thread_http_teardown()` (wired the identical way/placement as `festina_thread_set_db_close`'s own `db_close` hook, claude.md #207 -- called once, right before this thread's worker stops for good, whether that's an explicit `kill()` or `festina_thread_kill_all()` at process teardown) that, beyond closing every listener/connection (already-existing logic), now also actually `free()`s `g_conns`/`g_conn_free_slots`/`g_conn_index`/`g_listeners`/`g_poll_fds`/`g_poll_conn_ids` themselves -- confirmed clean by re-running the exact same leak_stress case afterward.

**Also found, and fixed, along the way: this project's own sanitizer scripts had never linked `festina_runtime_http.c` (or, for the client form, `festina_runtime_https.c`) at all.** `scripts/leak_stress.sh`/`scripts/thread_tsan_stress.sh` unconditionally link core/async/thread (pure POSIX) and PROBE graphics/audio (real, routinely-absent system dependencies) -- http had simply never been added to either list, since no stress test had ever needed it before this phase. Added `http` to both scripts' unconditional link set (matching thread/async's own reasoning: pure POSIX, no pkg-config dependency of its own) and a new `https` PROBE (mbedTLS -- a real, routinely-absent dependency, exactly like graphics/audio), needed because api.md's own `req.send()` doc comment states plainly that BOTH the plain and TLS client codepaths are always linked into any program using the client form at all, regardless of which scheme the url actually turns out to be at runtime -- confirmed directly: the first stress program using `req.send()` failed to LINK (`undefined reference to festina_register_tls_hooks`) before this fix, with no openSecurePort() in sight.
