**The stress test's own design had to work around a real, structural deadlock risk that has nothing to do with a bug -- documented, not just avoided by luck.** A single OS thread cannot simultaneously block making a client `req.send()` to its OWN listener and be the very loop that would accept/service that connection -- confirmed by reasoning through it before writing a line of the stress file (not discovered by a hang): from `on_load` (the combined loop hasn't started yet) or from that same thread's own `on message`/`on request` (the loop is synchronously blocked dispatching THIS handler, not concurrently polling), a self-directed client request would wait forever for a response nothing is left running to send. `tests/stress/thread_http_context_churn.f` avoids this by construction -- `worker`'s own `on message`, driven by TOTAL messages FROM MAIN, makes its blocking client request to MAIN's port, never its own; MAIN's own listener socket is already bound (`openPort()` is main's first top-level statement, well before any message is even sent) even though main's own accept LOOP may not have started polling yet at the moment the very first request arrives -- safe, not a race, since a bound-and-listening TCP socket accepts the SYN at the kernel level regardless of whether the application has called `accept()` yet, so the worst case is a brief wait for the response, never a failure. This same reasoning -- and the resulting one-directional design -- is now documented directly in api.md's own new "Per-thread HTTP context" section, not left as an implicit trap for the next person to rediscover by hanging.

**Coverage added:** `tests/test_threads.py` gains a new `TestThreadHttpContext` (12 tests) -- a request handler unlocks `openPort()`, `openPort()`/`closePort()`/`openSecurePort()` all separately rejected without one, the gate is proven order-independent (`on load()` calling `openPort()` textually BEFORE `on request`), each of the four handler names alone is enough to unlock the gate, a wrong `on request` signature and a duplicate `on request` are both still rejected, a pool thread may also declare an HTTP context, and bare `postMessage` works from inside `on request`. `tests/test_codegen.py` gains a new `TestThreadHttpContext` (3 real compile-and-run tests) -- a thread genuinely serves real HTTP traffic on its own private port (a real subprocess, a real `http.client` GET against it, via the existing `compile_and_run_server` fixture), a thread's own `on message` makes a real client request back to MAIN's own port and the response is verified byte-for-byte (proving both __thread-backed contexts run correctly and concurrently, not just that each compiles), and a thread with a declared handler but no `openPort()` call still starts and exits cleanly (the receive-only context doesn't hang or busy-loop). New `tests/stress/thread_http_context_churn.f` (2,000 full connect/send/receive/verify round trips, main and a thread each with their own private port, the thread's own client calls targeting main's, never its own) registered in `tests/test_leak_stress.py`'s coverage-completeness manifest. api.md gains a new "Per-thread HTTP context" subsection (the gate, the receive-only-context case, the client-form self-request deadlock warning, the port-collision note) and the Isolation paragraph's "may not call" list drops `openPort()`/`openSecurePort()` in favor of a cross-reference to it.

**Verified:** full suite green (2176 passed, 9 skipped, up from 2161/9 at claude.md #211) -- one real regression caught and fixed along the way: `TestThreadIsolation::test_disallowed_builtins_are_rejected_inside_a_thread[openPort(8080)]`, an old parametrize case asserting `openPort()` was flatly disallowed, now correctly removed (it's gated, not banned -- a different, more specific error, covered instead by the new `TestThreadHttpContext`). `scripts/leak_stress.sh`/`scripts/thread_tsan_stress.sh` against `thread_http_context_churn.f`, both clean AFTER the `festina_thread_http_teardown` leak fix above -- the TSan run specifically is what actually proves two genuinely concurrent `__thread`-backed HTTP event loops (main's own `festina_run_http_loop` and a thread's own combined loop, each servicing real accept/read/write traffic while the other does too) never race on anything, under real concurrency rather than by inspection alone -- the first place this project has ever had two such loops running at once.

213. `thread` EXTENSIONS, PHASE 5: LIVE CONNECTION HAND-OFF -- `NAME.giveRequest(r)`

The main program, having accepted a live request on its own port, may now hand it directly to a thread via `NAME.giveRequest(r)` -- that thread's own `on request` fires for it, on the connection's own live socket, exactly as if that thread had accepted it itself. Legal only from main (like `kill`/`live`/`isAlive`), only onto a thread that has declared its own `on request`, and only for a manually-managed `http?` value -- reusing `T?` (claude.md #202/#203) rather than building a new compile-time move-checker, per the explicit follow-up that reshaped this whole plan before implementation began. First cut: plain (non-TLS) connections only, matching the approved plan's own scoped-down v1.

**The genuinely new engineering is entirely at the OS-connection level, not the Festina-value level -- confirmed before writing a line of code, not discovered after.** The plan's own research had already shown `T?`'s existing no-clone-for-manually-managed machinery (`_emit_thread_clone_value`'s early return, `_thread_payload_release_fn`'s no-op release) already handles handing a manually-managed Festina VALUE across a thread boundary safely, for free -- so `giveRequest`'s own payload reuses the identical `FestinaHttpValue*` `req` already refers to, never cloned, exactly like any other `T?` argument to `postMessage` already would. What's genuinely new is the underlying **connection** -- the live fd, and every piece of per-connection parse/keep-alive/TLS state `FestinaConn` carries -- which has to move from main's own `__thread`-local connection table (claude.md #212) into the receiving thread's own, with `req.send()`/`.ok()`/etc. on the receiving side finding it there afterward.

**Design: detach/attach, mirroring `_emit_thread_clone_value`'s own "move the pointer, don't copy what it points to" shape at the OS-connection level.** New `festina_conn_detach(http_payload)` (festina_runtime_http.c) resolves the payload's own live connection, verifies it's still eligible (alive, plain/non-TLS, a request still being read -- not an upgraded WebSocket, not already responded to -- each a silent no-op otherwise, this runtime's own established "test, don't fail" convention for thread-related builtins), and moves it wholesale -- fd, buffers, every heap pointer `FestinaConn` owns -- into a heap-allocated copy via one shallow struct copy, recycling the now-empty slot into the calling thread's own free list exactly like `festina_conn_teardown` already does (minus actually freeing anything, since ownership moved rather than ended). The detached connection travels to the target thread as the `conn` half of a new `FestinaGiveRequestPayload{conn, http_value}` (deliberately defined in the SHARED header, festina_runtime.h -- both fields stay opaque `void*` there, since `festina_thread_give_request`, festina_runtime_thread.c, builds it without ever needing to know what `FestinaConn` looks like, and `festina_thread_deliver_given_request`, festina_runtime_http.c, is the only thing that ever unpacks it), riding a NEW `FESTINA_THREAD_MSG_GIVE_REQUEST` kind on `FestinaThreadMsg` (widened with a `kind` tag) through the target's ordinary inbound queue -- `festina_thread_try_dispatch_one` (claude.md #212's own dequeue helper) branches on it before ever touching `on_message`/`in_release`, calling a THIRD hook (`give_request_deliver`) `festina_thread_set_http_context` now wires alongside `service_pass`/`teardown`. On the receiving side, `festina_conn_attach` (mirroring `festina_conn_new_slot`'s own slot-acquisition shape, but installing already-real state rather than a blank one) inserts the connection into THAT thread's own `__thread`-local table, re-keyed under the SAME `conn_id` (never regenerated), before `g_request_handler` is ever called -- so `req.send()`/`.ok()` inside the receiving thread's own `on request` find it exactly where they already know to look.

**Refactored, not duplicated: `festina_dispatch_request`'s own post-handler-call logic (fallback 200, WebSocket-upgrade dispatch, keep-alive-vs-teardown) is now a shared `festina_finish_request_dispatch(conn_id, payload)`, called by both the ordinary accept path and the new hand-off delivery path.** A first draft considered hand-rolling an equivalent for the hand-off case; extracting the real, already-tested logic instead (rather than a second, inevitably-drifting copy of it) is what makes `tests/test_codegen.py::TestGiveRequest::test_a_thread_forgetting_to_respond_still_gets_the_default_200` -- a genuinely meaningful test, not a formality -- pass for free.

**A real ThreadSanitizer-caught data race, found on the very first stress run against real volume -- exactly what the approved plan itself predicted ("expect to find at least one real race the first time, budget for it"), not a surprise.** The first working draft had `festina_conn_detach` call `festina_retain(http_payload)` on success, reasoning (on paper, plausibly) that the payload needed to survive BOTH main's own still-pending `festina_finish_request_dispatch` release AND the receiving thread's own eventual one -- construction (+1), detach's own retain (+1), two releases (-1, -1), netting to zero. TSan disagreed immediately: both releases are the SAME plain, non-atomic decrement `festina_release_check` already uses everywhere in this runtime (a foundational, load-bearing invariant of the whole `thread` feature since claude.md #195 -- "no two threads ever share a mutable refcounted pointer, so every retain/release stays the plain non-atomic increment/decrement it already is"), and a handed-off connection's own http value genuinely IS reachable from two threads at once for a brief window -- exactly the case that invariant assumes never happens. **Fixed by removing the race at its root, not by reaching for an atomic decrement** (which would have carved out a narrower exception to an invariant this whole runtime otherwise leans on): a new `__thread` flag, `g_last_detached_conn_id`, is set by `festina_conn_detach` on success and read (and cleared) by THIS SAME calling thread's own very next `festina_finish_request_dispatch` call, which skips releasing the payload entirely when it names the connection just detached -- leaving the payload's one, original, construction-time reference to be released exactly once, by exactly one thread: the receiving one, whenever its own delivery eventually runs. No retain needed at all; the two `festina_finish_request_dispatch` calls (main's own skipped one, the receiving thread's own real one) never touch the same refcount concurrently again, because only one of them ever touches it at all. Confirmed by re-running the exact TSan case that first caught it -- clean.

**Coverage added:** `tests/test_threads.py` gains a new `TestGiveRequest` (8 tests) -- accepted onto a thread with `on request`, an ordinary (non-`?`) `http` argument rejected with a specific message, a target with no `on request` rejected (including one that declared some OTHER http handler, proving `has_http_handler` alone isn't specific enough), wrong argument count, called from inside a thread body rejected (mirroring kill/live/isAlive's own main-only gate), the "no such method" error names `giveRequest` too, and a pool instance receiver works. `tests/test_codegen.py` gains a new `TestGiveRequest` (2 real compile-and-run tests, via the existing `compile_and_run_server` fixture and a genuine `http.client` GET) -- a handed-off request is genuinely answered by the RECEIVING thread (not main), and a thread that forgets to respond still gets the shared fallback-200 path, not a hang. New `tests/stress/thread_giverequest_churn.f` (100 real, full connect/hand-off/respond/verify round trips -- `driver`, a THIRD thread, makes the real client calls so nothing here can hit the self-directed-request deadlock api.md's own new section documents; `worker` is the one receiving hand-offs) registered in `tests/test_leak_stress.py`'s coverage-completeness manifest. api.md gains a new "Live connection hand-off" subsection (the `T?` requirement, the main-only/`on request`-required gates, the v1 scope limits -- TLS/already-responded/already-upgraded all documented, not silently absent -- and the self-directed-hand-off deadlock warning) and a cross-reference from "Per-thread HTTP context"'s own receive-only-context paragraph.

**Verified:** full suite green (2187 passed, 9 skipped, up from 2176/9 at claude.md #212). `scripts/leak_stress.sh`/`scripts/thread_tsan_stress.sh` against the new `thread_giverequest_churn.f` -- both clean AFTER the retain/release race fix above (the TSan run is what actually caught the race in the first place, and re-confirms it's gone, not just patched over) -- the highest-stakes cross-thread resource transfer in the whole thread-extensions plan, verified under real concurrency rather than by inspection alone.

214. `thread` EXTENSIONS, PHASE 6: DOCS/TESTS/RELEASE CONSOLIDATION

The audit pass closing out the whole `thread` extensions plan (claude.md #208-#213) -- mirrors claude.md #201's own "audit, don't rebuild" shape, since every prior phase already updated api.md and added its own claude.md entry incrementally as it landed, not batched here.

**Audited, found essentially already current.** Read api.md's Threads and HTTP/WebSocket sections end to end: the "Isolation" paragraph's "may not call" list, the old "Threads are singletons"/"thread-private helper functions aren't supported" limitations, and the per-phase capability lists were all already updated in place, incrementally, exactly as each phase (claude.md #209-#213) landed -- confirmed by grepping for stale "singleton"/"not supported yet"/`onMessage(` leftovers across api.md and finding none. Found and fixed the one genuine gap: the "Sendable types today" paragraph's own closing sentence (`func`/`http`/`socket`/`regex`/`table` "never will be" sendable) predates claude.md #213 and, read in isolation, now reads as contradicting `giveRequest`'s own existence -- clarified in place (an ordinary `postMessage` still never sends a live `http`/`socket`/`regex`/`table` value, unchanged; a **live** `http` request is a separate mechanism entirely -- handed off, never cloned, never routed through `postMessage` at all) with a cross-reference to the new "Live connection hand-off" section. `todo.md` confirmed to carry zero remaining thread/http/pool-related gap entries -- grepped directly, not assumed.
