215. `thread pool[N]` MULTI-THREADED HTTP: EXAMPLE, BENCHMARK, AND A REAL DATABASE-CONFLICT GAP CLOSED

Two follow-ups requested directly against the just-finished thread-extensions plan (claude.md #212/#213): a real example/benchmark showing genuine multi-core HTTP concurrency, and a compile-time guard the plan's own design left open -- a `thread pool[N]` declaring its own `DatabaseURL` (which the existing per-thread-sqlite feature, claude.md #199, otherwise permits) would have every one of its `N` instances open an independent, uncoordinated connection into the SAME literal file at once.

**The gap: a pool shares one `_ThreadInfo`, and `DatabaseURL` lived on it unguarded.** `_emit_thread_pool_decl` loops the unchanged `_emit_thread_decl` once per mangled instance name, but `info.database_url` (read from the ONE shared `_ThreadInfo`) is the identical literal for every instance -- each instance's own `on_load` independently calls `festina_db_open` on it, so `pool[4] { DatabaseURL = './x.sqlite' }` would silently open 4 real sqlite3* handles into `x.sqlite` at once, each running its own transactions in an OS thread the others know nothing about. Confirmed as a genuine hazard (not the "never shared" isolation an ordinary singleton thread's own `DatabaseURL` already guarantees), not a false alarm -- SQLite tolerates multiple connections to one file via its own locking, but nothing here was making that decision on purpose. **Fixed** with a dedicated check in `analyze_thread` (semantic.py), positioned ahead of the existing "must be the first statement" check so a pool gets the SPECIFIC "cannot declare its own DatabaseURL" reason rather than a confusing pass-then-fail on the general one -- `_current_thread[0].database_url` therefore now provably stays `None` forever for any pool, which means the EXISTING `_SQLITE_BUILTINS` gate (claude.md #199 Phase 5's own "declared no DatabaseURL" check) already, for free, rejects `sqlite()`/`sqliteInt()`/`sqliteFloat()`/`sqliteText()` from inside a pool body too -- no second gate needed, confirmed directly with a real semantic.analyze() call.

**Example: `examples/threaded_http_server.f`.** A `thread pool[4] { on request(req:http) { ... } }` (claude.md #212's own private per-thread HTTP context, no `openPort()` of its own -- a receive-only context) computing a real, closed-form-resistant CPU-bound loop (the same polynomial-hash technique `benchmarks/loop_sum.f` already established, so an optimizer can't fold it away) per `/slow` request; main accepts every connection on the one real port and round-robins each live request to the next worker via `NAME.giveRequest(r)` (claude.md #213). `/` answers instantly, directly from main, with no hand-off at all -- proof the pool doesn't tax a request that never needed it. Manually confirmed 4 concurrent `/slow` requests (each ~29ms of real work alone) complete together in ~50ms, not ~116ms (4×29ms) -- genuine parallelism, not a lucky number.

**Benchmark: `benchmarks/http_threaded/`.** `server_single.f` (identical `/slow` work, computed directly on Festina's one HTTP event-loop thread -- every concurrent request queues up behind whichever one is currently computing) vs. `server_pool.f.template` (`thread NAME[N]` requires a compile-time-literal pool size, so this one substitutes `__POOL_SIZE__` as a plain token before compiling -- the identical technique `tests/conftest.py`'s own `__PORT__` substitution already uses, for the identical reason: Festina source is full of its own bare `{`/`}`, which `str.format()` would misparse). `run_http_threaded_benchmark.py` mirrors `benchmarks/http/run_http_benchmarks.py`'s own `wrk`-based structure (same output parsing, same `--update-doc` convention), defaulting the pool size to `os.cpu_count()`. Measured on this machine (4 CPUs): `/` performs about the same on both servers (the control, proving the pool's own round-robin dispatch adds no meaningful overhead to a request that never goes through `giveRequest`); `/slow` throughput roughly **2.8-3.2x** higher on the pooled server across repeated runs -- real speedup, bounded by core count as expected, not the full 4x a zero-overhead ideal would show (accept-loop/hand-off/the worker's own bounded-poll latency all cost something real, each already documented in claude.md #212/#213). New "HTTP: single-threaded vs. thread pool" section in benchmark.md, with the same auto-generated-results-block convention the cross-language HTTP section already uses.

**Coverage added:** `tests/test_threads.py::TestThreadPools` gains 2 new tests (a pool declaring `DatabaseURL` rejected with the specific message; a pool still correctly rejected from calling `sqlite()` with no database, proving the existing gate covers it for free). `tests/test_examples.py` gains a new `TestThreadedHttpServerExample` (compiles the real shipped example file, runs it as a background server, confirms `/` and four concurrent `/slow` requests -- matching the example's own `WORKER_COUNT` -- all answer correctly) -- `threaded_http_server.f` is also automatically covered by the existing `TestAllExamplesCompile` sweep, no wiring needed there. api.md's "Thread pools" section gains the DatabaseURL restriction, explained. README.md's examples table gains a row.

**Verified:** full suite green (2191 passed, 9 skipped, up from 2187/9 at claude.md #214).

216. `worker:thread` IS NEVER `null` -- MAIN BECOMES A REAL THREAD VALUE (`.main:bool`)

Phase 1 of a larger, directly requested messaging redesign: `worker`/`t` (the `on message(worker:thread, msg:T)` parameter) is never `null` any more -- when main is the sender, `worker` is a real, singleton `thread` value instead, distinguished from an ordinary worker's own handle by a new `.main:bool` field. The rest of the requested redesign -- a `.reply(T)`/`NAME.postMessage(x).callback(fn)` request/response mechanism, and removing `sqlite()`/`sqliteInt()`/`sqliteFloat()`/`sqliteText()` -- are separate, later phases of the same request, not part of this entry.

**Runtime: one process-wide singleton, not a second worker loop.** `festina_runtime_thread.c` gains `static FestinaThreadHandle g_main_handle = { .is_main = 1 }` -- a real, non-NULL `FestinaThreadHandle`-shaped value that is never `pthread_create`'d, never registered into `g_registry`, and never has `on_load`/`on_message`/`in_release` set; it exists purely as an identity token, returned by the new `festina_thread_get_main_handle()` and read by `festina_thread_is_main(void*)`. `struct FestinaThreadHandle` gains one new field, `int is_main` (0 for every ordinary `festina_thread_register`'d handle, via `calloc`'s own zero-fill -- no explicit code needed there). The ONE call site that used to pass literal `null` as `festina_thread_post`'s `sender` argument -- `NAME.postMessage(x)` called from main's own top-level code, codegen.py's ThreadType Member-call dispatch -- now calls `festina_thread_get_main_handle()` instead. Every thread-to-main send already passed a real, non-NULL `sender` (`h` itself, via `festina_thread_post_outbound`, claude.md #208) -- that path is completely unchanged; only main's own outbound direction needed a real value to send in place of `null`.

**semantic.py: `.main` is the one new field; comparing `thread` against `null` is now a compile error.** A new `ThreadType` branch in the field-access dispatch (alongside HttpType/SocketType's own field/method split) recognizes `.main`, returning `bool`; every other field name is a clear error naming `.main` as the one that exists. The `==`/`!=` compatibility check's old `ThreadType`-vs-`ThreadType` guard (claude.md #208: "may only be compared against null") is widened: `thread` vs. `null` on either side is now ALSO rejected, with a message pointing at `.main` -- `worker == null` used to be live, meaningful code; leaving it silently compiling to an always-false comparison after this change would be strictly worse than a clear error surfacing every call site that needs updating. `thread` vs. `thread` (two real values) stays rejected exactly as before, unrelated to this change (the pre-existing invalid-LLVM-IR hazard `struct == struct` already has).

**codegen.py: `.main` is a bare runtime call, no ownership question.** `_emit_http_socket_field` (the shared field-read codegen HttpType/SocketType already use) gains a `ThreadType` branch emitting `call i8 @festina_thread_is_main(ptr %obj)` -- `bool` is `i8` in this project's LLVM convention (not `i1` -- see `_llvm_type`'s own comment), matching `festina_thread_is_alive`'s identical shape exactly. `_release_owned_receiver` is called anyway for consistency with every other field-read branch here, though it's a genuine no-op for `ThreadType` (`_is_refcounted` gates it, and a `thread` value is a bare, non-refcounted `ptr` -- unchanged from claude.md #208).

**Verified:** every `worker == null` call site in the existing suite updated (`tests/test_threads.py`, one real usage in `tests/stress/thread_private_func_churn.f` -- both moved to `worker.main`). New coverage: `worker.main` reads `true` on a main-originated send and `false` on both a worker's own reply to main and a genuine thread-to-thread send (a discriminated round trip through a real second thread proves this isn't just "always false by accident" -- `tests/test_codegen.py`'s two new compile-and-run tests), `worker == null` is now a clear compile error naming `.main`, and the pre-existing `thread == thread` rejection still holds (`tests/test_threads.py`). api.md's "Sending and receiving" paragraph updated in place. Full suite green: 2194 passed, 9 skipped, up from 2191/9 at claude.md #215.

217. `t.reply(response)` / `NAME.postMessage(x).callback(fn)` -- REQUEST/RESPONSE MESSAGING

Phase 2 of the messaging redesign (claude.md #216 was Phase 1): a general request/response mechanism on top of the existing message-passing model, requested directly in the user's own words -- "For serialized responses, use `.reply(response:T)`, each thread can only have 1 reply type... the type must match the callback. If there is no callback, compile error because postMessage should be used. `.reply` also does not trigger the `on message` event." The originally-discussed `t.postMessage()`/transaction-id-as-a-visible-property design was superseded entirely by this `.reply()`/`.callback()` shape and never implemented -- the transaction id stayed a purely internal runtime correlation detail, never exposed to Festina code.

**The design: `.reply()`'s own receiving context fixes a reply type; `.callback(fn)` is checked against it.** `worker.reply(x)` is legal on ANY expression of the GENERIC `thread` type (there is no other way to obtain one, per `ThreadType`'s own doc comment, so gating purely on TYPE is exactly as precise as gating on "is this literally the `worker` parameter" would be). The FIRST `t.reply(...)` call site found textually inside a receiving context's own body (main's top-level `on message`, or a specific thread's own) fixes that context's `reply_type`; every later call in the same context is `check_assignable`'d against it (enum-coercion included, exactly like an ordinary parameter). Once a context has a `reply_type`, `.callback(fn)` becomes mandatory on every `NAME.postMessage(x)` call site targeting it -- the bare form included, so a worker sending to a main that replies must chain `.callback` too -- checked two ways: a NEW combined-pattern branch in `_infer_call` recognizes `X.postMessage(y).callback(fn)` as one AST shape (mirroring the existing `<text>.callback(fn)` file-loading precedent's own "match the shape directly" style, claude.md #165/#171) and validates `fn`'s signature; a bare (unchained) `postMessage(...)` reaching `ExprStmt`-level analysis is rejected if its target's `reply_type` isn't `None`. Together these cover the only two syntactically valid positions a postMessage call can appear in.

**Runtime: an ambient per-thread "which message am I answering" slot, plus a self-only pending-callback list.** `FestinaThreadMsg` gains `txn_id` (0 = no callback expected) and a new `FESTINA_THREAD_MSG_REPLY` kind. `.postMessage(x).callback(fn)` allocates a fresh id (`festina_thread_alloc_txn_id`, one atomic counter mirroring `festina_runtime_http.c`'s own `g_next_conn_id`), registers `(trampoline, fn)` on the SENDING handle's own `pending_callbacks` list (`festina_thread_register_callback`), then sends the ordinary message carrying that id. The dispatch loop on the receiving end (`festina_thread_try_dispatch_one` for a worker, `festina_thread_drain_impl` for main) sets a new `__thread g_current_reply_txn` right before calling `on_message` -- an ordinary message still triggers `on_message` completely normally, `.reply()` is purely additive. `worker.reply(x)` boxes `x` and calls `festina_thread_reply(self, dest, payload)`, which reads that ambient id and enqueues a REPLY-kind message to `dest` (the worker's own inbound queue, or -- via `dest->is_main` -- `self`'s own outbound queue, the exact path an ordinary bare send already uses to reach main). A REPLY message never calls `on_message`; it's looked up by `txn_id` in the RECEIVING handle's own `pending_callbacks` (`festina_thread_dispatch_reply`) and dispatched straight to a codegen-generated trampoline (`_emit_reply_callback_trampoline`, one per distinct `reply_type`, cached) that unboxes the payload, calls the user's `fn`, and releases the box. **`pending_callbacks` needs no lock at all** -- a handle's own sends and its own reply-dispatches always happen on that SAME OS thread (main's singleton included), so this list is self-only by construction, the same reasoning `festina_runtime_http.c`'s own per-thread connection tables already rely on.

**A real bug found and fixed along the way, unrelated to the new feature but exposed by reasoning through it carefully: `festina_thread_kill`'s leftover-message cleanup was already type-confused.** `festina_thread_free_msg_list` called `in_release` (the ORDINARY message's own release function) on every leftover queued message unconditionally -- including a GIVE_REQUEST message's `FestinaGiveRequestPayload*` (claude.md #213), a completely different struct. This was a pre-existing, latent type-confusion bug (a thread killed with a `giveRequest` still queued would call the wrong release function on the wrong struct shape); REPLY messages would have hit the identical hazard the moment this phase shipped. Fixed by making the cleanup kind-aware (only ORDINARY payloads go through `in_release`; a GIVE_REQUEST payload's own small wrapper is freed directly, documented as a narrow, accepted gap -- the connection it names is simply never returned to a listener; a REPLY payload is left unreleased, the same accepted "a reply that never arrives" leak `FestinaPendingCallback`'s own doc comment already covers). `festina_thread_kill` also now frees (never invokes) any callbacks the killed thread had registered for its own past sends, so a later `live()` respawn can't inherit stale registrations that could collide with an unrelated future send's own txn id.

**A real ThreadSanitizer-caught data race -- in this phase's own FIRST stress-test draft, not the feature itself.** `.callback(fn)`'s `fn` runs back on whichever OS thread originally sent the message -- for a worker sending to main via the bare form, that's the WORKER's own thread, not main's, a genuinely new characteristic (blob/img/aud's own `.callback()`, claude.md #165/#171, always marshals onto main via `festina_async_io_drain`; this one deliberately doesn't, matching the general-purpose, efficient design actually requested). The first draft of `tests/stress/thread_reply_callback_churn.f` had two independent callback streams (main replying to a worker, a worker replying to main) both touching a SHARED `maybeDone()` reading each other's counters -- a genuine cross-thread race, caught immediately by `scripts/thread_tsan_stress.sh`. Fixed by rewriting the file so the ONE stream that genuinely exercises the new off-main dispatch path (`worker2`'s own bare sends) owns counters touched by nothing else, with its own completion check relying on the SAME "main's top-level code always finishes before it can ever drain a reply" ordering guarantee every other close()-in-a-callback test in this suite already depends on. This new hazard -- `fn`'s body being ordinary, non-isolated code that can nonetheless run off main -- is now documented explicitly in api.md, its own paragraph, not left implicit.

**Coverage added:** `tests/test_threads.py::TestReplyCallback` (8 new semantic tests: round-trip type-checking, the two "must chain .callback"/"chaining onto a non-replying target" rejections, the callback-type-mismatch rejection, reply-type-fixed-by-first-call enforcement, main replying to a bare sender, and `.reply` only recognized on the generic `thread` type). `tests/test_codegen.py::TestThreadReplyCallback` (4 new compile-and-run tests: main-to-worker round trip, worker-to-main bare round trip -- synchronized via `setTimeout`, since the callback fires on the worker's own OS thread asynchronously relative to main's own `close()` -- `.reply()` never re-triggering `on message`, and two concurrent outstanding replies from the same sender resolving to the correct callbacks, not each other's). New `tests/stress/thread_reply_callback_churn.f` under both `scripts/leak_stress.sh` and `scripts/thread_tsan_stress.sh` (manifest-registered in `tests/test_leak_stress.py`). api.md gains the "Request/response" subsection plus the `fn`-runs-off-main hazard paragraph.

**Verified:** full suite green (2207 passed, 9 skipped, up from 2194/9 at claude.md #216). `scripts/leak_stress.sh` and `scripts/thread_tsan_stress.sh` both clean after the stress-test rewrite above (the TSan run caught a real race on the first attempt, confirming the sanitizer pass is pulling its weight here, not just a formality).

218. THREADING REVIEW: SIX REAL BUGS, TWO INEFFICIENCIES, AND A RESTRUCTURED api.md THREADS SECTION

A requested end-to-end review of everything `thread`-shaped -- the runtime translation unit, semantic.py's own thread paths, codegen's, and api.md's Threads section -- looking specifically for bugs, inefficiencies and documentation that no longer matches the implementation. Everything below was found by reading the code and then CONFIRMING each finding with a real compile-and-run, not by inspection alone.

**Bug: an out-of-range pool index registered a callback that could never fire.** `pool[i].postMessage(x).callback(fn)` emitted the txn allocation and `festina_thread_register_callback` BEFORE `_emit_thread_target_handle` opened its own bounds-checked block, so an out-of-range `i` registered a pending callback and then skipped the send -- `fn` could never run, and its slot sat on the sender's own `pending_callbacks` list for the life of the process. Registration and send are now emitted together, inside the block, so an out-of-range index is a complete no-op for the whole expression (argument included, matching what `pool[i].postMessage(x)` alone already did). Confirmed both ways with a real `pool[5]`-vs-`pool[0]` program. `giveRequest`'s own pool path was checked for the identical hazard and is already correct -- its `festina_conn_detach` call sits INSIDE the bounds-checked block, so an out-of-range hand-off never detaches a connection it then fails to deliver.

**Bug: `.reply()` outside a live dispatch silently dropped the reply AND leaked its payload.** `festina_thread_reply` read the ambient `g_current_reply_txn` without checking it was non-zero, so a reply with no message in flight was still malloc'd, enqueued, found no matching pending callback on arrival, and had its payload abandoned (nothing downstream could name the right release function). Two ways to reach it, both real and both confirmed by compiling programs that do it: a handler calling `.reply()` a SECOND time for one message (the first consumed the only pending slot), and a `thread` value stashed somewhere that outlives its own dispatch -- a struct field, an `arr[thread]`, a `map[thread]` are all accepted today -- replied to later from a timer or another handler. Now: nothing is enqueued and the payload is released immediately.

**Bug (the same leak, generalized): a reply with nothing to dispatch to had no release path at all.** `FestinaThreadMsg` gained a `release` field, recorded by the SENDER at reply time from codegen's own `_thread_payload_release_fn(reply_type)` -- the receiving side only ever knows its own inbound type, never the sender's reply type, which is exactly why this leak existed. Every path that can drop a reply now releases it properly: the undispatchable case on both the worker-side (`festina_thread_try_dispatch_one`) and main-side (`festina_thread_drain_impl`) branches, and a reply still queued when its target is `kill()`'d (`festina_thread_free_msg_list`, which previously documented the leak rather than fixing it). `tests/stress/thread_reply_callback_churn.f` now replies TWICE to every one of its 5,000 messages -- 5,000 deliberately-dropped replies per run -- and `scripts/leak_stress.sh` is clean.

**Bug: `festina_thread_give_request` left fields uninitialized.** It `malloc`s a `FestinaThreadMsg` and set every field except `txn_id` (and, after this entry, `release`). Harmless only because the GIVE_REQUEST dispatch branch happens to return before reading either -- the kind of "true today, silently wrong the moment someone adds a read" gap worth closing rather than documenting. Both are now explicitly zeroed.

**Bug: `type_name()` had no `ThreadType` case at all,** so every user-facing message about a thread value fell through to `str(t)` and printed this compiler's own Python repr: `cannot assign value of type ThreadType(None) to int`. It says `thread` now (and `thread 'name'` for a specific declared one). Two more error-message fixes alongside it: `log(w)`/`` `${w}` `` on a thread value fell through to generic fallbacks (the template one didn't even name the FILE, reporting `<string>:0:0`) and now get img/aud's own specific "has no text form" message; the "thread has no field X" error suggested `.postMessage()` as the fix, which is not a method on a thread VALUE at all (it's a method on a declared thread's NAME) -- it now names `.main`/`.reply(x)` and shows the `someThread.postMessage(x)` spelling; and the "cannot cross a thread boundary" error listed every unsendable type EXCEPT `thread` itself, which became a real holdable value in claude.md #208/#216.

**Inefficiency: the pending-callback list was O(N^2) for the ordinary case.** `festina_thread_register_callback` PREPENDED, and `festina_thread_dispatch_reply` scans linearly -- but replies come back in the order their sends went out (a target thread drains its own inbound queue strictly in order), so the entry every arriving reply wanted was always at the END of the list. N outstanding sends cost N^2/2 pointer hops. Appending at a tail pointer instead makes that same common case an O(1) head hit. **Measured by building the identical stress program both ways** (prepend vs append, nothing else changed): 5,000 in-flight sends, 0.06s -> 0.04s; 20,000 in-flight sends, 0.92s -> 0.47s. The gap widening with N is the actual point -- the constant factor is modest at small N and unbounded at large N, which is what removing a quadratic gets you.

**Inefficiency: two mutex acquisitions per message on the hottest path.** A thread with no HTTP context locked `in_lock`, waited on its condvar, unlocked, then called `festina_thread_try_dispatch_one`, which locked `in_lock` AGAIN to dequeue -- two full round trips for every single message delivered. The wait now happens INSIDE that function, under the same acquisition that dequeues (a new `blocking` parameter; the HTTP-context loop passes 0 and keeps polling, unchanged). Same predicate, same spurious-wakeup behavior, half the mutex traffic.

**Measured and documented rather than changed: a thread pool compiles its body once per instance.** `_emit_thread_pool_decl` loops `_emit_thread_decl` over N mangled instance names, which is what makes instances genuinely independent with zero runtime indirection -- but it means N copies of the generated code. Measured on a ~12-line body: ~136 lines of LLVM IR per instance, so `pool[32]` emits 4,758 IR lines against `pool[1]`'s 542 (8.8x). Sharing one body across instances would need per-instance state reached indirectly rather than through fixed globals -- a real redesign, not a tweak -- so this is now stated plainly in api.md as a compiled-size decision instead of a surprise.

**api.md's Threads section: 428 lines, zero subsections, and a false claim.** Every other major section in this file (HTTP, Graphics, Files) uses `###` subsections; Threads had grown to 428 lines of bold-paragraph markers, in the order the features happened to be built rather than the order anyone reads them, with every cross-reference pointing at the section anchor `#threads` instead of the thing being referenced (and one, "see Thread-private functions above", pointing the wrong direction entirely). It now has ten real subsections -- sending/receiving, request/response, private state, private functions, lifecycle, isolation, database, pools, HTTP context, hand-off -- ordered basics-then-advanced, with every cross-reference resolving to a real anchor. A checker over the whole file found one genuinely broken pre-existing link (`#http--websocket-servers`, from back when that heading used `&`) and it is fixed; all 30 intra-doc anchors now resolve. Corrected on the way through: the claim that "`thread`'s only other operation is `.postMessage()`" -- exactly backwards, a `thread` value has `.main` and `.reply()` and specifically does NOT have `.postMessage()`. Newly documented because it was true but unwritten: reply at most once per message, a stashed `thread` value replies to nothing, `kill()` drops pending callbacks, a `thread` value has no text form, and the pool code-size cost above.

**Verified:** full suite green (2213 passed, 9 skipped, up from 2207/9 at claude.md #217 -- 6 new regression tests, one per bug above). An earlier run of the same suite showed 2 failures in `TestFullscreenAndDecorations`; both pass in isolation and on a re-run, a window-manager timing flake unrelated to anything here (nothing in this entry touches X11). `scripts/leak_stress.sh` and `scripts/thread_tsan_stress.sh` both clean, the former now exercising 5,000 deliberately-dropped replies per run.

219. REMOVED `sqliteInt()`/`sqliteFloat()`/`sqliteText()` -- `sqlite()` ITSELF, `table`, AND `DatabaseURL` UNTOUCHED

Requested directly, narrower than the full sqlite removal considered (and explicitly cancelled) alongside the messaging redesign in claude.md #216-#218: only the three single-value-query convenience wrappers `sqlite()` grew in claude.md #94 come out. `sqlite()`, `table`, and `DatabaseURL` are unaffected -- every ordinary query, insert, and per-thread private database keeps working exactly as before.

**Why these three specifically earned removal.** They existed to avoid declaring a `table` (which CREATES a real table via claude.md #28-31's schema sync) just to receive one scalar value like a `count(*)`. But a `struct` -- unlike a `table` -- creates no real table when used as a query target (claude.md #97's own struct-as-query-target feature), so `arr[SomeStruct] x = sqlite('SELECT count(*) AS n FROM ...')` already gave the identical schema-free round trip through `sqlite()`'s own one prepare-and-bind-and-step path. Three near-duplicate builtins, each differing from `sqlite()` only in how it stepped and unwrapped the first column, were paying an ongoing "one more thing to learn and gate per-thread" cost for a capability the general path already had for free.

**semantic.py/codegen.py: delete, don't deprecate.** `BUILTIN_FUNCTIONS` and the builtin return-type dict lose their three entries; `_SQLITE_BUILTINS` shrinks to `frozenset({"sqlite"})` (the per-thread `DatabaseURL`-gates-`sqlite()` check in `_infer_call` and the bound-parameter-array mixed-type carve-out both key off this set, so both narrow automatically -- no separate code path to remove for either). codegen.py's `_emit_sqlite_scalar` method and its three `festina_sqlite_scalar_int/_float/_text` LLVM `declare` lines are deleted outright, not stubbed -- a program still calling `sqliteInt()` now gets the same clear "no such function" compile error any other removed builtin gets, not a silent no-op or a deprecation warning. The runtime C functions themselves (`festina_runtime.c`/`.h`) are deleted too; nothing else called them.

**Every remaining call site across tests/stress/docs rewritten onto the struct-target pattern, not just deleted.** `tests/stress/thread_db_churn.f` and `structs_and_rows_churn.f` (both under `scripts/leak_stress.sh`, the latter also under `scripts/thread_tsan_stress.sh`) had their `sqliteInt('SELECT count(*) FROM ...')` calls replaced with `arr[T] counted = sqlite('SELECT count(*) AS <field> FROM ...')` against an already-declared `table`/`struct` in each file, preserving the exact same coverage (real concurrent sqlite traffic across two OS threads' own separate databases, still racing on the shared prepared-statement cache registry) rather than thinning it. `tests/test_codegen.py::TestScalarQueries` (5 tests exercising the wrappers directly, including JSON1 and FTS5 passthrough) became `TestStructTargetScalarQueries` (4 tests: the no-extra-table proof, no-match-is-an-empty-array in place of the old no-match-is-null semantics -- the struct-array path doesn't have a null-scalar case, since a query matching no rows now returns a zero-length `arr[T]` rather than a value to compare -- and JSON1/FTS5 passthrough re-verified through the new pattern rather than dropped). api.md's "Single-value queries" and "JSON and full-text search" subsections rewritten to show the `struct`-target idiom directly rather than describing removed functions with a note.

**Coverage added:** none new -- this is a pure removal plus a like-for-like rewrite of existing coverage onto the surviving mechanism, so no new behavior needed a new test. Confirmed instead: `sqliteInt(...)` now raises the ordinary "no such function" `CompileError` any unrecognized identifier would.

**Verified:** full suite green (2212 passed, 9 skipped, down from 2213/9 at claude.md #218 -- net -1 from replacing `TestScalarQueries`'s 5 tests with `TestStructTargetScalarQueries`'s 4, equivalent coverage through the surviving mechanism). `scripts/leak_stress.sh` and `scripts/thread_tsan_stress.sh` both clean on the two rewritten stress files.

220. `thread NAME[] { ... }` -- AUTO-SIZED THREAD POOLS

Requested directly: `thread NAME[] { ... }` (empty brackets, no literal `N`) sizes itself to `os.cpu_count()` minus every other thread the program declares, floored at 1; `thread NAME { ... }` (no brackets at all) stays exactly what it always was, a singleton -- stated by the user for contrast, not a behavior change.

**The one real design fork: compile time or run time.** The literal reading of "os.cpu_count()" is "however many cores the machine actually RUNNING the binary has" -- but claude.md #218's own "pool compiles its body once per instance" finding already established that today's pool codegen has no shared, runtime-indexed body at all: `_emit_thread_pool_decl` compiles `N` full, independently-named copies of the body, and emits a compile-time-sized `[N x ptr]` global array of handle pointers. Making `N` a genuine runtime value would need exactly the redesign that finding already flagged as out of scope (share one body, reach per-instance state indirectly) -- a multi-day undertaking, not a same-day feature. Put to the user directly: compile time (the count is read on the machine COMPILING the program, baked into the binary as an ordinary literal -- fits the existing architecture exactly, but the binary's pool size won't adapt if later run on a different machine) vs. run time (the more literal reading, but needs the large pool-codegen redesign). Compile time was chosen.

**semantic.py: a new pre-pass, resolving a parser sentinel before anything else reads `pool_size`.** The parser leaves `pool_size = "auto"` on the AST node for empty brackets (a new one-token lookahead in `parse_thread_decl`: `[` immediately followed by `]`, distinct from `[` `NUMBER` `]`). A new pre-pass at the very top of `analyze()` -- alongside the existing struct/table/enum name pre-pass and the function-hoisting pre-pass, the same "resolve names/facts before anything needs them" shape those already use -- walks `program.body` once, sums every OTHER thread's own fixed instance count (`None` counts 1, an explicit `NAME[N]` counts `N`; another `NAME[]` auto pool is deliberately NOT counted, so two auto pools in the same program don't have to solve a system of equations between them -- each sizes independently against the same fixed total, at the cost of both getting the full remaining budget rather than splitting it, a simple and order-independent rule stated plainly in api.md), then mutates each `"auto"` node's `pool_size` into `max(1, os.cpu_count() - that total)`. Every later reader -- the rest of semantic.py (`_ThreadInfo.pool_size = node.pool_size`), all of codegen.py (`decl.pool_size`, `pinfo["pool_size"]`) -- sees an ordinary positive int and needs zero changes; the "auto" sentinel exists for exactly the span between parsing and this one pre-pass.

**Coverage added:** `tests/test_threads.py::TestThreadPools` gains 6 semantic tests (`os.cpu_count()` monkeypatched for determinism): auto-sizes to the full cpu count with nothing else declared, subtracts a singleton's 1, subtracts an explicit pool's own N, floors at 1 when other threads already exceed the cpu count, two auto pools each get the same (unsplit) remaining budget, and an auto-sized declaration indexes (`pool[0].postMessage(...)`) exactly like an ordinary one. `tests/test_codegen.py::TestThreadPools` gains a real compile-and-run proof (`cpu_count()` monkeypatched to 3, one singleton declared alongside): the resolved pool genuinely has 2 live instances (`pool[0]`/`pool[1]` alive, `pool[2]` out of range) -- not just that the resolved-size program compiles. api.md's "Thread pools" section gains a paragraph on `[]` and the two-auto-pools rule.

**Verified:** full suite green (2219 passed, 9 skipped, up from 2212/9 at claude.md #219 -- 7 new tests: 6 semantic, 1 compile-and-run). `scripts/leak_stress.sh` and `scripts/thread_tsan_stress.sh` both clean (codegen.py is untouched by this entry -- an auto-sized pool becomes an ordinary compile-time-sized pool before codegen ever runs, so nothing new for either sanitizer to exercise beyond the existing pool coverage both already have).

221. REMOVED `exec(args, callback)` -- THE NON-BLOCKING FORM

Requested directly, first of a batch of smaller fixes and removals covering threading/leak/scoping questions across the codebase. `exec(args)` (the blocking, single-argument form, claude.md #150) is unaffected -- only the non-blocking, 2-argument form claude.md #177 added is gone.

**Why:** claude.md #218's own threading review already flagged this specific gap while covering something else entirely -- `exec`'s comment block noted its 2-argument form's callback "is documented to run on MAIN's OS thread regardless of which thread dispatched it... a real cross-thread-isolation violation." That was true the whole time this form existed: a thread calling `exec(args, callback)` could hand `callback` a closure over its own private state, and that closure would then run on a DIFFERENT OS thread (main's) than the one that captured it -- exactly the class of bug this language's whole thread design (deep-copy-everything-crossing-the-boundary, no shared mutable state) exists to make impossible everywhere else. Removing the form closes the gap outright rather than continuing to special-case it.

**semantic.py:** the arity-dependent `if name == "exec":` handling (1 argument -> int, 2 -> void with a structurally-checked `func[int]:void` callback) collapses to the single 1-argument form. The dedicated `exec(args, callback)`-inside-a-thread rejection (a specific error naming the cross-thread hazard, checked ahead of the ordinary arity check) is deleted -- with only one arity left, the ordinary "exec() expects 1 argument" error now covers a 2-argument call site everywhere, thread body included, with nothing thread-specific left to say.

**codegen.py/runtime:** the 2-argument branch (dispatch through `festina_process_exec_dispatch`, the async-io background worker) is deleted from `_emit_call`'s exec handling; `_emit_exec_callback_trampoline` (the generic, payload-data-driven `void(ptr)` bridge every 2-argument call site shared) is deleted entirely, along with its cached-symbol field. `runtime/festina_runtime.c`/`.h` lose `festina_process_exec_dispatch`, `FestinaExecPayload`, `festina_exec_worker`, and `festina_exec_payload_free` -- `festina_run_argv` (the shared fork/execvp/waitpid core both forms called) stays, now with only `festina_process_exec` (the blocking form) as its one remaining caller, and its own doc comment simplified to match.

**Coverage:** `tests/test_codegen.py::TestExecCallback` (8 tests, all specific to the removed form) is deleted; a single new negative test on `TestExec` confirms `exec(args, callback)` is now a plain "expects 1 argument" error. `tests/test_async_io.py::TestExecCallbackSemantics` (9 tests) is replaced by a 3-test `TestExecArity` covering the same shape (1-arg fine, 2-arg rejected, first-argument-type-checking still works) without the now-dead callback-signature-checking tests. `tests/test_threads.py`'s own thread-specific rejection test is updated to expect the ordinary arity error instead of the deleted thread-specific message. `tests/stress/exec_callback_churn.f` (a program that only exists to exercise the removed dispatch/payload/trampoline path under ASan) is deleted, and its manifest entry in `tests/test_leak_stress.py` removed with it. api.md's own "Running without blocking: `exec(args, callback)`" subsection is deleted outright (not just edited); the Threads section's `#thread-limitations` paragraph is rewritten to cover only the still-real HTTP-client-callback hazard, with a note that `exec()` no longer has this problem at all.

**Verified:** full suite green (2206 passed, 9 skipped, down from 2219/9 at claude.md #220 -- net -13 from deleting 17 tests specific to the removed form and adding 4 covering its removal). One unrelated flake seen in a full run (`test_audio_demo_plays_through_the_null_alsa_device`, an audio-channel-pool timing test under the null ALSA device -- passes cleanly in isolation; nothing here touches audio). `scripts/leak_stress.sh` (no more `exec_callback_churn.f` to run) and `scripts/thread_tsan_stress.sh` both clean -- this entry only removes code, touching no runtime path either sanitizer suite would newly need to cover.

222. `.callback(fn)` NOW FIRES ON MAIN'S OWN OS THREAD FOR A SEND ADDRESSED TO MAIN -- NOT THE SENDING WORKER'S

Requested directly: "fix callback(fn) not running on main thread (or current thread if one worker uses callback on another)." Fixes exactly the hazard claude.md #217/#218 both already named but left as documented, accepted behavior: a worker's own bare `postMessage(x).callback(fn)` (always addressed to main) had `fn` fire back on the SENDING WORKER's own OS thread once main replied, not main's -- a real cross-thread-isolation violation for a language whose whole thread story is "no shared mutable state to race on." A worker messaging ANOTHER worker directly is unaffected by design (the user's own "or current thread" clause) -- `fn` still fires on the sending worker's own thread there, since that send never touches main at all.

**Why only the bare-to-main case was broken.** `.callback(fn)` registers `(txn_id -> trampoline, fn)` on the SENDING handle's own list (self-only, no lock -- claude.md #217's own design). A reply is delivered to `dest` -- the ORIGINAL sender's handle -- via `festina_thread_reply`: if `dest->is_main`, it's enqueued on the replying handle's own OUTBOUND queue (drained by main); otherwise it's enqueued on `dest`'s own INBOUND queue (drained by `dest` itself). Main-sent-to-worker traffic always has `dest->is_main` true (dest is main's own singleton) -- correctly drained and dispatched by main, since main is both the original registrant and the drainer, no fix needed. Worker-sent-bare-to-main traffic has `dest` = the WORKER's own real handle (whoever the sender was, per the `on message(worker, msg)` parameter) -- `dest->is_main` is FALSE, so the reply lands on the WORKER's own inbound queue, and the worker's own dispatch loop found and ran the trampoline INLINE, on itself. Worker-to-worker traffic follows the identical "lands on the sender's own inbound queue" path, dispatched by the sender -- already exactly the "current thread" behavior wanted, untouched by this fix.

**The fix: a compile-time-known flag on the registration, consulted at dispatch time to decide inline-vs-marshaled.** `FestinaPendingCallback` gains `dispatch_on_main` (1 only for a worker's own registration of the bare form -- codegen's own AST shape at the `.callback()` call site already knows this: `pm_callee` is a bare Identifier for the bare form, a Member for a named one). `festina_thread_dispatch_reply` (called from BOTH the worker's own inbound-queue loop and main's own outbound-drain loop -- the single place that decides whether to call `trampoline` at all) now branches on it: unset, call `trampoline` inline exactly as before (worker-to-worker, and every main-registered entry, which is never bare); set, wrap `(trampoline, fn, payload)` in a small malloc'd struct and hand it to `festina_async_io_dispatch` -- the SAME cross-thread-safe mechanism `blob`/`img`/`aud`'s own `.callback()` already uses (a no-op `work_fn`, since the reply payload already arrived fully formed; the real work happens in `callback`, which `festina_async_io_dispatch`'s own contract guarantees runs on MAIN, once `festina_async_io_drain()` next runs from main's own event loop). `festina_thread_register_callback` gains the flag as a 5th parameter; codegen passes `handle is None` (the bare-form AST test already used to choose which send-emission function to call) as a literal `i8 1`/`0`. Emitting a bare-form registration also now sets `self.uses_async_io = True`, so the real worker pool and hooks are actually linked -- without it, `festina_async_io_dispatch`'s own documented fallback (no hook registered) runs the job INLINE, on whatever thread called it, silently defeating the fix.

**A real, previously-latent data race found and fixed along the way -- not hypothesized, caught directly by ThreadSanitizer the first time this path was ever exercised.** `festina_async_io_dispatch`/`_run` had never before been called from any thread but main (blob/img/aud's `.callback()` is ordinary program code; the one other caller, `exec(args, callback)`'s own dispatch, was removed in claude.md #221, and was itself blocked from thread bodies for the identical reason this whole entry exists). `festina_async_io_outstanding_impl`'s own `g_outstanding` read was deliberately unlocked, reasoned as safe because every write also came from main -- true right up until this fix made a WORKER thread a second writer. `scripts/thread_tsan_stress.sh` caught it immediately on `thread_reply_callback_churn.f` (5,000 bare sends from a worker): a genuine multi-writer race on `g_outstanding`, `festina_runtime_async.c:117`. Fixed by locking the read under the pool's own existing `g_lock` -- cheap (called once per main-loop iteration, uncontended in the common case) and now correct regardless of which thread writes.

**Coverage:** no new semantic-level tests -- this is a pure runtime dispatch-thread fix, invisible to semantic analysis (no new syntax, no new compile error). `tests/test_codegen.py::TestThreadReplyCallback`'s `test_worker_to_main_bare_reply_round_trip` docstring corrected (it used to explicitly document the bug as intended behavior); `tests/test_threads.py::TestThreadWiderBuiltinAccess`'s own docstring updated for consistency with claude.md #221's exec() simplification. `tests/stress/thread_reply_callback_churn.f`'s own top comment rewritten to describe the fixed behavior (its 5,000-bare-sends-per-run shape is what caught the g_outstanding race, and now serves as its regression guard) -- confirmed the fix's own honest limit directly: Festina exposes no OS-thread-identity primitive a pytest-level test could check, so a synthetic "prove it happened on this thread" ordering test was tried, found to not actually discriminate the two cases (both the buggy and fixed builds produced identical output ordering, confirmed by literally reverting the fix locally and re-running), and discarded rather than kept as a misleading green check -- the decisive proof is the ThreadSanitizer race above, real and directly attributable to this exact code path. api.md's own `.callback()`-off-main hazard paragraph rewritten: the remaining hazard is scoped to worker-to-worker sends only, with the main-addressed cases (both directions) now explicitly safe by construction.

**Verified:** full suite green (2206 passed, 9 skipped, unchanged from claude.md #221 -- this entry adds no new test, only corrects a docstring and a stress file's own comment). `scripts/leak_stress.sh` and `scripts/thread_tsan_stress.sh` both clean, the latter only after the `g_outstanding` fix above -- confirmed failing (a real, reproducible race) before it, clean after, on both the single-file and full-suite runs.

223. FIXED: `toStruct()`/`toArr()`'S PARTIAL-PARSE-FAILURE LEAK -- api.md'S OWN DOCUMENTED "ONE REAL, HONEST LIMITATION"

Requested directly, next in the same batch as claude.md #221/#222: the leak api.md itself already documented -- a JSON value that fails to parse *partway through* being built (a struct's third field turning out to be the wrong type, having already parsed the first two; an array's fourth element failing, having already collected three) leaked whatever was already built for that one call. The exact same structural class as `throw`'s own "any intermediate frame between the `try` and the `throw` leaks" limitation (claude.md #157), just at a specific, previously-uninvestigated call site.

**Root cause: every generated `_from_json_*_fn_for` function is itself an intermediate frame.** `.toStruct(T)`/`.toArr(T)` compile to a call into a per-type, cached, generated function that builds the struct/array/map field-by-field or element-by-element, calling `festina_throw` directly (via `festina_json_read_*`'s own error paths) the moment something doesn't match -- but that function had no `try` of its OWN. A throw partway through unwound straight past it via `llvm.eh.sjlj.longjmp`, skipping every local cleanup exactly the way claude.md #157 already documents for ordinary user code, except here the "user" is generated code with no way to write a `try` around itself.

**The fix: each generated from-json function now installs its own local catch frame around its own build loop.** Two new shared codegen.py helpers, `_emit_json_catch_prologue`/`_emit_json_catch_epilogue`, hand-roll the identical `llvm.eh.sjlj.setjmp`/`frameaddress`/`stacksave` shape `_emit_try` already uses for a real `try` statement -- emitted right after the function's own fresh struct/array/map header (`out`) is allocated, so a throw ANYWHERE in the recursive read that follows (a nested field, element, or entry, possibly several `_from_json_*_fn_for` calls deep) lands in a catch block that releases `out` (correctly freeing whatever was already stored in it -- a struct/array/map's own release function already walks "whatever is actually there" regardless of completeness, so no new release logic was needed) and re-throws the same message outward via an ordinary `festina_throw`. This converts every generated from-json function into the one frame shape claude.md #157's own reasoning already says is leak-free: one that directly contains its own `try`. `_from_json_struct_fn_for`, `_from_json_arr_fn_for`, and `_from_json_map_fn_for` all now call this pair; the struct and map builders additionally track a `key_slot` (the in-flight JSON key text, read before its value, freed only once the value is stored) via `_emit_json_catch_epilogue`'s new `extra_free_slots` parameter, since that temporary isn't `out` itself and would otherwise leak if the throw lands between the key being read and its own ordinary free.

**A second, separate leak found one frame further up, by the same Valgrind run: the `.toStruct()`/`.toArr()` CALL SITE itself.** Fixing the builder function moved the leak, it didn't remove it -- the call site in `_emit_call` (the `callee.prop in ("toStruct", "toArr")` branch) allocates a `festina_json_cursor` and holds the receiver's own text before calling into the (now leak-free) builder, but its own `festina_json_cursor_free(cursor)`/text-temp cleanup sat AFTER that call, on the normal-return path only. When the builder re-threw, `cursor` and the receiver's own owning text both leaked right there -- the identical "intermediate frame" shape, one level up. Fixed the same way: the call site wraps its own call into the builder in a local catch frame (reusing `_emit_json_catch_prologue`, a bespoke epilogue since nothing has been "built" yet at this point -- just `cursor`/`recv_val` to free before re-throwing).

**`volatile` is not optional here -- confirmed empirically, not just added out of caution.** A first version of `key_slot`'s tracking used a plain (non-`volatile`) `alloca ptr`/`store`/`load`. It compiled and ran fine unoptimized, but leaked 32 bytes under this project's real default `-O2` (confirmed directly via Valgrind against a minimal repro): LLVM's optimizer dead-store-eliminated the per-loop-iteration store, because unlike `out` (defined once, on the same CFG edge that reaches the catch block via the ordinary `setjmp` branch), a store inside the loop has no PROVABLE reader on any edge the optimizer's dataflow analysis recognizes -- `llvm.eh.sjlj.longjmp`'s own jump into the catch block is invisible to it, the exact class of hazard C's own `setjmp`/`longjmp` has always required `volatile` to guard against, now confirmed to apply identically to this project's own sjlj-based mechanism. Every store/load touching `key_slot` (in both the struct and map builders, and in `_emit_json_catch_epilogue`'s `extra_free_slots` loop) is now `store volatile`/`load volatile`. The call site's own `cursor`/`recv_val` did NOT need this treatment -- both are plain SSA values defined in a straight-line block before the `setjmp`, with no loop involved, so they trivially dominate the catch block on the normal branch edge.

**A genuine environmental discovery along the way: AddressSanitizer cannot run ANY program using `try`/`throw` in this environment.** The obvious plan -- add a new stress file to `tests/stress/` and run it through `scripts/leak_stress.sh` like every other fix in this project -- crashed with "Illegal instruction" (SIGILL) the moment the new file was compiled with `-fsanitize=address`. Bisected down to a minimal, completely unrelated-to-this-session repro: a bare `try { risky(5); risky(-1) } catch (e:text) { }` with no JSON involved crashes identically. This is pre-existing (confirmed: no file in `tests/stress/*.f` used `try`/`throw` before this session) and matches api.md's own long-standing note that `throw`'s own leak-freedom was "measured directly under Valgrind" rather than under ASan -- Valgrind was already the right tool for this class of program, just never previously turned into automated, repeatable coverage.

**New: `scripts/valgrind_stress.sh` + `tests/valgrind_stress/`, a permanent home for try/throw-using stress programs.** Mirrors `scripts/leak_stress.sh`'s shape (compile, run, fail on a leak) but needs none of its ASan-specific machinery (no instrumented runtime build, no IR-attribute stamping) -- it just runs an ORDINARY compiled binary (the real `festina.cli compile` pipeline, `-O2` and all) under `valgrind --leak-check=full --error-exitcode=1`. `tests/test_valgrind_stress.py` mirrors `test_leak_stress.py`'s own per-program parametrization and "the suite covers what it claims to" guard. `tests/valgrind_stress/json_parse_fail_churn.f` deliberately fails PARTWAY THROUGH at every shape the fix applies to (a flat struct, a nested struct field, an array, a `map[T]` field, a self-referencing struct one level deep, and malformed JSON syntax itself), 400 iterations of each, every pass -- so a regression is a real, reported leak.

**Verified:** `valgrind --leak-check=full` against `tests/valgrind_stress/json_parse_fail_churn.f` (2,400 catches, 400 x 6): **0 bytes definitely lost, 0 errors** (115 bytes "still reachable" at exit -- the same benign program-exit-time pattern already seen elsewhere in this codebase, not a leak). Confirmed both fixes are independently necessary: with only the builder-frame fix, Valgrind still showed the call-site's `cursor` leak; with both, clean. `scripts/valgrind_stress.sh` runs clean. Full pytest suite: 2207 passed, 9 skipped, 1 failed (up from 2206/9 at claude.md #222 -- 2 new tests: `TestValgrindStress`'s per-program parametrization and its own "suite covers what it claims to" guard). The one failure, `test_graceful_shutdown.py::TestHttpGracefulShutdown::test_an_in_flight_connection_still_completes_before_exit`, is the same pre-existing, timing-sensitive socket flake claude.md #173/#174 already documented -- confirmed unrelated (this entry touches no HTTP/socket/shutdown code at all) and reproduces the same way in isolation, independent of any change here. `scripts/leak_stress.sh`/`scripts/thread_tsan_stress.sh` both re-run and clean (this entry adds no new file to either -- `json_parse_fail_churn.f` cannot run under either, by design, and nothing else in this entry touches threading or the ASan-covered stress files). api.md's own "one real, honest limitation" paragraph rewritten to state the fix and the new Valgrind-based verification, with a note on the ASan/sjlj incompatibility.

224. SCOPED: `rows()[0]`'S OWN ARRAY LEAK -- A REAL FIX EXISTS, DELIBERATELY NOT RUSHED IN

Investigated directly, next in the same batch as claude.md #221-223: the deliberate, twice-already-documented leak (#85, #119, todo.md) where a computed-index table row (`getRows()[0]`, a query-result array never bound to a name) leaks the whole array, because a row has no refcount header of its own to retain past its container.

**A real fix is buildable, and was prototyped far enough to confirm its shape.** The blocker #119 named -- "nothing to retain" -- has a direct answer, the same one claude.md #11-16 already used for `text` (also header-less): copy the WHOLE row into its own fresh buffer instead of trying to share the original. A row's layout is fully known at compile time (`self.tables[name]`, the same column list `_emit_table_row_release_fn` already walks) and every TableType row is built with `want_rowid=1` unconditionally (see `_member_ptr_from`'s own `.rowid` comment), so its total width -- declared columns + the presence-mask slot + the rowid slot -- is an exact, static constant. A per-table `_emit_table_row_copy_fn` mirroring `_emit_table_row_release_fn`'s own unrolled column walk is straightforward: `malloc` a same-size buffer, blit every slot, then `festina_text_own` (plain strdup) each text column and `festina_retain` each blob/img/aud column -- both already-existing runtime primitives, no new C code needed, since a row's own blob/img/aud columns are genuinely refcounted handles (`festina_image_free` etc. already go through `festina_release_check`, the same generic mechanism every other refcounted type uses) even though the ROW wrapping them is not.

**Why it stops there rather than being wired in.** A fresh row copy is only half the fix -- todo.md's own escape hatch ("bind the array to a name first and it reclaims normally") already proves the OTHER half: a `TableType`-typed local today is never released at scope exit at all, unconditionally, by design (`_emit_table_row_release_fn` is deliberately reachable only from an array's own cascade, per its own comment, specifically so an ordinary row-typed binding never double-frees a row its array still owns). Making the copy above actually stop leaking requires giving `TableType` the same "always owned once bound, always released at scope exit" symmetry `text` has -- and that means auditing and changing every site that treats a `TableType` local as a costless, unreleased borrow: `VarDecl`, reassignment, a row passed as a function argument, a row returned from a function, anywhere one is stored in a struct field, array or map. `text`'s own version of this exact change was #11-16 -- SIX dedicated, individually-verified sections, each with its own ASan/LeakSanitizer pass, because getting the owned/borrowed symmetry wrong in either direction is a double-free or a UAF, not a leak, and this codebase's whole discipline is verifying that class of change directly rather than reasoning about it. Attempting the equivalent for `TableType` inside this one batch entry -- alongside four other unrelated items -- is exactly the kind of rushed, unverified surface area this project's own established practice (see nearly every entry above) refuses to ship.

**The other option -- copy-on-mint ONLY at the `rows()[0]` extraction site, leaving every other `TableType` binding untouched -- was checked and rejected as not actually a fix.** Without scope-exit release for `TableType` locals, a fresh copy minted at the extraction site would still never be freed when the local holding it goes out of scope: the array's leak would simply become a same-sized row's leak, once per access instead of once per array, worse in a loop that calls `rows()[0]` repeatedly rather than binding the array once. Half-measures here trade a bounded, well-understood, already-documented leak for an equally real, LESS bounded one -- not a net improvement.

**What stays true, unchanged.** The leak is bounded (at most one array per `rows()[0]`-shaped call site, never accumulating across the array's own contents) and has a zero-cost, already-documented workaround (bind the result to a name first). todo.md's own wording is accurate as written and needs no correction. A real fix is a genuine `TableType`-ownership-model project, comparable in size to claude.md #11-16, and belongs in its own dedicated, fully-verified round -- not a line item alongside #221-225. Recorded here rather than left as silent inspection: the fix's exact shape (per-table copy function, `festina_text_own`/`festina_retain` per column, then real scope-exit release wiring for `TableType` locals) so a future round does not have to re-derive it. No code changed by this entry; `tests/test_leak_stress.py`'s own canary (`test_the_harness_can_actually_fail`) still relies on this exact leak being real, so nothing here could have silently fixed it without that test itself telling us.

225. SCOPED: `giveRequest`'S TLS GAP, THREAD-SIDE `.upgrade()`, AND HANDING OFF A LIVE `socket`

Investigated, next in the same batch: three related `giveRequest`-adjacent gaps api.md's own "First-cut scope" note already flags or implies. Findings, not implementation -- each is a genuinely different size of work, and none of the three is a quick patch alongside #221-224.

**TLS hand-off (`openSecurePort()` connections) is blocked by a real concurrency hazard in mbedTLS's own design, not just missing plumbing.** `festina_conn_detach` (`festina_runtime_http.c`) rejects any connection with `c->tls != NULL` outright. Reading `festina_runtime_https.c`'s own structures explains why that is not simply an unfinished case: one `FestinaTlsListener` (built once per `openSecurePort()` call) holds the `mbedtls_ctr_drbg_context`/`mbedtls_entropy_context` every connection accepted on that port draws randomness from -- required not just at handshake time but for every TLS record's own IV generation on `mbedtls_ssl_write`, for the connection's entire lifetime. mbedTLS's `ctr_drbg` context has no internal locking. Today this is safe by accident: every connection on a port is serviced by the SAME thread that owns the listener, so draws are already serialized by construction. Handing a TLS connection to a WORKER thread would have that worker keep calling `mbedtls_ssl_write`/`read` against a `ssl_context` whose `->conf` still points at the ORIGINAL thread's listener -- and if that original thread (main, ordinarily) is still accepting and handshaking NEW TLS connections concurrently, both threads draw from the identical unsynchronized `ctr_drbg` at the same time. A real fix needs one of: a mutex around every `ctr_drbg` draw (mbedTLS's own documented workaround, `MBEDTLS_THREADING_C`-style, at a real per-handshake/per-write cost on the hot path every OTHER connection on that port pays too), or a genuinely independent RNG per connection (seeded once, no ongoing shared state -- more code, no ongoing cost). Either is a real, bounded, implementable fix; neither is a quick patch to `festina_conn_detach`'s own `if` alone.

**Thread-side `.upgrade()` on a handed-off request already works by construction -- and is completely unverified.** `festina_http_upgrade` (`festina_runtime_http.c`) reaches its connection purely through `festina_live_conn`/`festina_conn_by_id`, which read the CALLING thread's own `__thread`-local `g_conns`/`g_conn_index` -- exactly the tables `festina_conn_attach` (the receiving half of a hand-off, claude.md #213) installs a handed-off connection's state into. Nothing about `.upgrade()`'s own code path is main-specific or listener-specific; a worker calling it on a connection it received via `giveRequest` mutates that connection's `mode` to `FESTINA_CONN_WEBSOCKET` in its own table, the identical operation a directly-accepted request's own `.upgrade()` performs. Whatever polls that connection's fd afterward for `on socketMessage` traffic is the SAME per-thread combined loop already driving that thread's own accepted connections -- there is no second, listener-only poll loop this connection would be invisible to. This is very likely already correct, not merely plausible -- but "very likely" is not this project's own bar (every claim in this file up to here was CONFIRMED by a real compile-and-run, not reasoned from code reading alone), and `TestGiveRequest` in `tests/test_codegen.py` has no test combining hand-off with a subsequent `.upgrade()` at all. This is the cheap item of the three: add `test_a_handed_off_request_can_upgrade_to_a_websocket_on_the_receiving_thread` (real client, real handshake, a message sent after hand-off, confirmed to arrive at the worker's own `on socketMessage`) as a real next step -- likely a test-only change, confirming rather than building anything, but not yet DONE, so not claimed done here.

**Handing off an already-live `socket` (an upgraded WebSocket connection) is a genuinely new mechanism, not an extension of the existing one.** `giveRequest` moves an `http?`-typed value mid-request, dispatching into the receiving thread's `on request`; a `socket` is a different declared type (see `types.py`'s own `socket`-shaped `on socketMessage`/`on socketClose` handler signatures) representing a connection ALREADY past that point, with a different receiving-side dispatch target (`on socketMessage`/`on message`, not `on request`) and a different sender-side gate (would need its own manually-managed `socket?` the same way `http?` exists today, since the identical "main's own auto-release races the receiving thread" hazard applies identically). `festina_conn_detach` already refuses a `FESTINA_CONN_WEBSOCKET`-mode connection outright (the "already upgraded... cannot be handed off either" line api.md already documents) -- lifting that restriction usefully needs its own message kind (a `FESTINA_THREAD_MSG_GIVE_SOCKET` alongside `GIVE_REQUEST`), its own semantic.py gate (a `NAME.giveSocket(s)`-shaped call, checked against the receiving thread declaring `on socketMessage`/`on socketClose` the same way `giveRequest` checks for `on request`), and its own codegen dispatch path -- real, comparably-sized new surface, not a bug fix to the existing one.

**Net scope for a future round, in priority order:** thread-side `.upgrade()` (cheap -- one compile-and-run test, likely already correct), TLS hand-off (bounded but real -- a `ctr_drbg` thread-safety fix, one of two known shapes), live-socket hand-off (a new feature comparable in size to `giveRequest` itself, claude.md #213). None implemented here; api.md's existing "First-cut scope" note already states the TLS and post-upgrade restrictions accurately and needs no correction.

226. SCOPED: SHARING ONE COMPILED BODY ACROSS A THREAD POOL'S INSTANCES

Investigated, next in the same batch: whether `thread NAME[N] { ... }`'s own "compiles its body once per instance" cost (measured and first documented in claude.md #218: `pool[32]` emits 4,758 LLVM IR lines against `pool[1]`'s 542, an 8.8x blow-up on a ~12-line body) is worth closing. Reaffirmed rather than re-derived from scratch -- #218 already correctly diagnosed the root cause (`_emit_thread_pool_decl` loops `_emit_thread_decl` over N mangled instance names, which is what makes every instance's own private state reachable through a fixed, dedicated global rather than any runtime indirection) and already named the shape of the real fix ("share one body across instances... per-instance state reached indirectly"). This entry adds the concrete design sketch #218 didn't need to spell out, and a recommendation.

**The concrete shape.** Every thread-private global `_emit_thread_decl` generates today (one dedicated LLVM global per instance, per declared private var) would become ONE array, sized to the pool's own instance count, with every private-state access site (message handlers, thread-private funcs, the spawn entry point) rewritten to index into `array[instance_id]` instead of referencing a fixed symbol -- the same "dedicated global becomes an indexed slot" shift claude.md #1-3 already did once for `arr[T]`/`map[T]`'s own indirect representation, applied here to a thread pool's private state instead of a container's elements. Every function this pool's body compiles (its `on message` handler, every thread-private func reachable from it) would need an implicit instance-index parameter threaded through -- systematically, at every private-var reference site, not just at the function boundary -- so ONE compiled copy of each function serves every instance, the index supplying which slot of the shared state array it's currently operating on. The N pthreads themselves are unaffected either way -- this is a compiled-CODE-size change only, never a runtime-thread-count one; each of the N spawned OS threads would call the SAME shared entry point with its own instance index baked in as an argument, instead of each calling its own dedicated, identically-shaped function.

**Why this is scoped rather than built.** The systematic parameter-threading this needs touches every private-state access site a thread pool's body can contain -- comparable in kind (not necessarily in raw line count) to the arr[T]/map[T] representation change that itself took claude.md #1-7, several fully-verified rounds, to land correctly the first time this codebase did an indirection-introducing change like this. Getting the threading wrong at even one access site is a genuine cross-instance data corruption bug (instance 3 reading/writing instance 5's own private state), not a leak or a cosmetic issue -- exactly the class of mistake this project's own established practice insists on ASan/TSan-verifying in full before landing, never reasoning about in isolation.

**Recommendation: not worth pursuing without a concrete need.** The cost is compiled artifact size only (LLVM IR line count, and by extension object/binary size) -- it has zero effect on runtime behavior, correctness, or the pool's own per-instance isolation guarantees, which stay exactly as strong either way (still N independent, unshared globals today; still N independent, index-isolated slots under the redesign). A program with a very wide pool (dozens to hundreds of instances) and a substantial per-instance body is the only realistic case where this would matter in practice, and this project's own established pattern for exactly this shape of tradeoff -- todo.md's media-formats bullet: "revisit only with a concrete need" -- applies identically here. No code changed by this entry.

227. SCOPED: THE GENERAL `throw`-THROUGH-A-CALLED-FUNCTION LEAK

Investigated, last of the batch's scoping items: whether claude.md #157's general leak -- a function that merely CALLS something which eventually throws, with no `try` of its own, never gets the chance to run its own cleanup -- is fixable with the same technique claude.md #223 just used to close the narrower `.toStruct()`/`.toArr()` instance of this exact problem. It is buildable, in principle, using the identical mechanism; it is NOT a small extension of #223's own fix, and is not attempted here.

**Why #223's own technique doesn't just generalize directly.** #223 worked because each generated from-json function has exactly ONE thing being incrementally built (`out`, the struct/array/map header) plus a small, FIXED number of well-known in-flight temporaries (`key_slot`) -- a single local catch frame around the whole function, releasing `out` via its own already-correct release function (which already handles "however much is actually there"), was enough. An ARBITRARY user function has an unbounded, call-site-dependent SET of live cleanup-needing locals at any given point in its body -- `text a = f()  int b = g()  free a  arr[int] c = h()` has a DIFFERENT live set depending on exactly where a threw call sits relative to `a`/`b`/`c`'s own declarations and frees. A single top-of-function catch block cannot know which of a function's own locals were live at the moment of a deeper throw unless EVERY one of them is tracked the way `_key_slot` was: a `volatile`-tagged current-value slot, re-stored at every point that local's value changes (declaration, reassignment, an inner scope's own exit) -- because, per #223's own confirmed finding, `llvm.eh.sjlj.longjmp`'s jump into a catch block is invisible to LLVM's dataflow analysis, so a plain (non-`volatile`) local's last real value is not reliably recoverable there.

**The actual shape of a general fix.** For every function whose body contains a call that could transitively throw (a call graph reachability question, decidable at compile time -- exactly the kind of whole-program fact `_is_cyclic_type` already computes for a different purpose in #120), every LOCAL of a cleanup-needing type declared inside it would need its storage to go through (or be shadowed by) a `volatile` slot kept current at every write, with a generated top-of-function catch block that, on a throw, inspects every one of THAT function's own slots and releases whichever currently holds a live value, then re-throws. This is not a variant of #223's fix -- it is the SAME "give every function its own local `try`" idea #223 proved out, but multiplied across every local in every function that can reach a `throw`, not one well-known temporary in a handful of generated functions. Functions that cannot reach a `throw` at all (the overwhelming majority in a typical program -- no call in their own transitive call graph ever throws) need none of this and pay nothing, the same "cost proportional to what's actually used" shape #120's own cycle-detection already established for a different feature.

**Why this is scoped, not built, here.** In size this is comparable to (likely larger than) claude.md #11-16's own text-refcounting project or #1-10's own arr[T]/map[T] indirection work -- both were multi-round, individually-verified undertakings specifically BECAUSE getting an ownership-tracking change wrong corrupts memory (a double-free or use-after-free), not merely leaks it. Applying `volatile`-shadowed tracking to every cleanup-needing local in every throw-reachable function, correctly, at every declaration/reassignment/scope-exit site across the whole compiler, in one batch entry alongside #221-226, is exactly the kind of rushed, unverified surface area this project's own established practice refuses to ship (the same conclusion #126 and #128 already reached for their own differently-shaped "real fix exists, but it's a project" gaps).

**Why it stays low priority regardless of size.** The leak is strictly error-path (a normal, non-throwing run leaks nothing) and bounded PER THROW (never unbounded, never accumulating across a loop of successful calls) -- todo.md's own characterization remains accurate. #223 already closed the one concrete, previously-documented instance of this pattern a real feature (`.toStruct()`/`.toArr()`) actually exercised structurally, at volume, every call. The remaining general case requires a specific, unusual shape to bite at all -- a `try`-free function whose own locals are still live at the exact moment a callee (however many frames down) throws -- which is a real but comparatively rare pattern in practice, not a load-bearing one any existing feature depends on. No code changed by this entry; todo.md's own wording (already updated by #223 to describe exactly this general case) needs no further correction.

228. ANSWERED: CAN HTTP HAVE ITS OWN LOOP SEPARATE FROM GRAPHICS?

Investigated, last of this batch: whether HTTP (`openPort()`/`on request`/...) can run its own event loop independent of graphics (`render()`/window handlers), and what that would cost. The answer is yes, in the sense that matters, and it already ships -- the interesting finding is that the real separation this question is really asking for already exists as a documented feature, and building a SECOND way to get it would be pure redundant engineering.

**Standalone, HTTP already has its own loop -- no graphics code in the binary at all.** A program using `openPort()` with no graphics call anywhere links `festina_run_http_loop` (`festina_runtime_http.c`, poll()-based, POSIX-only) and never touches `festina_runtime_graphics.c` -- cli.py's own per-feature object file selection (claude.md #1xx-era "slim binaries" principle) means the graphics translation unit, X11, Cairo, none of it, is even linked. This has been true since claude.md #151 and needed no new work to confirm.

**Combined with graphics IN THE SAME (main) THREAD, no -- by design, and claude.md #166 already explains the real reason: main only ever blocks in one place.** `_emit_main_and_entry` picks exactly one blocking call for main -- `festina_run_event_loop` (graphics, X11 select()-based) when graphics is used, `festina_run_http_loop` otherwise. When a program's TOP-LEVEL code uses both, #166's fix services HTTP FROM INSIDE the graphics loop (a hook seam, `festina_http_service_hooks`, bounding the select() wait whenever HTTP has outstanding work) rather than running two loops on one thread, which is not something one thread can do at all without exactly this kind of cooperative multiplexing (or a state machine neither loop's existing code is written as). The one real, already-documented cost of THAT choice: the combined path skips `festina_run_http_loop`'s own graceful-shutdown grace period entirely (api.md's http Limitations, security.md's single-threaded-availability bullet) -- a real, accepted simplification, not silently absent.

**The genuine separate-loop answer already exists, one layer over: put the HTTP server in a `thread`.** claude.md #114's private per-thread HTTP context (`api.md`'s own "A thread's own HTTP context") gives a `thread` that declares `on request`/etc. and calls `openPort()` a **fully private** connection table and listener set, serviced by that thread's own combined message+HTTP loop, running on its own genuinely independent OS thread -- never sharing a select()/poll() call with main's graphics loop at all. A program with a window AND an HTTP server that must never share a loop can have exactly that TODAY, at zero new engineering cost, by moving the `on request`/`openPort()` declarations inside a `thread { }` block instead of top level. The cost of THIS route is the one this whole language already asks any thread-using program to pay: no shared mutable state between the graphics side and the HTTP thread (message-passing via `postMessage`/`.reply()`, or a live connection via `giveRequest`, instead of direct calls), and the same lifecycle rules every other thread follows (`kill()`, main-exit-kills-children, `on exit` semantics already covered by `TestThreadGracefulShutdown`).

**Why building a THIRD option -- true loop separation while keeping `openPort()` at the TOP level alongside graphics, with no `thread` involved -- is not worth it.** It would mean spawning an implicit second OS thread for one of the two responsibilities under the hood whenever a program's top-level code uses both, essentially auto-threading what `thread { }` already lets a program do explicitly. The cost is real and this project has already paid it once, for the wrong shape: `festina_run_http_loop`'s own graceful-shutdown grace-period logic would need porting to whichever loop runs standalone (exactly the gap #166 already left open for the COMBINED case, not yet closed there either), plus new signal/exit coordination between two now-genuinely-concurrent top-level loops -- a smaller version of the exact coordination `thread`'s own kill()/main-exit semantics already solve correctly and are already tested. Since the capability (two independent OS threads, two independent loops, no shared blocking call) is already fully available via `thread`, adding a second, implicit way to get the identical result would be new surface area with no new capability behind it -- worse, since two different constructs would each need their own graceful-shutdown story to get right, doubling the maintenance surface #166 already flagged as unfinished in its one existing form.

**Answer, plainly: yes, HTTP can have its own loop separate from graphics, and this ships today two ways** -- automatically, whenever a program uses HTTP without graphics at all, and by explicit choice, by declaring the HTTP server inside a `thread` when a program wants both. The one combination that does NOT get separate loops -- `openPort()` and graphics both declared at the TOP level, no `thread` -- is a deliberate design choice (claude.md #166), not a gap, because the alternative is either impossible on one OS thread or a strictly worse, redundant re-implementation of what `thread` already provides. No code changed by this entry -- purely an analysis, as asked.
