230. FIXED: A THREAD'S SECOND-EVER `.reply()` WAS SILENTLY DROPPED -- A STALE TAIL POINTER, NOT A DESIGN LIMIT (uraikus/festina#89, #90)

Reported directly, two related GitHub issues: #89 (a thread's reply mechanism delivers successfully only the FIRST time, for that handle's entire process lifetime -- every reply after that from the same sender is silently dropped, no error) and #90 (api.md's own "Reply at most once per message" wording contradicts that observed "per thread lifetime, ever" behavior, and asks which one is supposed to be true). Both close together: the runtime was wrong, not the docs -- api.md needed no edit at all.

**Root cause: `festina_thread_dispatch_reply` (claude.md #217/#222) removed a node from `pending_callbacks` without ever fixing `pending_callbacks_tail` when that node happened to be the tail.** The list is a classic head-pointer-plus-tail-pointer singly-linked list (`festina_thread_register_callback` appends at `pending_callbacks_tail` in O(1), claude.md #218's own fix for what used to be an O(N^2) prepend-and-scan). Removal used the `FestinaPendingCallback **link` head-relative-pointer idiom -- correct for unlinking the node from the chain itself, but it never checked whether the node being removed WAS `pending_callbacks_tail`, so a removal that emptied the list (removing the one and only remaining node -- which is exactly what "the last node" and "the tail" both are at that moment) left `pending_callbacks` correctly `NULL` but `pending_callbacks_tail` pointing at now-freed memory. The very next registration on that same handle (`festina_thread_register_callback`) trusted the stale tail: `if (self->pending_callbacks_tail) self->pending_callbacks_tail->next = cb;` wrote through the dangling pointer into already-`free()`'d memory (a real use-after-free write, not just a logic bug) and never touched `pending_callbacks` itself, which stayed `NULL` -- so the new registration was reachable from nowhere, and the corresponding reply, when it eventually arrived, found nothing in the list to match its txn id and was silently discarded (the existing, deliberate "should never happen" fallback for that case, per that function's own doc comment).

**Why every existing test and stress program missed this.** The only shape that triggers it is a list draining to genuinely EMPTY between registrations -- a single outstanding request-at-a-time, request-then-fully-resolve-then-request-again. `tests/test_codegen.py::TestThreadReplyCallback::test_two_outstanding_replies_resolve_to_the_right_callbacks` registers BOTH callbacks before either reply is dispatched, so neither removal ever empties the list. `tests/stress/thread_reply_callback_churn.f`'s own 5,000-message batch (`worker2`) sends every message up front in one tight loop, for the identical reason -- the list never drains to empty until the very last removal in the whole run. Both are real coverage of everything they were built to cover; neither happens to be the sequential-round-trip shape that empties and refills the list, which is exactly what #89's own repro (`sendA` at t=100ms, `sendB` at t=1000ms, each a completely separate round trip) does on every single call after the first.

**The fix: track `prev` explicitly during the scan instead of the head-relative `**link` idiom, and correct `pending_callbacks_tail` to `prev` whenever the removed node was the tail.** `prev` is `NULL` exactly when the removed node was also the head (the list is now fully empty), which is exactly the correct new tail value in that case too -- one branch handles both "removed the tail of a longer list" and "removed the only node" correctly. `runtime/festina_runtime_thread.c`'s `festina_thread_dispatch_reply` is the only site that needed this -- `festina_thread_register_callback` (the append) was already correct, and the kill()-path bulk-clear (claude.md #217, further down the file) already resets both `pending_callbacks` and `pending_callbacks_tail` to `NULL` together when discarding the whole list at once, so it was never exposed to the same partial-removal hazard.

**Coverage, in both directions.** `tests/test_codegen.py::TestThreadReplyCallback::test_a_second_sequential_reply_still_delivers` -- a real compile-and-run, deterministic (no timer: `onA`'s own callback body is what sends the second message, so it provably runs only once the first round trip has genuinely finished) reproduction of #89's exact repro shape, confirmed failing on the pre-fix runtime and passing after. `tests/stress/thread_reply_callback_churn.f` gains a second, independent churn path (`worker3`/`onSeqReply`, 1,000 real sequential round trips, each one triggered from the PREVIOUS reply's own callback -- genuinely emptying and refilling `pending_callbacks` on every iteration, unlike the file's own pre-existing batch) alongside its original 5,000-message batched one, both required to finish (and both sums checked) before the program exits cleanly -- confirmed hanging forever on the pre-fix runtime (the sequential chain simply stops advancing once the corruption hits, exactly #89's own "TIMEOUT" symptom) and completing correctly, both sums exact, after the fix. `scripts/leak_stress.sh` and `scripts/thread_tsan_stress.sh` both clean on the updated file -- the fix touches no new shared state and needs no new synchronization (`pending_callbacks`/`_tail` were already documented as self-only, touched exclusively by their own owning handle's OS thread, and stay exactly that after this fix).

**#90 (the docs issue) needed no doc change at all.** api.md's "Reply at most once per message" bullet, and the whole Request/Response section's framing around it (the worked example implying many independent round trips over a thread's life, each getting its own reply), were already correct -- they described the INTENDED behavior, which the runtime bug above was failing to actually provide. Fixing the runtime made reality match the documentation instead of the other way around.

**Verified:** the exact program from #89's own bug report, compiled and run directly -- prints `TIMEOUT` and exits 1 on the pre-fix runtime (confirmed reproducing the reported bug byte for byte), prints `A: 2` / `B: 4` and exits 0 after the fix. `tests/test_codegen.py::TestThreadReplyCallback` (9 tests, the new one included) green. `scripts/leak_stress.sh`/`scripts/thread_tsan_stress.sh` both clean on the updated `thread_reply_callback_churn.f`, run individually; the buggy pre-fix runtime hangs on it forever (the sequential chain simply stalls once the corruption hits), confirmed directly rather than assumed. Full pytest suite: 2206 passed, 9 skipped, 3 failed (up from claude.md #229's own 2207/9/1 -- net +1 collected test, the new regression case above) -- all 3 failures are pre-existing, unrelated flakes (`TestFullscreenAndDecorations`'s own X11-window-manager-under-Xvfb timing, claude.md #218; `TestHttpGracefulShutdown`'s own signal-timing race, claude.md #173/#174), confirmed passing cleanly in isolation immediately afterward rather than assumed -- none touch threading or the reply mechanism at all.

231. NEW: `NAME.drain()` -- BLOCK UNTIL A THREAD'S OWN QUEUE IS FULLY PROCESSED (uraikus/festina#91)

Requested directly: no way existed to guarantee work already sent to a `thread` had actually completed before the main program exits, including the ordinary "user closes the window" path -- making a thread with its own `DatabaseURL` unsafe for anything that must durably survive program exit (the issue's own worked repro: a `postMessage` fired from `on close()` to persist a final value, silently lost every time, confirmed directly under Xvfb with a real `WM_DELETE_WINDOW`). `NAME.kill()` (and process-exit's own identical teardown, `festina_thread_kill_all`) explicitly discards anything still queued rather than draining it -- correct for "stop now," wrong for "make sure this landed first."

**The fix: `NAME.drain()`, the deliberate opposite of `kill()`'s own discard-don't-wait choice.** Blocks the calling (main) thread until the target's own inbound queue is fully processed -- everything queued at the moment the call is made, no new arrivals meanwhile changes that -- then returns with the thread still running, still accepting new messages, nothing stopped. Same main-only, no-argument shape `kill()`/`live()`/`isAlive()` already have (added to the same allow-list, the same main-only gate, and the same `pool[i].<method>()` indexing all four already share).

**Runtime: two new fields on `FestinaThreadHandle`, both guarded by the SAME `in_lock` the inbound queue itself already uses.** `dispatching` (a plain flag, set the moment a message is dequeued, cleared once its own `on_message`/`in_release` -- or the GIVE_REQUEST/REPLY equivalent -- has fully finished) and `drained_cond` (a condvar, broadcast on every clear). "The queue is empty" alone is NOT "drained" -- a message can be dequeued (head already `NULL`) while still being processed, exactly the window a naive `in_head == NULL` check would race. `festina_thread_try_dispatch_one` sets `dispatching = 1` while STILL HOLDING `in_lock` at dequeue time (so there is no window where a concurrent `drain()` could see both "queue empty" and "not dispatching" for a message still genuinely in flight), then calls a new shared helper (`festina_thread_mark_drained`) on every one of its own "processed one message" exit paths (ordinary, GIVE_REQUEST, REPLY alike) to clear the flag and broadcast. `festina_thread_wait_drained(h)` -- **not** `festina_thread_drain`, which already exists and means something entirely different (drains every thread's own OUTBOUND queue into main, part of the existing hook triple main's event loops poll; confirmed the collision by compiling before naming anything, not assumed) -- loops `while (in_head || dispatching) pthread_cond_wait(...)` under the lock; not alive at all (never `live()`'d, or already `kill()`'d) returns immediately rather than waiting on a condvar nothing will ever signal again.

**Codegen/semantic:** `"drain"` added everywhere `"kill"` already appears -- the allowed-method tuple (both the ordinary-thread and pool-index branches share one check), the main-only-body gate, and a semantic branch mirroring `kill()`'s own (no arguments, returns nothing). Codegen emits `call void @festina_thread_wait_drained(ptr {handle})`, the identical shape `kill()`'s own call site already has, pool bounds-checking included for free (the same `_emit_thread_target_handle` every lifecycle method already goes through).

**Verified end to end, both directions.** The exact repro shape from the issue (a `table Written`, a `writer` thread with its own `DatabaseURL`, an INSERT inside `on message`, `postMessage` then immediately `close(0)`): without `drain()`, the row is silently lost (`SELECT * FROM Written` on the resulting file returns nothing -- confirmed directly). With `writer.postMessage(42); writer.drain(); close(0)` inserted between them, the row survives every time. `tests/test_codegen.py::TestThreadDrain` pins this positively (a real compile-and-run, then the thread's own `.sqlite` file inspected directly from Python once the process has actually exited -- the same pattern every other thread-DB test in this suite already uses, since a thread and main can never share one `DatabaseURL` per the existing isolation gate) plus two no-op-safety cases (a never-`live()`'d thread, a `kill()`'d one) -- 3 new compile-and-run tests. `tests/test_threads.py::TestThreadLifecycleMethods`/`TestThreadPools` gain 4 semantic tests (accepted with no arguments, rejected with one, rejected from inside a thread body alongside the other three, accepted on a pool instance).

**New stress coverage: `tests/stress/thread_drain_churn.f`.** 800 iterations of the tightest possible interleaving (`postMessage` immediately followed by `drain()`, every single cycle) on an ordinary thread, plus 200 more spread across a 4-instance pool, proving `drain()` composes with `pool[i]` indexing the same way the other three lifecycle methods already do. This is genuinely NEW shared state nothing before this entry ever exercised -- a race between the worker's own clear-and-broadcast and `drain()`'s own predicate check would be exactly the kind of thing only ThreadSanitizer catches, and a leaked/double-freed message exactly what LeakSanitizer catches. `scripts/leak_stress.sh` and `scripts/thread_tsan_stress.sh` both clean on this file specifically, and added to `tests/test_leak_stress.py`'s own coverage-guard set.

**api.md:** the `### Lifecycle` subsection heading and its own worked example both widened to include `drain()`, with a dedicated paragraph explaining exactly the durability hazard it closes (`on close()`/`on exit(code:int)` firing a final `postMessage` that a graceful-shutdown-driven `kill()` could otherwise discard, unprocessed, in the exact same teardown that already runs) and the `on close()`-plus-`drain()` idiom the issue itself suggested, spelled out as a real worked example rather than left implicit.

**Verified:** `tests/test_threads.py` (142 tests, the 4 new drain() semantic cases included) and `tests/test_codegen.py::TestThreadDrain` (3 new compile-and-run tests) both green. `scripts/leak_stress.sh` and `scripts/thread_tsan_stress.sh` run in FULL (every stress program, not just the new one) both clean, confirming this entry's own runtime changes to the shared dispatch path (`festina_thread_try_dispatch_one`) didn't disturb anything the other 25/10 stress files already cover. Full pytest suite: 2215 passed, 9 skipped, 1 failed (up from claude.md #230's own 2206/9/3 -- net +9 collected: 4 semantic + 3 compile-and-run new tests here, plus the two `TestFullscreenAndDecorations` flakes #230 saw not recurring this run). The one failure, `test_graceful_shutdown.py::TestHttpGracefulShutdown::test_an_in_flight_connection_still_completes_before_exit`, is the same pre-existing, unrelated signal-timing flake claude.md #173/#174/#230 already documented -- confirmed passing cleanly in isolation immediately afterward.

232. `drain()` HARDENED: EDGE CASES PINNED, THE PER-MESSAGE LOCK PAID BACK, AND THE REPLY LIST'S LAST UNTESTED REMOVAL SHAPE COVERED

Requested directly, over the two freshest pieces of PR #92 (claude.md #230's reply-list fix and #231's `drain()`): look for edge cases, write more complex and dynamic tests, and make sure the code is efficient. Findings first, then what changed.

**Efficiency: #231 as first shipped re-introduced exactly the cost claude.md #218 had removed from this path.** `festina_thread_mark_drained` was called after every processed message -- a full `lock / clear flag / unlock / broadcast` round trip, on the hottest loop this whole feature has, for the benefit of a `drain()` call most programs never make. #218 had specifically collapsed that loop to ONE mutex acquisition per message. Fixed by folding the clear into the acquisition the worker already makes at the top of its next `festina_thread_try_dispatch_one` call (a new `static inline festina_thread_note_dispatch_finished_locked`, run before the blocking wait so an idle worker never leaves a waiter holding a stale flag, and on the kill path too), and gating the `pthread_cond_broadcast` on a new `drain_waiters` count (incremented/decremented by the waiter itself, under the same lock) so it is skipped outright when nobody is waiting. The flag now stays set only for the handful of instructions between one dispatch returning and the next lock being taken -- an interval during which the worker is provably not idle, so no waiter can observe anything different. **Measured**, the same way #218 measured its own change -- identical 400,000-message fire-and-forget program (`bench_msgs.f`, kept out of the tree), 20 runs each, both binaries built from the same tree with only this change differing: **min 208 -> 171 ms, median 300 -> 225 ms.** The wall clock includes main's own send loop, which is unchanged, so the worker-side saving is larger than the headline ratio suggests.

**Robustness: the wait predicate now includes `alive`, and a stopping thread broadcasts on its way out.** As shipped, a `drain()` blocked on a thread that then stopped would have slept forever (nothing would ever clear `dispatching` or empty the queue again). Unreachable from Festina today -- only main may call `drain()` or `kill()`, and `kill()` joins synchronously, so the two can never overlap -- but a correctness property that holds only because of a caller-side gate two files away is exactly the kind of thing worth making locally true instead. `festina_thread_main` now clears the flag and broadcasts (waiter-gated) right where it sets `alive = 0`.

**Edge cases found and pinned as real compile-and-run tests (`tests/test_codegen.py::TestThreadDrain`, +5):**
- *The blocking guarantee itself, dynamically.* Batches of 1, 7, 3, 25, 1, 60, 12, 100, 2 messages -- the queue draining fully to empty and refilling, repeatedly, on purpose -- with the worker appending one byte per message to a file and main re-reading it after every `drain()`. The byte count must equal everything sent so far at every step; a drain that returned with a message dequeued-but-mid-append, or still queued, fails at that exact batch. Checked from inside the program, not after it exits.
- *A thread with its own HTTP context.* That thread runs the OTHER worker-loop shape (`festina_thread_main`'s bounded-poll branch, which never blocks on its condvar). The flag lives in the shared dispatch function both shapes call, so it works there too -- now proven rather than assumed. api.md notes the one visible difference: a drain there can take up to one poll interval (~20ms) longer to notice an idle queue.
- *`on exit(code:int)` driving the final write* -- #91's own scenario verbatim, via `close(0)`.
- *The signal path* (`tests/test_graceful_shutdown.py`, +1): the process idling in its event loop, a real `SIGTERM`, `on exit` fires the last write and drains, and the row is on disk once the process is gone. The row's value is `code + 100` = 243, which doubles as proof the handler saw the real signal code, not a stale 0 -- the "user closes the window" shape, minus the window.
- *`drain()` returns BEFORE a pending reply's `.callback(fn)` runs on main* -- an easy thing to assume the other way. drain waits for the worker to finish (its own `.reply()` included), but a reply reaches `fn` via main's own event loop, which only runs once top-level code returns. Pinned as a forced output order, and stated plainly in api.md: drain is about the worker's side effects, not round-trip completion.
- *An out-of-range `pool[i].drain()`* is the same silent no-op every other pool lifecycle method already is -- and the in-range drains right after it still genuinely wait.

**The reply-list fix (#230) had one removal shape neither of its own tests reached: removing the TAIL of a list that is not thereby emptied.** #230's regression test empties a one-entry list; the pre-existing two-outstanding test removes the HEAD of a two-entry list. Neither exercises "tail removed, head survives, `pending_callbacks_tail` must walk back to the surviving node" -- the exact branch where the fix sets `tail = prev` to a non-NULL node. Two new tests (`TestThreadReplyCallback`, +2): a deterministic one (a deliberately slow thread registered first, a fast one second -- the fast reply removes the tail while the head survives, then the slow reply empties the list, then a third send proves it is still usable; output order is forced, not racy), and a dynamic one (a 4-instance pool, each lane a 30-deep chain of send-reply-send, so main's single list has entries removed from head, middle and tail in whatever interleaving four real OS threads produce this run, with new registrations appending at the tail throughout -- 120 callbacks, each exactly once, pinned by count and checksum).

**Nothing about the runtime's own semantics changed for any existing program** -- every pre-existing thread test, the full `scripts/leak_stress.sh` and `scripts/thread_tsan_stress.sh` sweeps, and the new dynamic tests all pass on the folded version; the only behavioral difference is that `drain()` can no longer hang on a dead thread. Version 0.40.

**Verified:** full pytest suite 2224 passed, 9 skipped, 0 failed (up from claude.md #231's own 2215/9/1 -- the 8 new tests above, plus the `test_graceful_shutdown.py` signal-timing flake #173/#174/#230/#231 all saw simply not recurring this run; a fully clean sweep, the first one in this batch). `scripts/leak_stress.sh` (26 programs) and `scripts/thread_tsan_stress.sh` (11) both run in full and clean on the folded runtime.

233. CODE REVIEW: THE JSON CLEANUP STACK (claude.md #223 REDONE), TWO JSON MEMORY BUGS, A DEEP-NESTING CRASH, AND WHY CI ON `main` HAD BEEN RED ON ALL THREE PLATFORMS

Requested directly: another code review of the freshest work, looking for bugs, inefficiencies and poor documentation. The review started from #223, #230, #231 and #232 (the newest code) and then followed the evidence to GitHub Actions, where every `CI` run on `main` had been failing on linux, macos AND windows for as far back as the run list goes. Findings first, in severity order; then what changed; then the things checked and found sound.

**1. claude.md #223 removed `.toStruct()`/`.toArr()` from two CI-verified platforms and broke it on a third -- a regression from this same batch.** #223 closed the partial-parse leak by putting a real `llvm.eh.sjlj.setjmp` catch frame inside every generated `__festina_from_json_*` function and at the call site, and (correctly, given that design) set `CodeGen.uses_try` for it. But `uses_try` is the one flag `cli.py`'s wasm32-wasi gate and `_check_darwin_try_supported` key off. Confirmed three ways: (a) `festina compile --target=wasm32-wasi` of any program using `.toStruct()` failed with "try/catch/throw is not supported when compiling to WASM" on the current tree and compiled fine on a pre-#223 worktree; (b) the macos CI job's skip count rose by exactly 21 between the merge before #223 and the merge after it -- `conftest.py`'s `compile_file_or_skip` turns the "unsupported platform feature" category into a *skip*, so every JSON parsing test on macOS had quietly stopped running rather than failing; (c) the windows CI job gained exactly 9 new failures at the same merge, all of them `test_json_parse.py`'s throw tests -- there the frame compiled, but the builder's own catch never ran (empty output; one case died with `0xC0000374`, heap corruption). So: the sjlj-frame approach was wrong in kind, not just in detail.

**The replacement: a per-thread cleanup stack in the runtime (`festina_cleanup_push(ptr, release_fn)` / `festina_cleanup_pop()`, `runtime/festina_runtime.c`).** Generated code registers each value it holds "mid-expression" -- a builder's own half-built struct/array/map right after it is allocated, each JSON key from its read until its own free, and at the call site the cursor, the temporary receiver text and the finished value -- and pops it on the ordinary path; `festina_try_push` records the stack depth in the catch frame, and `festina_throw` releases everything above that depth, newest first, before its `longjmp`. Strictly LIFO by construction (nested builders push and pop above their caller's entries), which is also what makes the release order right: an inner half-built value goes before the outer one it would have been stored into. Plain portable C with no `setjmp` of its own, so `uses_try` is untouched by JSON code; where `festina_throw` is the `fail()` stub (wasm32-wasi, macOS) a parse failure still ends the program as any uncaught throw does and none of this is reached. The frames, the malloc'd `FestinaCatchFrame` per builder call, and the `volatile` key-slot machinery are all gone from codegen (`_emit_json_cleanup_push/_pop` replaced `_emit_json_catch_prologue/_epilogue`). The `runtime/festina_runtime_http.c` async worker's hand-written `__builtin_setjmp` frame goes through the same `festina_try_push`, so it records a depth too, automatically. **Measured** on the same 100,000-object `.toArr(Person)` x5 benchmark #223 used, 7 runs each of three binaries from the same tree: pre-#223 min 183 / median 223 ms, #223 as shipped min 221 / median 233 ms, this entry min 191 / median 225 ms -- the setjmp-per-builder overhead is essentially paid back.

**2. A real double free in #223's builders.** A duplicate `text` key whose SECOND value fails to parse (`{"name":"first","name":5}`) -- the struct builder freed the first value BEFORE reading the second (the refcounted-field path already did load/read/store/release in the right order; the text path did not); the read throws, and the throw-time release of the half-built struct then freed the same buffer again. Confirmed under Valgrind: one "Invalid free()" per iteration. Not reachable before #223 (nothing released the half-built value then), so this was #223's own. Fixed by giving the text path the same load-old / read-new / store / free-old order.

**3. A real leak in #223's call site.** Trailing data after a COMPLETE value (`'{"id":1} trailing'.toStruct(T)` inside a `try`): `festina_json_expect_end` throws after the builder has already returned the finished value, and the call site's catch released the cursor and the receiver text but not the value -- confirmed under Valgrind, one definitely-lost block per iteration. The call site now keeps the finished value registered across that final check.

**4. A pre-existing crash the new stack's bound turns into a throw.** The builders' own recursion for a self-referencing struct had no depth cap at all (claude.md #192's cap only covered an *unknown* field's skipped value): `{"n":1,"next":` repeated 300,000 times SIGSEGV'd (exit 139, confirmed) -- reachable through `req.toStruct()` on a network body. The cleanup stack is a fixed-size `__thread` array (2048 entries, ~32KB per thread; malloc'd growth would leak per exited worker thread, which the thread churn stress programs would flag), and overflowing it releases the value being registered and throws `JSON nested too deeply (more than 1024 levels)` -- the same catchable error, and Valgrind-clean after the ~1024 already-built levels cascade-release.

**5. Why CI on `main` was red, per platform, and what changed.** *linux:* 4 tests hard-failed with `FileNotFoundError: 'xwd'`/`'xprop'` -- ci.yml installed `xvfb xdotool openbox` but not `x11-apps`/`x11-utils`, and those four tests (three `TestCanvasPathsRenderRealPixels` real-pixel reads through `_xwd_pixels`, one `TestFullscreenAndDecorations` `xprop` probe) lacked the skip guard their siblings have. Both fixed: the packages are installed on CI, and a new `_require_x11_tool` skips cleanly (or fails loudly under `FESTINA_STRICT_DEPS`, so the strict linux job never silently sheds them). *macos:* `test_no_orphaned_thread_survives_after_the_parent_exits` reads `/proc/<pid>/task`, which macOS does not have -- now `skipif` non-Linux; and `test_manually_managed_struct_free_then_read_is_null` did `log(c.x)` after `free c` and expected `0` -- the IR is a load through a null pointer, undefined, printing 0 on Linux and a heap address on macOS and Windows. What `free` actually promises (api.md) is `c == null`; the test asserts that now, and api.md's `free` section says plainly that a field read through a freed struct binding is undefined like an out-of-range index. *windows:* 69 of the 88 failures were one bug -- `festina_runtime_http.c` has used `pthread_mutex_t` unconditionally since claude.md #212's connection-id counter, but included `<pthread.h>` only in its POSIX branch, so the http runtime did not compile there at all ("unknown type name 'pthread_mutex_t'"); the include is unconditional now (as `festina_runtime_thread.c`/`_audio.c` already do -- MSYS2's winpthreads provides it) and the "http" feature links `-pthread` like "audio"/"threads" already did (glibc 2.34+/macOS fold libpthread into libc, which is why the omission never failed a link elsewhere). The 9 JSON throw tests are #1 above. The SIGTERM/143 tests in `test_graceful_shutdown.py` can't work on Windows (`send_signal(SIGTERM)` is `TerminateProcess` there: exit 1, no handler) -- module-level `skipif`, matching api.md's own documented Windows graceful-shutdown gap. `_default_output_name("tool.wasm.f", target="wasm32-wasi")` came out `tool.wasm.exe` on a Windows host (the wasm branch had nothing to append, so the win32 branch appended `.exe`) -- fixed, with an explicit `platform_name="win32"` test so every platform covers it. The remaining Windows failures -- `test_a_value_escaping_inside_a_catch_body_survives` (access violation), two `exec()` tests, one `doctor --fix` prompt test -- predate this batch (present in the pre-#223 run too) and are not touched here; they are Windows-specific work of their own. I cannot run macOS or Windows here: those changes are verified by reasoning from the CI logs plus the identical mechanisms already working elsewhere in the tree, and the CI runs on this PR are the real check.

**6. Documentation that had gone stale.** `runtime/festina_runtime.c`'s JSON section still carried the pre-#223 "ONE REAL, DOCUMENTED LIMITATION" paragraph describing the partial-parse leak as live; api.md named the Valgrind program as `tests/stress/json_parse_fail_churn.f` (it lives in `tests/valgrind_stress/`) and described the sjlj design; `todo.md`'s throw entry likewise; `tests/CONTRACT.md`'s status narrative referenced nothing past #219; api.md's Threads section listed `drain()` in its lifecycle subsection but not in the two method lists. All updated, and wasm.md/macos.md now say explicitly that JSON parsing is unaffected by the `try` gate.

**Checked and found sound (no change):** #223's sjlj frame balance (a `festina_throw` pops the frame it unwinds *to*, and `festina_try_error` transfers message ownership -- the frames were correctly balanced; the design was wrong for other reasons); `festina_thread_drain_impl` (#230) dispatches with `out_lock` released, no deadlock; the arr builder's per-element `alloca` sat inside the loop body, which reads as a per-iteration stack allocation, but a 3,000,000-element `toArr(int)` parsed fine (LLVM hoists a constant-size alloca) -- moved to the entry block anyway so nothing depends on the optimizer for it.

**Tests added:** `test_json_parse.py` +5 (the double free at 200 rounds -- glibc aborts on the double free it detects, so this fails without Valgrind too; trailing data after a complete value, 100 rounds; 5000-level self-referencing nesting caught, not crashed; and `TestJsonParsingNeedsNoSjlj`, which pins `uses_try is False` and no `llvm.eh.sjlj.setjmp` *call* in the IR for a JSON program, and the opposite for an explicit `try`), `test_wasm.py` +2 (`.toStruct()`/`.toArr()` compiling AND running under wasm32-wasi -- the regression itself; the win32-host `.wasm` suffix case), `test_platform.py::TestOnMacOS` +1 (`.toStruct()` compiles and runs on the darwin job, through `compile_file` directly so it cannot be skipped away). `tests/valgrind_stress/json_parse_fail_churn.f` gained the duplicate-text-key, trailing-data and 2000-level nesting shapes.

**Verified:** full pytest suite 2231 passed, 10 skipped, 0 failed (up from claude.md #232's own 2224/9/0: the 10 tests above are new, and the one extra skip is the platform-gated macOS `.toStruct()` test; the first run had 3 failures, all `test_platform.py::TestAudioFeatureConfig` tests that pinned "http links no extra flags" -- updated to the new `-pthread`, since the old expectation was the bug). `scripts/leak_stress.sh` (26 programs) and `scripts/thread_tsan_stress.sh` (11) run in full and clean on the new runtime -- the cleanup stack's `__thread` array and `festina_throw`'s unwind are new state on every thread; `scripts/valgrind_stress.sh` clean with the three new shapes. A `.toStruct()`/`.toArr()` program compiles and runs under `--target=wasm32-wasi` again. The macOS and Windows halves are verified by this PR's own CI runs, not locally.

234. `img` AS A LAYER: PER-IMAGE TRANSFORMS AND STATE STACK, CLEARS, AND `img.drawImage` (uraikus/festina#93)

Requested directly: add the features in issue #93's "Proposed API". The issue's own case is festina-game, which paints its world as one composited 384x384 `img` per chunk -- and every brush stamp had to be `clearCanvas(); drawImage(c.bg, 0, 0); paint...; img snap = saveCanvas(); c.bg = snap.clip(...)`: two window-sized copies plus a chunk blit per stamp, per overlapped chunk, at mouse-move rate, purely because the brush needed one rotated rect and the eraser one `clearCircle`, neither of which could target an image. Three gaps, each closed as a method form on `img` mirroring the canvas call name-for-name:

1. **A per-image transform and state stack.** `img.translate(dx, dy)`, `img.rotate(degrees)`, `img.scale(sx, sy)`, `img.resetTransform()`, `img.saveState()`, `img.restoreState()`. The transform lives on `FestinaImageBox` itself (a `cairo_matrix_t` plus the same lazy-init flag the canvas's `g_transform_ready` is), identity from creation, completely independent of the canvas's -- which stays never-applied to image draws, unchanged from claude.md #134. Every image drawing/clearing/compositing call now goes through one new `festina_image_context(box)` (the img counterpart of `festina_canvas_context`) so the image's transform applies to all of them uniformly, exactly as the canvas's applies to the canvas versions. The state stack holds only that image's transforms -- style state is global and stays with the canvas's `saveState()`, the split the issue itself proposed -- and is a malloc'd, doubling per-image array allocated on the first `saveState()` (a fixed 64-matrix array would cost every 16x16 sprite 3KB it never uses), freed with the image, with the canvas's own 64-deep limit and the same two loud failures (`img.restoreState(): nothing was saved`, `img.saveState(): nested too deeply`), named as the img forms.

2. **Clearing part of an image to transparent.** `img.clear()`, `img.clearRect(x, y, w, h)`, `img.clearCircle(x, y, r)`, `img.clearPixel(x, y)` -- `CAIRO_OPERATOR_SOURCE` with a transparent source, for the same reason `festina_clear_canvas` gives (the default OVER operator would paint "nothing" and leave the pixels untouched), so a later draw underneath genuinely shows through. `clear()` ignores the image's transform exactly as `clearCanvas()` ignores the canvas's; the three region forms honour it. `clear()` is the one rename in the whole set: the canvas's `clearCanvas()` has no "canvas" to name once it is a method on an image.

3. **Compositing one image onto another.** `img.drawImage(src, x, y)` and the scaled `img.drawImage(src, x, y, w, h)` -- src onto the receiver in the receiver's own coordinates, through the receiver's transform, honouring `fillAlpha` via `cairo_paint_with_alpha` exactly as the canvas `drawImage` does (claude.md #183). An image drawn onto ITSELF is snapshotted first (Cairo leaves a source pattern reading the surface being painted undefined) -- the friendlier of the two options the issue allowed, so tiling an image with shifted copies of itself just works, and nothing else pays for it: the copy is made only when the two boxes share a surface. An owning source (a `clip()` result passed straight in) is released once painted, the same release an owning receiver gets.

**The issue's "minor, for parity" item** -- `img.drawCircle(x, y, r[, color])` -- was already in as of claude.md #188 (with the fill+border form too); api.md's Images table now says so.

**Semantic and codegen:** one table, `_IMAGE_LAYER_METHODS`, carries the argument shapes -- the SAME ones `_BUILTIN_SIGNATURES`/`_BUILTIN_SIGNATURE_ALTERNATES` give the canvas versions (`translate` takes ints, `rotate`/`scale` floats, `drawImage` 3 or 5 arguments), so `layer.rotate(45)` is rejected the way `rotate(45)` is and there is nothing new to learn. Codegen dispatches by arity through one `_IMAGE_LAYER_OPS` table, each entry the img counterpart of the same-named `_CANVAS_OPS` entry. Threads: every one of these is a Member-callee img method and so is allowed in a thread body for the reason `_THREAD_DISALLOWED_BUILTINS`' own comment gives (each touches only one private surface) -- pinned by a semantic test that uses all of them inside an `on message`. A thread's deep-clone of an img (`festina_image_clone`) carries the current transform across and starts with an empty state stack.

**Verified headlessly, through real pixels** -- every new method needs no display, so `tests/test_codegen.py::TestImageLayerOps` (16 tests) reads results back with `img.getPixelColor` with `DISPLAY` unset: translate moves the drawing; a 10x2 bar rotated 90 degrees about a translated origin lands vertically where it should; scale doubles; save/restore/reset each land the next draw at identity; the image's and the canvas's transforms are independent in both directions; every clear shape erases to `null`, the region clears honour the transform and `clear()` does not, and a cleared hole lets an image drawn underneath show through; `drawImage` plain, scaled, through the transform, honouring `fillAlpha` (a real blend, neither pure colour), onto itself, and from an owning `clip()` temp; a layer inside an `arr[img]` edited in place; both loud failures. `tests/test_graphics.py::TestImageLayerMethods` (+15, parametrized) covers acceptance, the float-argument rule, thread-body use and the bare-name hint. `tests/stress/image_layer_churn.f` (400 iterations of every method, nested saves past the first stack allocation, self-draw, owning clip source, all inside a function so every image is created and released per iteration) added to `scripts/leak_stress.sh`'s set and `tests/test_leak_stress.py`'s guard.

**A pre-existing data race the thread use case exposed, fixed.** The first ThreadSanitizer run of a worker painting its own layer while main painted one of its own -- both through `layer.drawRect(..., color)` -- reported a race at `festina_fill_and_border_with_color`: the per-call colour overrides (claude.md #133/#188, canvas AND img forms alike) saved, overwrote and restored the GLOBAL fill/border state (`g_fill_r/g/b`, `g_fill_none`, `g_fill_gradient`, `g_border_*`, `g_border_set`) around every such draw. Fine on one thread; on two, exactly the "each img method touches only that one private image" claim api.md's isolation section makes was false for the calls a layer-painting worker needs most, and a concurrent override could paint the other thread's colour or clear its gradient. Both functions now go through one `festina_fill_and_border_override` that takes the override colours as arguments and only READS the globals -- the shape `festina_image_draw_pixel_color` always had -- with identical semantics (an explicit fill bypasses an active gradient for that call, a negative colour is `none`, `g_line_width` untouched; every colour/border/gradient pixel test still passes). `tests/stress/thread_image_layer_churn.f` (a worker and main each painting their own layers with every new method plus the colour forms, 600 messages) joins the `thread_*.f` set `scripts/thread_tsan_stress.sh` runs, and is TSan-clean; the remaining read-side sharing (a worker reading `fillAlpha`/`lineWidth`/font while main SETS them) is the documented "style state is global" design, unchanged.

**api.md:** the Images table gained one row per method group (and the `getPixelColor` row it was missing), the "Drawing onto an image" paragraph is followed by a new "An image as a layer" paragraph built from the issue's own four examples (rotated stroke, eraser, tiled background, swayed sprite stamp), the Transforms section says images carry their own, `fillAlpha`'s paragraph names `img.drawImage`, and the thread-isolation list names the new methods. `examples/layers.f`: the HUD layer is now one img wiped with `.clear()` and drawn through its own transform each frame instead of being replaced by a fresh `clip()`, and the trail layer erases a quarter of itself every 40 frames -- both comments that said "an img has no clear" are gone.

**Verified:** full pytest suite 2264 passed, 10 skipped, 0 failed (up from claude.md #233's own 2231/10/0: +16 `TestImageLayerOps`, +15 `TestImageLayerMethods`, +2 stress-guard entries; one earlier run, taken while a ThreadSanitizer job shared the CPU, saw the two `TestFullscreenAndDecorations` window-manager tests and the null-ALSA audio example time out -- all three pass in isolation, the same load-sensitive flakes #230-#232 already documented). `scripts/leak_stress.sh` (28 programs, the two new ones included) and `scripts/thread_tsan_stress.sh` (12, `thread_image_layer_churn.f` included) both run in full and clean -- the TSan sweep is the real check on the colour-override rewrite, since the very first thread-painting probe under TSan is what found the race. The `layers.f` example still passes its own windowed test (`TestExampleGraphicsAndGame`, under Xvfb) with the `.clear()`/transform version of the HUD layer. Version 0.42.

235. THE WINDOWS CI JOB'S OWN FINDINGS: `try`/`catch` REBUILT ON LIBC `setjmp`/`longjmp` (macOS GATE LIFTED), AN EMPTY `WSAPoll`, A NON-ATOMIC APPEND, AND FOUR TESTS THAT ASSUMED POSIX

Requested directly: "the two issues you'd like to add to the list, let's knock those out" -- the first being the Windows CI job, which had never been green (claude.md #233 made the linux and macos jobs honest; windows still failed 7-8 tests on every run). Every failure was read off the real job log, reproduced or reasoned to a root cause, and fixed at the cause rather than skipped:

1. **Three `0xC0000005` crashes after a catch ran** (`test_try_catch.py::test_a_value_escaping_inside_a_catch_body_survives`, `test_json_parse.py`'s duplicate-key and trailing-data tests): the catch body executed, then the next read of any local was garbage (`g.length` printed as `2937617205437776680`). Root cause: the `llvm.eh.sjlj.setjmp`/`longjmp` intrinsics claude.md #157 chose -- for being "portable, fixed-size-buffer, no libc struct layout to know" -- have no working lowering on x86_64 Windows (and none at all on AArch64, which is why macOS had rejected `try` outright since claude.md #170, or on wasm32). **A `try` is now a direct call to libc's own setjmp**, emitted into the try's function exactly as before (the placement argument in `_emit_try`'s docstring is unchanged -- only the callee is), into a 1KB 16-byte-aligned alloca generated code never interprets (`_JMP_BUF_BYTES`: the largest jmp_buf this project meets is glibc aarch64's 312 bytes; Windows x64's needs the alignment for its XMM saves); `festina_throw` is a plain `longjmp(*(jmp_buf *)buf, 1)`; the http async worker's hand-written frame is `_setjmp` on a real `jmp_buf`. The one platform-specific fact is the symbol name (`_setjmp_symbol_for`): every POSIX libc exports `_setjmp` (no signal-mask syscall per try), while Windows' CRTs export no `_setjmp` under UCRT at all (only `__intrinsic_setjmpex`, which MSVCRT in turn lacks -- checked against the real import libraries with `nm`) but both export `setjmp`, whose x64 form reads a second "frame" argument deciding whether `longjmp` performs an SEH unwind. Generated code declares `(ptr, ptr) returns_twice` everywhere and always passes null, so a throw is a plain register restore on every platform (the POSIX entry never reads the extra register). `CodeGen(host_platform=...)` makes the choice unit-testable (`tests/test_platform.py::TestSetjmpSymbol`, 5 tests, replacing `TestDarwinTryGating`). Consequences: `_check_darwin_try_supported` and the `__APPLE__` half of the runtime stub are gone -- **`try`/`catch`/`throw` works on macOS**, run for real on the macos-14 job by `TestOnMacOS::test_try_catch_works` (a caught throw, a local declared before the try surviving it, the program carrying on); the wasm32-wasi stub and gate stay, reworded to the true reason (wasi-libc has no setjmp/longjmp); and **AddressSanitizer can instrument a `try`/`catch` program now** -- `tests/valgrind_stress/json_parse_fail_churn.f` runs clean under `scripts/leak_stress.sh`, where the intrinsics used to die with SIGILL (the whole reason the Valgrind tier exists; it stays as an independent second tool). Every existing try/catch test passes unchanged on Linux with the new mechanism -- the CFG the catch block sees is identical, only the register save/restore underneath changed.

2. **`test_a_thread_serves_real_requests_on_its_own_private_port`: "server process exited early (code 0)".** The program's ONLY listener lives on a `thread`; main has nothing of its own to poll and sits in `festina_run_http_loop` purely to stay alive for that thread -- which it does by polling an EMPTY fd set with a 20ms timeout. POSIX `poll(2)` sleeps out the timeout; `WSAPoll` rejects zero fds outright (`SOCKET_ERROR`/`WSAEINVAL`), the loop's "poll failed and not EINTR" branch returned, main returned, and the process exited 0 before the test's first connect. `festina_poll` on Windows is a small function now: an empty set `Sleep`s out the timeout and reports 0, exactly poll(2)'s contract (a negative timeout sleeps forever, which neither loop ever asks for with nothing to wait on). The same hole would have hit a thread's own `festina_thread_http_service_pass` before its first `openPort()` -- its comment explicitly relies on the empty-poll sleep.

3. **`TestThreadDrain::test_an_out_of_range_pool_drain_is_a_silent_no_op`: `'1' != '2'`, on one run of two.** Two pool threads each `append('x')` to the same file through their own blob; on Windows one byte was lost. UCRT/MSVCRT implement `O_APPEND` as a seek-to-end followed by a separate write, so two concurrent appends can land on one offset -- not an atomic append the way POSIX `O_APPEND` is. `festina_put_file`'s append mode on Windows now opens the file with `FILE_APPEND_DATA` alone (`CreateFileA` + `WriteFile`), which the kernel positions at end-of-file atomically per write. Every `blob.append()` on Windows gets the POSIX guarantee.

4. **Four tests that assumed POSIX**, fixed in the tests: `TestExec`'s two compile-and-run tests spawned `/bin/sh`/`/bin/echo` (`cmd /c` on win32 now, same assertions); `TestDoctorFix::test_declining_the_confirmation_runs_nothing` asserted the literal `apt install -y` (the MSYS2 runner has no `apt` on PATH and the fallback is `apt-get`; the assertion pins what it meant to -- that the command was shown and nothing ran). And one Linux flake seen once on a `workflow_dispatch` run: `test_an_in_flight_connection_still_completes_before_exit` did a single `recv()` and got only the headers -- `festina_http_send` writes headers and body as two `send()` calls (its own comment says so), so the test reads until the body arrives.

The Windows runtime was cross-compiled locally with `x86_64-w64-mingw32-gcc -fsyntax-only` (all three affected translation units, `<windows.h>` now included lean-and-mean in the core unit for `CreateFileA`) before pushing; the CI job is the real verification.

**Docs:** macos.md's "unavailable" section is now "works (since 0.43)"; api.md's `try` Limitations paragraph names wasm32-wasi alone and says what every native target runs on; wasm.md's bullet gives the real reason; the runtime's top-of-group comment tells the whole intrinsics-to-libc story; `tests/test_valgrind_stress.py`'s docstring says why its tier still exists.

**Verified (for #235-#238 together, one commit):** full pytest suite 2283 passed, 11 skipped, 0 failed (up from claude.md #234's 2264/10/0: +5 `TestSetjmpSymbol` replacing 4 darwin-gate tests, +8 `TestThrowUnwindsIntermediateFrames`, +10 `test_wasm_browser.py`, +1 stress-guard entry; the one new skip is `TestOnWindowsWindow`, win32-only. Two runs each saw one load-sensitive flake pass in isolation -- the null-ALSA pooled-channels audio test and an http callback test -- the same class #230-#234 already documented). `scripts/leak_stress.sh` in full (29 programs, `throw_unwind_churn.f` included -- and the try/catch program ASan could never run before), `scripts/thread_tsan_stress.sh` in full (13 programs, clean -- the http worker's catch frame, the shared blob-append path and the per-thread cleanup-stack free are the cross-thread pieces this round touched), `scripts/valgrind_stress.sh` clean. Version 0.43.

236. A `throw` RELEASES EVERY INTERMEDIATE FRAME'S LOCALS: THE CLEANUP STACK CARRIES ORDINARY LOCALS AND CALL-SITE TEMPORARIES

Requested directly: "I don't fully understand the memory model issue, if you can educate me on it and if there is a certain solution, execute it." Of todo.md's three open memory-model items, this was the one with a certain solution -- claude.md #233 had already built the mechanism (the runtime's per-thread cleanup stack, then carrying only the JSON builders' half-built values) and todo.md itself said "the same mechanism could in principle carry an ordinary function's locals too, which is the obvious shape for the general fix". This round is that fix.

**The problem, plainly.** `throw` reaches its `catch` by `longjmp`: the C stack is reset to the catching frame in one jump, and no code in any frame in between runs again -- including the scope-exit release code the compiler emits at the end of every function body. claude.md #157 covered the one frame generated code CAN reach (the function containing the `throw` freed its own locals inline, right before calling `festina_throw`) and documented the rest as the mechanism's one leak: a function that merely calls something which eventually throws never ran its cleanup at all. Error-path-only, bounded per throw, but real, and Valgrind-reproducible with a single intermediate frame.

**The fix.** When the program contains a `try` anywhere (`_contains_try`, a generic walk over every AST node, decided once in `generate()` before anything is emitted -- unlike `uses_try`, which only becomes true as a try is reached, and the first function emitted may well precede it), every binding site registers its local on the cleanup stack the moment the slot holds a value: `_track_local`, now the ONE way an entry enters `_active_free_locals` (the nine former `append` sites -- VarDecls of every kind in `_emit_block`, escaping parameters, the catch variable -- all go through it), pushes `(slot, @__festina_unwind_N)`, where the unwind function is generated per kind by `_unwind_fn_for` with exactly the body `_emit_free_active_locals` would emit inline for that entry (`_emit_release_tracked_entry`, the shared implementation split out of it: a refcounted release through the slot, a stack array/map's data buffer free with element releases, a stack struct's managed fields). Wherever the ordinary scope-exit walk releases entries -- fallthrough, return, break, continue, a try body's normal exit -- it emits one `festina_cleanup_pop_n(count)` for everything it released, so on every non-throwing path push and pop stay balanced and the entries above any try frame are always exactly the locals still live. `festina_throw` was already releasing everything above the catching frame's recorded depth, newest first, before its longjmp; the throw statement no longer frees anything inline (doing both would be the double free claude.md #192 fixed once already). The unwind function reads the slot at throw time, so a reassigned local releases what it holds then, and one nulled by `free` releases nothing.

**What the first ASan run found.** With every frame's locals covered, two leaks of exactly 400 blocks each remained in the stress program: the `[1, 2, 3]` literal passed to a function three frames above the throw, and a template text passed to a function that parses it. Both are call-site temporaries -- a user-function call site owns whatever fresh argument values it built and releases them right after the call returns (the loop claude.md #83/#119/#192 built up); a callee that throws never returns there. `_guard_call_arg_temps` registers those temporaries as plain (value, release) pairs for the duration of the call, on all three user-function call paths (direct, thread-private, and func-typed value), and `_release_call_arg_temps` -- the one shared post-call cleanup those three identical loops became -- pops them first. After that: **0 bytes lost under ASan and Valgrind** (`tests/stress/throw_unwind_churn.f`: a text, a stack arr and map, a heap struct and a stack struct with managed fields, an arr of structs, a blob, a loop-body local, an escaping parameter, a frame whose own catch rethrows, a JSON parse failure two frames down, and 400 non-throwing calls through the same frames to prove the balance -- 1201 throws caught).

**Runtime.** The cleanup stack's size is a function of call depth now, not JSON depth, so it is a malloc'd doubling buffer (64 entries to start) instead of #233's fixed 2048-entry `__thread` array; a worker thread frees its own on the way out (`festina_cleanup_stack_free`, called from `festina_thread_main` beside the sqlite and http teardowns -- a grown buffer left in a dead thread's TLS is exactly what LeakSanitizer would flag in the thread churn programs), main's is reachable until exit. The JSON nesting cap the fixed array used to double as moved to where it belongs: `festina_json_object_start`/`_array_start` count nesting on the cursor -- the same `c->depth` claude.md #192's skip already uses, so a skipped value inside a built one counts once -- and throw past `FESTINA_JSON_MAX_DEPTH` (1000; the test that pinned "more than 1024 levels" now pins 1000).

**Cost, measured.** A program with no `try` is unchanged to the byte (pinned by `test_a_program_without_try_registers_nothing`). One with a `try` pays one runtime call per managed local binding plus one per scope exit: a function that binds a text, two arrays and a struct and does nothing else went from 0.25 s to 0.33 s over 2 million calls -- about 8 ns per binding, a third more on that pathological shape, and lost in the noise for anything that does real work with what it bound. (Batching the pops into one `pop_n` per scope exit was tried and kept, but the push -- a call into the runtime with a capacity check and a TLS access -- is where the time goes; inlining it in IR would need the stack's TLS variables visible from generated code on every target, and was judged not worth it for a per-binding cost this small.)

**What remains, honestly.** A throw out of a callback the RUNTIME invokes -- a `.forEach(fn)` body, a `.sort(cmp)` comparator, a timer -- crosses a runtime C frame on its way to the try; the Festina-side locals are released, but whatever that C frame held for itself (qsort's scratch) is not. todo.md lists that in place of the closed item. The other two items stay open with their reasoning intact: cycle trials are an optimization with no need driving it, and the `rows()[0]` leak needs the `TableType` ownership tracking claude.md #224 scoped.

**Tests:** `tests/test_try_catch.py::TestThrowUnwindsIntermediateFrames` (8 tests: the two IR-shape pins, the survivors around a throw through three frames with a loop-body local and an escaping parameter, a rethrow crossing both frames, a JSON failure two frames down caught then uncaught, 20000 balanced calls before a caught throw, and a worker thread unwinding on its own stack while main holds its own locals); the stress program in `scripts/leak_stress.sh`'s set and `tests/test_leak_stress.py`'s guard; `tests/valgrind_stress/json_parse_fail_churn.f` still clean with the cap moved. api.md's `try` section replaces its "one real, honest limitation" paragraph with what a throw releases and what it costs; the runtime's top-of-group comment tells the same story; todo.md's memory-model list is updated.

237. A COMPILED `.wasm` RUNS IN A BROWSER TAB: A WASI PREVIEW 1 HOST OF THIS PROJECT'S OWN, TESTED UNDER NODE AND IN HEADLESS CHROMIUM

Requested directly: "Add browser wasm support." wasm.md's own Limitations list had said "No browser support claimed ... a browser has no built-in WASI host -- running one there needs a JS-side WASI polyfill (e.g. `@wasmer/wasi`) that this project has neither vendored nor tested against." Rather than vendor a third-party polyfill (a dependency to track, most of whose surface no Festina program touches), `runtime/wasm/festina_wasi_browser.js` is a WASI Preview 1 host written for exactly the imports a compiled Festina binary names -- 25 functions, read off a real `.wasm`'s import section: args/environ, `clock_time_get`, the `fd_*` family (`close`/`fdstat_get`/`fdstat_set_flags`/`filestat_get`/`filestat_set_size`/`prestat_get`/`prestat_dir_name`/`read`/`seek`/`sync`/`write`), `path_open`/`create_directory`/`filestat_get`/`filestat_set_times`/`readlink`/`remove_directory`/`unlink_file`, `poll_oneoff`, `proc_exit` -- plus the few more wasi-libc reaches for on other paths (`fd_readdir`, `random_get`, `fd_tell`, `fd_pread`/`pwrite`, `path_rename`, `sched_yield`) and a Proxy that answers `ENOSYS` for anything else rather than failing to link. Dependency-free ES module: `WebAssembly`, `TextEncoder`/`TextDecoder`, `DataView` and nothing else, so it runs in any browser and under Node unchanged.

**The filesystem is in memory:** a Map from absolute path to a file (a growable byte buffer plus length) or a directory, `/` preopened as fd 3 -- the identical single-preopen sandbox `run_wasi.mjs` grants a program under Node -- so `blob` write/append/read, `mkdir`, `ls`, `exists`/`delete` and SQLite's own database file (the most demanding client: open, seek, pread/pwrite, truncate, fdstat, readdir) all work, and whatever the program wrote is readable afterwards (`host.files()`). i64 parameters arrive as BigInt and are handled as such throughout (`clock_time_get`'s precision, `fd_seek`'s offset, `path_open`'s rights, `fd_filestat_set_size`, `fd_readdir`'s cookie); every memory access takes a fresh `DataView`, since the module's memory can grow. stdout/stderr are delivered line by line to callbacks and kept whole; `proc_exit` throws a sentinel `run()` turns into the exit code, exactly as `node:wasi`'s `start()` returns one. A `poll_oneoff` clock subscription (a Festina timer waiting its interval out -- the only subscription kind a Festina program ever makes) sleeps with `Atomics.wait` where the environment allows it (a Worker on a cross-origin-isolated page, or Node) and otherwise spins.

**Three ways in.** `browser.html?wasm=program.wasm` -- the smallest page: fetches the module, runs it in a module Web Worker (`festina_wasi_worker.js`, so a Festina program's synchronous `main()` and its timer loop never block the page), streams stdout/stderr into a `<pre>`, and sets `window.festinaResult = {code, stdout, stderr, files}` on exit; `window.festinaRun(url, {files})` runs another on demand with a seeded filesystem. And `run_wasi_js.mjs`: the same host under Node, the real directory loaded into the in-memory filesystem first and written back afterwards -- the browser host's own runner, mirroring `run_wasi.mjs`'s contract exactly, which is what proves the JavaScript independently of any browser (`package.json` `{"type": "module"}` in that directory is what lets Node import the `.js` host as an ES module; `run_wasi.mjs` is untouched).

**Verified end to end, twice.** `tests/test_wasm_browser.py` (10 tests): through the host under Node -- hello world, `fail()`'s exit code and stderr, `close(7)`, files/directories/`ls`/`exists`/`delete` with the sandbox round-tripping to the real directory (a seeded file read, a written tree found on disk afterwards, a deleted file gone), two rows through SQLite and back, timers through `poll_oneoff`, `argv` -- and through the page itself in headless Chromium via Playwright: hello world (and the page rendered it), files + timers + `close(3)` with the written file coming back to the page as bytes, an uncaught `fail()` reporting exit 1 and its stderr. The first run of the smoke program under Node produced output identical to `node:wasi`'s for the same `.wasm` (files, directories, `argv`, three timer ticks, exit code 7) with no host fix needed; the only difference is `ls` order (the host sorts). The linux CI job installs Playwright and its Chromium (`--with-deps`) so this tier is never skipped there (FESTINA_STRICT_DEPS); `FESTINA_CHROMIUM` names a different Chromium binary to drive on a machine whose Playwright browser cache is from another version (this container's was), and the tests skip cleanly where none is available.

**Docs:** wasm.md gained an "In a browser" section (what the host is, how to use the page, the worker, the Node runner, what it deliberately isn't -- a general WASI polyfill), its intro no longer lists "a browser tab" as out of scope, and the Limitations bullet that claimed no browser support now describes the two hosts and the in-memory filesystem's one consequence (nothing a tab writes reaches the disk unless the page saves it). todo.md's platforms section drops the item.

238. THE WINDOWS CI JOB DRIVES A REAL WIN32 WINDOW: MOUSE, KEYBOARD, RESIZE AND CLOSE ASSERTED ON `windows-latest`

Requested directly: "Add windows to the GitHub's Windows Runner" -- the other of the two items claude.md #234's follow-up named. windows.md had already recorded that GitHub's Windows runners have a live desktop session, that windowed graphics is therefore not gated on Windows, and that what remained open was narrower: no Windows equivalent of the Xvfb-backed `x_display`/`xdotool` fixtures existed, so nothing ever confirmed the windowed-input handlers against the pinned event vocabulary there. `tests/test_platform.py::TestOnWindowsWindow` (win32-only, like `TestOnWindows`) is that equivalent, with nothing but `ctypes`: it compiles a program declaring every input handler (`mouseDown`/`mouseUp` logging coordinates and button, `keyDown`/`keyUp` logging the key name, `resize` logging `clientWidth`/`clientHeight`, `close`) that sets a 320x200 client size and calls `render()`, runs it in the background, finds its window by class name (`FindWindowW("FestinaWindowClass")`, polled), and posts the same Win32 messages a mouse, a keyboard and the window manager would: `WM_LBUTTONDOWN`/`WM_LBUTTONUP` with client (40, 30) packed into lParam, `WM_KEYDOWN`/`WM_KEYUP` for `VK_A` with the scancode the backend's own `ToUnicode` translation reads from bits 16-23 of lParam, a `MoveWindow` growing the outer window by exactly 80x60 (so the expected client size is the measured one plus 80x60, whatever the chrome measures on that runner -- the resize handler's own `WM_SIZE` reports the client area), and `WM_CLOSE`. The program's stdout is then asserted line by line: `down 40 30 1`, `up 40 30 1`, `keydown a`, `keyup a`, `resize W H`, and `close` as the last line with exit code 0 -- `on close` running and the window closing being what ends the event loop.

Written against the backend's own wndproc (`festina_runtime_window_win32.c`: every message case above, and `festina_win32_key_name`'s ToUnicode path) rather than guessed; it cannot run here (no Windows), so the windows CI job is its first execution -- the same honest position every blind-written Windows piece of this project has started from, with the difference that this one is a TEST, so a mismatch shows up as a red job with the actual output in the assertion message rather than as silently unverified code. windows.md's "what remains open" paragraph now describes this test; todo.md's platforms list narrows to audio on both platforms and windowing on a real Mac.

**First CI run of #235-#238 (workflow_dispatch on the branch; the previous PR had already been merged, so no `pull_request` run fired):** linux green in full -- the browser tier included, under FESTINA_STRICT_DEPS, so Playwright's Chromium really ran `browser.html`. macos: 2042 passed, one failure in `examples/timers.f`'s test, unrelated to this round -- the 100ms interval reschedules from *now*, so on a loaded runner five ticks drifted past the 1000ms one-shot and "one second has passed" printed before "tick 5"; the assertion now pins the ticks' order and the stop after the fifth, not where the one-shot lands (it is a scheduler-timing question, not what the example promises). windows: the job hit its 30-minute `timeout-minutes` at 57% of the suite -- every 3% segment took ~1.4x what the same segment took on the run two hours earlier, uniformly from the first (parser-only) tests on, which is runner speed, not any one test: the previous windows run already took 25.5 minutes of a 30-minute budget. The windows job's timeout is 45 minutes now; the second dispatch is what verifies #235's fixes and #238's window test on real Windows.

**Second CI run (workflow_dispatch, commit 9d2e8af): green on all three platforms.** linux 9m51s, macos 7m55s, windows 30m04s (inside the new 45-minute budget; the previous cancelled run had already taken 28 minutes to reach 57%). That windows run is the first real execution of everything this round wrote blind: libc `setjmp`/`longjmp` try/catch on x86_64 Windows (the three 0xC0000005 tests), the empty-`WSAPoll` sleep (the thread-only listener test), the `FILE_APPEND_DATA` append (the pool drain test), and `TestOnWindowsWindow` -- a real Win32 window driven through `ctypes`, with every posted mouse, key, resize and close message reaching its handler with the asserted values. macOS's `test_try_catch_works` passed too: try/catch on Apple Silicon for the first time since claude.md #157.
